cards.t: Venous valves, reflux and venous hypertension
q: what is venous hypertension
how do vein valves work
how are venous disorders related to each other
cards.x:
Chronic venous disease is the umbrella term for problems caused by too much pressure inside the leg veins. It runs from telangiectasias (tiny dilated veins in the skin) through varicose veins to the severe end, chronic venous insufficiency. That high pressure is called venous hypertension. It comes from four things: a weak calf muscle pump, leaky valves (which let blood flow backward, called reflux), a clot in a vein, or some other blockage of the veins that is not a clot.

Veins have one-way valves. A healthy valve keeps blood moving one way, toward the heart. A diseased valve lets blood move both ways, so pressure climbs. That pressure first stretches the veins (venous dilation). Then it changes the skin or breaks it down into an ulcer.

The conditions are linked. A deep vein clot can scar the valves and become chronic venous insufficiency (post-thrombotic syndrome) 6 to 24 months later. Long-standing varicose veins can progress to it too.

cards.t: Deep vein thrombosis: what it is and where it happens
q: what is a deep vein thrombosis
where do DVTs form
why is a DVT dangerous
cards.x:
Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is a blood clot in the deep veins, usually in the legs. Deep vein thrombosis plus pulmonary embolism (a clot that has traveled to the lungs) together are called venous thromboembolism.

A leg clot is about 10 times more common than an arm clot. It usually starts in the calf and then grows upstream to the popliteal, femoral and iliac veins. The most common proximal (upper) sites are the femoral and popliteal veins in the thigh. The most common distal (lower) sites are the peroneal veins in the calf. In pregnancy the pelvic veins are the usual site.

Arm clots make up only 5 to 10% of all deep vein clots, though they are rising every year. They most often follow a pacemaker, an implantable cardiac defibrillator or a central venous catheter left in the vein.

The danger is that part of the clot can break off and travel to the lungs. A pulmonary embolism complicates up to 6% of arm clots but 15 to 30% of leg clots.

cards.t: Virchow triad: why clots form in veins
q: what is the Virchow triad
what are the three causes of a venous clot
what is the most common inherited hypercoagulable state
cards.x:
Virchow triad is a three-category way to think about why a clot forms in a vein: slow blood flow, blood that clots too easily, and injury to the vessel lining. Learn the three arms, then the examples under each.

- Venous stasis (slow or altered blood flow): immobilization such as long flights, prolonged sitting or inactivity after surgery (about a 20-fold higher risk), venous insufficiency, heart failure.
- Hypercoagulable state (blood that clots too easily): inherited, such as factor V Leiden (the most common inherited cause), prothrombin gene mutation, protein C or S deficiency, antithrombin deficiency; or acquired, such as cancer, oral contraceptive pills (more so with smoking or obesity), postmenopausal estrogen, pregnancy.
- Endothelial trauma (injury to the vessel lining): surgery, especially knee or hip replacement or hip fracture repair, trauma, burns, injection drug use in the leg. Smoking and hypertension are also filed here.

Arms often act together: a hip fracture injures the vessel and then keeps the patient immobile.

cards.t: Other risk factors for deep vein thrombosis
q: what else raises the risk of DVT
how much does a prior clot raise risk
does air travel cause DVT
cards.x:
Besides the Virchow triad, a list of other things raises the odds of a deep vein clot, and it is worth asking about every one of them, especially personal and family history.

A personal or family history of a deep vein clot or pulmonary embolism matters: a previous episode markedly raises the risk of another. Ask how many clots, how long ago, and who in the family had one and at what age.

The rest of the list:
- Age older than 60, overweight or obesity, and slightly higher risk in males.
- Smoking, heart failure, high blood pressure, chronic kidney disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis).
- Cancer and chemotherapy.
- Air travel and a sedentary lifestyle.
- Hormones: estrogen-containing contraceptives, postmenopausal hormone replacement, and the first 6 to 12 weeks after delivery.

cards.t: How a deep vein thrombosis presents
k: calf cramp that won't go away
q: what are the signs of a DVT
is the Homan sign useful
how does an arm DVT present
cards.x:
In the leg, suspect a deep vein clot when there is swelling, pain and warmth, with or without redness. Swelling is the most common finding: it is present in 97% of patients with a clot (97% sensitive), pain in 86% and warmth in 72%. A calf cramp or "charley horse" that does not settle and worsens over the next few days should keep you asking questions.

Where the symptoms sit depends on where the clot is. An isolated clot in the lower (distal) veins keeps symptoms in the calf. A clot in the upper (proximal) veins may involve just the calf or the whole leg.

The Homan sign (calf pain when the foot is pulled upward) may be present, but it is neither sensitive nor specific, so a positive or negative sign settles nothing.

An arm clot often shows up as nothing more than arm swelling and discomfort.

cards.t: What else looks like a deep vein thrombosis
q: what can mimic a DVT
how do you tell a Baker cyst from a DVT
which drugs cause leg swelling
cards.x:
Several problems give a swollen, painful leg, so the history and exam decide which to chase.

- Ruptured popliteal (Baker) cyst: severe, sudden calf discomfort.
- Cellulitis: leg pain with redness, possibly with fever and chills.
- Post-thrombotic (postphlebitic) syndrome: symptomatic chronic venous insufficiency that follows a clot, from 6 to 24 months later.
- Superficial thrombophlebitis: a tender cord along a vein just under the skin.
- Lymphedema: chronic swelling of the limb, usually with a history of pelvic surgery, cancer or radiation.
- Calf muscle pull or tear: there is usually an injury in the history, and there may be bruising at the ankle.
- Drug-induced edema: a common side effect of some drugs, including dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine. The swelling is often in both legs with no signs of inflammation.

Each has its own clue: an injury in the history for a muscle tear, usually a history of pelvic surgery, cancer or radiation for lymphedema, possible fever and chills for cellulitis, and swelling that is often in both legs, with no signs of inflammation, for drug-induced edema.

cards.t: Wells criteria for deep vein thrombosis (the points)
q: how do you calculate the Wells score for DVT
what are the items in the Wells criteria
does a long flight count in the Wells score
cards.x:
The Wells criteria estimate how likely it is that a swollen leg is a deep vein clot, before any test. They are used only in the outpatient and emergency department setting, not for hospitalized patients.

Add 1 point for each of these:
- active cancer (treatment or palliation within 6 months)
- bedridden recently for more than 3 days, or major surgery within 12 weeks
- calf swelling more than 3 cm larger than the other leg (measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity)
- collateral (nonvaricose) superficial veins
- the entire leg swollen
- tenderness along the deep veins
- pitting edema only in the symptomatic leg
- paralysis, weakness or a recent cast (plaster) on the leg
- a previously documented deep vein clot

Subtract 2 if another diagnosis is at least as likely as a clot.

A common trap: long travel is a risk factor but it is not a Wells item. The bedridden item means bedridden after surgery or immobilized in a cast, so a long flight scores nothing.

cards.t: Reading the Wells score: what to order next
q: what do I order for a low Wells score
when do you skip the D-dimer
what if the ultrasound is negative in a high-risk patient
cards.x:
The Wells total sorts the patient into likelihood groups: zero or less is low, 1 to 2 is moderate, and 3 or more is high. The work-up pathway shows what to order for the low and high groups.

- Low likelihood: D-dimer first. If it is negative, stop; the clot is ruled out. If it is positive, order an ultrasound of the thigh, and if that is negative, stop.
- High likelihood: skip the D-dimer and order the ultrasound of the thigh. A D-dimer is optional here, and even a negative one would still lead to the ultrasound.

If the ultrasound is positive, the diagnosis is made and treatment starts. If it is negative in a high-likelihood patient, there are three options: an ultrasound of the lower leg, phlebography (venography), or a repeat thigh ultrasound in 1 week.

cards.t: D-dimer: sensitive but not specific
q: what does a positive D-dimer mean
why is D-dimer a rule-out test
when should you order a D-dimer
cards.x:
D-dimer is a blood test that goes up when the body is breaking down clots (increased fibrinolysis). It is sensitive but not specific. Sensitive means a clot almost always raises it, so a negative result is reassuring. Not specific means many other things raise it too. So a positive result only implies increased clot breakdown somewhere in the body, not necessarily a clot in the leg.

That is why D-dimer is useful as a rule-out test for deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. In the Wells pathway it is the first test for a low score. A negative one helps close the case. A positive one is just a reason to get an ultrasound.

Do not order it reflexively. Know what you will do next with either answer. With a high Wells score you skip it and go to ultrasound, and even a negative D-dimer would not end the evaluation.

cards.t: Imaging for deep vein thrombosis: ultrasound vs venography
q: what is the best imaging for DVT
why did ultrasound replace venography
what if the ultrasound is nondiagnostic
cards.x:
Venous duplex ultrasound of the affected limb is the imaging test used to diagnose a deep vein clot. It is noninvasive and has replaced the older test.

That older test, contrast ascending venography, is still called the "gold standard" because it is definitive. It uses contrast dye to show the veins. But it is invasive, so it has been replaced by venous duplex ultrasound.

A positive ultrasound ends the work-up and treatment begins. If the ultrasound is negative in a patient whose Wells score was high, there are three options: an ultrasound of the lower leg, phlebography (another name for venography), or a repeat thigh ultrasound in 1 week.

When you order the ultrasound, say on the request why you are ordering it.

cards.t: Anticoagulation: the mainstay of deep vein thrombosis treatment
q: how do you treat a DVT
what are the strategies for anticoagulation
when should you not anticoagulate
cards.x:
Anticoagulation (blood thinning) is the mainstay of deep vein clot treatment. Depending on the situation, a patient may also need thrombolysis (a procedure that breaks down the clot) and/or lifelong anticoagulation.

There are three main strategies:
- The classic one, which is waning in use: start heparin, then bridge to warfarin.
- Parenteral (injected or intravenous) therapy, switched after 5 days to dabigatran (a direct thrombin inhibitor) or edoxaban (an anti-factor Xa drug).
- Oral monotherapy with a loading dose, then a maintenance dose: rivaroxaban or apixaban, both anti-factor Xa drugs.

The drug groups to place: low molecular weight heparin (enoxaparin); unfractionated heparin, given by intravenous bolus then infusion and adjusted by the activated partial thromboplastin time; fondaparinux (an indirect factor Xa inhibitor); warfarin (a vitamin K antagonist, monitored with the international normalized ratio).

Do not give them with active bleeding, acute intracranial hemorrhage, major trauma or severe bleeding disorders: a blood thinner would make a bleeding patient bleed more.

cards.t: How long to treat a deep vein thrombosis
q: how long do you anticoagulate for a DVT
what is an unprovoked DVT
what counts as a major transient risk factor
cards.x:
The first episode of a deep vein clot or pulmonary embolism gets at least 3 months of treatment for every patient. After that, the length depends on whether something obvious triggered the clot.

- Provoked by a major transient (reversible) risk factor: 3 months. Examples are surgery under general anesthesia for more than 30 minutes, hospitalization or bed rest for 3 days or more, and major trauma or fracture.
- Provoked by a minor transient risk factor: 3 to 6 months. Examples are estrogen therapy, pregnancy, minor surgery, prolonged travel and a minor leg injury.
- Unprovoked first clot (no risk factor found): indefinite treatment.

The logic is about what you know. With a major reversible cause, you know why it happened and it is over. With an unprovoked clot, no source was found, so an undiscovered clotting condition cannot be excluded.

cards.t: Outpatient vs inpatient treatment of a deep vein thrombosis
q: who can be treated for DVT at home
when should a DVT patient be hospitalized
what do you do for DVT with kidney disease
cards.x:
Many patients with a deep vein clot can be treated at home, but only if they are safe to be there. Outpatient treatment fits patients who are hemodynamically stable (steady blood pressure and heart rate). They also need a low bleeding risk, no renal insufficiency, good support and reliable follow-up.

It is not appropriate with an iliofemoral (proximal) clot, a concurrent symptomatic pulmonary embolism, a high bleeding risk, or other conditions that call for inpatient care.

Outpatient options are:
- Rivaroxaban.
- Apixaban.
- Low molecular weight heparin (enoxaparin) or fondaparinux for 5 days, then dabigatran or edoxaban.
- Low molecular weight heparin or fondaparinux for 5 days overlapping with warfarin until the international normalized ratio is above 2.

The choice rests on clinician experience, bleeding risk, other conditions, preference, cost and convenience.

With chronic renal disease and a creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min, the patient is hospitalized to start. Unfractionated heparin is given together with warfarin. The overlap lasts at least 5 days and until the international normalized ratio is above 2 for at least 24 hours.

cards.t: Bleeding on anticoagulants and the reversal agents
q: how do you reverse heparin
what reverses dabigatran
what is the antidote for warfarin
cards.x:
Bleeding is the most serious side effect of treating a clot. So each blood thinner has its own antidote for life-threatening or intracranial (inside the skull) bleeding. Match the drug to the antidote:

- Unfractionated heparin or low molecular weight heparin: protamine sulfate.
- Dabigatran: idarucizumab.
- Apixaban and rivaroxaban: andexanet alfa (also used off-label for edoxaban).
- Warfarin: four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate, fresh frozen plasma or intravenous vitamin K. Oral vitamin K is the usual outpatient choice.

A way to keep them straight: protamine goes with the heparins, idarucizumab with dabigatran, andexanet alfa with apixaban and rivaroxaban. Warfarin is the odd one out, reversed with vitamin K, plasma or prothrombin complex concentrate.

cards.t: Inferior vena cava filters and thrombolysis
q: when do you place an IVC filter
when is thrombolysis used for DVT
is a filter routine for DVT
cards.x:
Blood thinners are the treatment for a deep vein clot. Two other tools are reserved for special situations.

An inferior vena cava filter is a device placed in the big vein that returns blood from the legs to the heart. It keeps a clot from traveling to the lungs. It is used for an acute proximal deep vein clot in the leg when the patient cannot take anticoagulation (for example active bleeding). In other words, the filter is for patients who cannot take blood thinners, not an add-on for everyone.

Thrombolysis (using tissue plasminogen activator to dissolve the clot) and thrombectomy (removing the clot) are reserved for selected large clots, such as a large proximal clot. Neither is routine treatment. Anticoagulation remains the mainstay.

cards.t: Intermittent pneumatic compression to prevent clots
q: how do sequential compression devices prevent DVT
when is DVT prevention needed
which arm of the Virchow triad do they treat
cards.x:
Intermittent pneumatic compression (sequential compression devices) are inflatable sleeves that squeeze the legs in cycles, first one section, then the next, up the leg. They are used especially when a patient must stay immobilized after surgery or through a long hospital stay.

The idea ties straight to the Virchow triad. When you lie still, the calf muscles are not squeezing the veins, so blood slows down and pools. That is venous stasis, one of the three causes of clots. The device does the calf muscles' job, pushing blood along so it does not stagnate. It is prevention aimed at the stasis arm.

cards.t: Complications of a deep vein thrombosis
q: what are the complications of DVT
why is pulmonary embolism the biggest risk
can DVT cause chronic venous insufficiency
cards.x:
The biggest complication is pulmonary embolism: part of the clot breaks off and travels to the lungs. Every patient with a deep vein clot should be asked about breathing difficulty right away, rather than waiting to see if shortness of breath appears.

Without adequate treatment, the risk of a fatal pulmonary embolism rises with the size of the embolism. It is lowest, under 1%, in patients with a symptomatic leg clot and no pulmonary embolism, and higher with a non-massive and then a massive pulmonary embolism.

Other complications:
- Post-thrombotic syndrome, which is symptomatic chronic venous insufficiency 6 to 24 months after the clot.
- Recurrence: a prior deep vein clot or pulmonary embolism markedly raises the risk of another.
- Bleeding from the treatment itself.

cards.t: Superficial phlebitis vs thrombophlebitis
q: what is the difference between phlebitis and thrombophlebitis
what causes superficial thrombophlebitis
how is thrombophlebitis diagnosed
cards.x:
Superficial phlebitis is inflammation of the wall of a vein just under the skin, with no clot. Superficial thrombophlebitis is the same inflammation with a clot inside. The two are told apart because the treatment differs.

Common causes and risk factors:
- Varicose veins, the most common cause in the leg.
- A recent intravenous catheter, the most common cause in the arm. The most common type is a peripherally inserted central catheter, a long line threaded into a vein from the arm.
- Inactivity, local trauma or a procedure on the veins, pregnancy or estrogen, cancer or a hypercoagulable state (blood that clots too easily).

What you find is a tender, red, hard (indurated) cord along the vein, warm to the touch, which you can trace by hand.

History and exam make the diagnosis. Venous duplex ultrasound confirms it: the vein will not compress. Wall thickening alone is phlebitis. Wall thickening with a clot inside is thrombophlebitis.

cards.t: Treating superficial thrombophlebitis
q: do you give heparin for superficial thrombophlebitis
what is the treatment for thrombophlebitis
when should you recheck a thrombophlebitis
cards.x:
Superficial thrombophlebitis rarely causes serious complications, so treatment starts simple. Use warm compresses, compression, elevating the limb, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs, for example ibuprofen or diclofenac) for pain and inflammation.

Anticoagulation (unfractionated heparin, enoxaparin or fondaparinux) is added only when the clot burden is extensive or the risk of thrombosis is intermediate or higher. That means when there is a really big concern. So in a case like a red, painful, swollen arm with varicose veins and no extensive clot, the answer is an anti-inflammatory drug, not heparin.

Examine again within 7 to 10 days to see whether it is resolving or progressing. If signs persist or worsen, repeat the duplex ultrasound.

The outlook is good: it rarely embolizes (sends a clot to the lungs). Many patients worry they have a dangerous clot, so counseling matters.

cards.t: Septic (suppurative) thrombophlebitis
q: what is septic thrombophlebitis
how do you recognize an infected vein
what history should you ask about
cards.x:
Septic (suppurative) thrombophlebitis is thrombophlebitis in which the vein itself has become infected. It is uncommon without a history of venous cannulation (a venipuncture or a catheter), so always ask about a recent intravenous line.

Suspect it when you see high fever, fluctuance (a soft, fluid-filled feel under the skin) or purulent (pus) drainage. Also suspect it when the redness extends significantly beyond the margin of the vein, not just along it.

The key skill is recognizing these infection signs, because a missed infection can leave the patient septic.

cards.t: Arteriovenous fistula made for hemodialysis
q: what is an arteriovenous fistula
how do you examine a dialysis fistula
what should you do if a dialysis fistula has no bruit
cards.x:
An arteriovenous fistula is an abnormal connection between an artery and a vein that bypasses the capillary bed, so blood flows directly from artery to vein. Some are made on purpose: surgeons create one for long-term hemodialysis access. The upper extremity is most common (the upper arm or forearm), and it is preferred over the leg.

A healthy dialysis fistula is not silent. You can feel a diffuse thrill (a buzzing vibration) and hear a soft bruit (a whooshing sound) with the stethoscope, both with systolic and diastolic components. It also collapses completely when the arm is raised.

If you cannot hear a bruit, refer the patient.

cards.t: Acquired (iatrogenic) arteriovenous fistula
q: how do acquired fistulas form
why are lower extremity fistulas usually iatrogenic
how do you treat an acquired AV fistula
cards.x:
An acquired arteriovenous fistula is an unwanted artery-to-vein connection that arises from trauma or from a medical procedure (iatrogenic means caused by medical care). The classic one is in the leg. The groin, with the femoral vessels, is a common site of access for arterial and venous procedures such as cardiac catheterization. That is why lower extremity fistulas are most commonly iatrogenic and affect the femoral vessels.

After the procedure, examine the puncture site with a complete lower extremity vascular exam. Compare the pulses with those before the procedure to be sure nothing changed. Duplex ultrasound confirms a suspected iatrogenic fistula. Computed tomography angiography or angiography gives its location and size.

Treatment of an acquired fistula is surgical: remove the fistula or decrease its size. A congenital fistula is different. It is hard to treat because the connections can be numerous. It is managed with elastic support hose, and sometimes embolization removes it.

cards.t: Nicoladoni-Branham sign and fistula complications
q: what is the Nicoladoni-Branham sign
what are the complications of an AV fistula
why can a fistula cause heart failure
cards.x:
The Nicoladoni-Branham sign is a reflex: if you compress a large arteriovenous fistula, the heart rate slows. Do not hold the fistula closed to demonstrate it on a patient.

Watch for trouble over time: chronic venous insufficiency, heart failure and ischemia (poor blood supply). Also watch for infection. A fistula is one of the less common causes of chronic venous insufficiency.

In primary care the job is to keep the fistula free of infection, decide whether it is congenital or acquired, find out how it was acquired, and refer appropriately.

cards.t: Chronic venous insufficiency: what it is and what causes it
q: what is chronic venous insufficiency
what is the most common cause of CVI
what is the difference between primary and secondary CVI
cards.x:
Chronic venous insufficiency is the severe, advanced end of venous disease. It is long-lasting high pressure in the leg veins (venous hypertension) that shows up as edema, skin changes and venous ulcers. When it follows a deep vein clot it is called post-thrombotic syndrome, but not all chronic venous insufficiency comes from a clot.

It is classified by where the problem starts:
- Primary: the vein wall or valves are abnormal on their own, causing valve reflux (backward flow).
- Secondary: an outside cause, such as obstruction or valve damage from a prior deep vein clot.

A prior deep vein thrombosis is one of the most common causes. About 25% of these patients have no known clot history, and there may instead be leg trauma or surgery. So ask "have you had a clot before?" and about leg surgery.

Another common cause is progressive superficial venous reflux. Other causes are congenital or tumor-related blockage of the pelvic veins and an arteriovenous fistula (congenital or acquired).

cards.t: Why chronic venous insufficiency causes leg swelling
q: how do the valves fail in CVI
why does CVI cause edema
what happens to superficial and deep veins
cards.x:
The valves fail for two reasons. Either their leaflets are thickened and scarred (as after a clot, post-thrombotic syndrome), or they sit in a dilated vein where they cannot close properly. Chronic clot or scarring higher up can add a blockage on top.

Either way, the valves cannot stop blood from flowing back toward the foot. Blood pools, and pressure in the veins of the lower leg climbs (venous hypertension). That pressure bears on the veins and tissues of the lower leg. The result is edema.

The problem also spreads. The superficial veins expand and their valves stop closing. The deep system becomes incompetent because of the expanded superficial veins. And the superficial veins cannot empty into the deep system during walking.

cards.t: Symptoms of chronic venous insufficiency
q: what is the main symptom of CVI
what makes venous leg symptoms better or worse
how does early CVI present
cards.x:
Early chronic venous disease is often asymptomatic. The primary presenting symptom is progressive pitting edema of the leg, usually the lower leg, with dull discomfort that gets worse with standing. Document and grade the pitting so you can follow it over time.

Other symptoms are itching of the lower-leg skin, often starting around the medial malleolus (the bony bump on the inner ankle). Others are leg heaviness, aching, pain, throbbing, hyperesthesia (heightened skin sensitivity) or burning.

The pattern gives it away. Symptoms get worse with standing or with sitting for a long time with the feet down. They get better with elevating the leg and with walking.

cards.t: Venous skin changes: stasis dermatitis, hemosiderin, lipodermatosclerosis
q: what is stasis dermatitis
why is venous skin brown
what is lipodermatosclerosis
cards.x:
Long-standing venous hypertension changes the skin in a recognizable way.

- Stasis dermatitis: inflamed skin. The earliest sign is redness, scaling and slight darkening just above the inner ankle.
- Hemosiderin staining: brown or blue-gray discoloration from hemosiderin deposits. It helps separate a venous cause from an arterial one. The ankle skin is also shiny and taut from swelling.
- Lipodermatosclerosis: scarring of the skin and fat of the lower leg in long-term disease. The area is firm and indurated, with the skin tacked down to the tissue underneath. It is commonly at the inner ankle and can form a constricting band around the leg.

Cellulitis on top of venous insufficiency causes blanching redness, with or without pain. It is hard to diagnose. Drawing around the edge with a marker and dating it lets you follow progression.

cards.t: Venous ulcer: how it looks and why it fails to heal
q: what does a venous ulcer look like
where do venous ulcers occur
how long do venous ulcers take to heal
cards.x:
A venous ulcer is the open sore at the end of the chain of venous hypertension. It sits usually above the ankle on the medial (inner) or anterior (front) side. It is painful, with a clean base covered in fibrinous exudate (a fibrin-rich coating) and possibly serous drainage (clear or light yellow, see-through fluid).

It heals with a thin scar that breaks down easily with minor trauma or increased leg swelling.

Ulcers will not heal unless edema is controlled and compression is applied. Refer to wound care; complete healing can take 4 to 6 months, and an ulcer that has not fully healed needs more work-up for infection or other causes.

cards.t: Other causes of leg swelling and leg ulcers to tell from venous disease
q: what else causes bilateral leg swelling
how do you tell lymphedema from venous insufficiency
how is an arterial ulcer different
cards.x:
History and exam often point to venous insufficiency. But they are not enough on their own to prove a venous cause or rule out other causes. So know the look-alikes.

Leg swelling:
- Heart failure, chronic kidney disease or decompensated liver disease: bilateral edema of the lower legs.
- Medications: calcium channel blockers, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, thiazolidinediones.
- Lymphedema: swelling on one side, no varicose veins, pitting present, and brawny (hemosiderin) discoloration is rare.
- Lipedema: bilateral, symmetric swelling just above the ankles, in women.

Leg ulcers: diabetic neuropathic ulcers, autoimmune disease, sickle cell anemia, erythema induratum (both legs, back of the lower leg), and arterial insufficiency.

The key contrast: venous ulcers are on the inner ankle, shallow and clean. Arterial ulcers are dry, punched out and painful, at the toes and usually (but not always) the lateral (outer) ankle, with weak pulses. A punch biopsy can help rule out other causes when unsure.

cards.t: Testing in chronic venous insufficiency: duplex and ankle-brachial index
q: what is the first test for CVI
why do you order an ABI in venous disease
when is venography needed
cards.x:
Venous duplex ultrasound is the first test. It checks venous patency (is there a deep vein clot?) and valve competence (is there reflux?). It confirms the diagnosis, finds the cause, rules out a clot, and maps the level and anatomy of the disease. In chronic venous insufficiency it shows incompetent valves with backward flow.

Cross-sectional venography (computed tomography or magnetic resonance) looks at deep veins that ultrasound cannot see well. Catheter-based venography is the gold standard but is rarely needed for diagnosis. It is done before an invasive procedure.

Alongside this, do an arterial pulse exam and an ankle-brachial index (ABI) in any patient with a leg wound and in older patients. Peripheral artery disease must be ruled out before compression is started.

cards.t: Conservative care for venous insufficiency: elevation, exercise, skin
q: how high should you elevate legs for CVI
what exercise helps venous disease
what skin care does stasis dermatitis need
cards.x:
Initial management is always nonoperative: skin care, leg elevation, exercise and compression.

Leg elevation must put the feet above the level of the heart. That improves blood flow in the skin and reduces swelling. Legs resting a little higher than the hips do nothing, so ask the patient to show you what they call elevation.

Exercise means daily walking and ankle flexion, and avoiding long periods of sitting and standing. It builds calf muscle strength, and a strong calf pump pushes blood up the leg.

Skin care means gentle cleansing and emollients to keep the skin barrier intact, prevent dryness and cracking, and reduce scratching. Barrier creams such as petrolatum or zinc oxide help, and stasis dermatitis with redness, inflammation, itching or blisters may need a mid-potency topical corticosteroid.

cards.t: Compression therapy and why peripheral artery disease must be excluded first
q: how does compression help venous disease
what does graduated compression mean
who should not wear compression stockings
cards.x:
Compression (stockings or bandages) is the standard treatment for chronic venous insufficiency. It improves oxygen delivery to the skin and tissue under it, decreases swelling, reduces inflammation and squeezes the dilated veins back down.

Stockings must be graduated, meaning the pressure is greatest at the ankle and less as you go up the leg. That squeezes blood upward, speeding flow, preventing pooling, and lowering the chance of a clot.

The safety rule: peripheral artery disease must be ruled out before compression is started.

Some patients cannot tolerate compression, so explain why they are wearing it. Swelling comes back if the socks are not worn consistently.

cards.t: Treating infection, ulcers and surgery in chronic venous insufficiency
q: what drugs help venous insufficiency
what is the surgery for CVI
how do you treat cellulitis with venous insufficiency
cards.x:
Cellulitis on a leg with venous insufficiency is treated with oral antibiotics (cephalexin or clindamycin). Ulcers need edema control and compression, plus referral to wound care.

Classically no oral medication is considered proven for venous disease; current guidelines suggest pentoxifylline or flavonoids only as add-ons to compression for ulcer healing. Flavonoids are used to increase vein tone, and aspirin may speed healing of venous ulcers.

Surgery aims to block off or remove the affected vessels, restore proper blood flow and lower venous hypertension. Valvuloplasty (repairing the valve) is occasionally successful, but the rate of a deep vein clot after the operation is high. Venous bypass is successful in select patients.

The long-term key is steady control of swelling: the edema returns when compression socks are not worn consistently, and a healed ulcer leaves a thin scar that breaks down easily.

cards.t: When to refer chronic venous insufficiency to a vascular specialist
q: when do you refer a venous patient
which referral is urgent
what counts as a nonhealing ulcer
cards.x:
Refer to a vascular specialist for:
- Arterial insufficiency. This is the urgent one: it calls for an as-soon-as-possible, same-day referral.
- Nonhealing ulcers, and ulcer recurrence (the same place again and again).
- Persistent stasis dermatitis, or suspected contact dermatitis.
- Diagnostic uncertainty: if you are not sure of the diagnosis, consult someone.
- Significant saphenous reflux, and to control swelling long-term so ulcers do not recur.

Arterial insufficiency is the one that cannot wait: it needs an as-soon-as-possible, same-day referral, and compression must not be started until peripheral artery disease is ruled out.

cards.t: Spider veins, reticular veins and varicose veins: how they differ
q: what is the difference between spider veins and varicose veins
how big is a varicose vein
what are reticular veins
cards.x:
Chronic venous disease is a spectrum, and for the early stages the difference is mostly size and depth. Telangiectasias (spider veins) are tiny dilated venules within the skin, under 1 millimeter. Reticular veins are dilated bluish veins just beneath the skin, 1 to 3 millimeters. Varicose veins are dilated veins in the tissue under the skin (subcutaneous), 3 millimeters or more.

At the far end is chronic venous insufficiency itself: chronic severe edema, skin changes and venous ulceration. Advanced disease can look like pigment change on both sides of the ankle with a healed ulcer. It can also look like a small clean active ulcer, or a leg with massive pitting edema and red skin that suggests cellulitis.

cards.t: Risk factors for chronic venous disease
k: who gets varicose veins and venous insufficiency
q: what are the risk factors for chronic venous disease
does pregnancy raise the risk of venous insufficiency
why does a prior clot cause venous insufficiency
cards.x:
Chronic venous disease is more likely with:
- Advancing age and female sex.
- A family history of venous disease, or certain hereditary conditions.
- Ligamentous laxity (loose, stretchy ligaments, for example in flat feet).
- A higher body mass index and smoking.
- Lower extremity trauma or a prior venous thrombosis.
- Higher parity (more pregnancies) and high estrogen states.

A prior deep vein clot deserves special attention. Through scarring of the valves and obstruction of the vein, it is one of the most common causes of chronic venous insufficiency, the severe end of the disease. When that happens the condition is called post-thrombotic syndrome.

cards.t: Varicose veins: cause, risk factors and symptoms
q: what causes varicose veins
what is the most common symptom of varicose veins
what is the most common risk factor for varicose veins
cards.x:
Varicose veins are dilated, twisting veins under the skin caused by venous reflux (backward flow through leaky valves) together with venous hypertension. They usually involve the superficial veins, most often the great saphenous vein, and also the short saphenous vein.

Risk factors:
- Family history, the most common predisposing factor. If positive, ask who and at what age it started.
- Periods of high venous pressure, from prolonged standing or heavy lifting (think of occupation).
- Women after pregnancy.

Some people have no symptoms. If symptomatic, the most common symptom is a dull, achy heaviness or fatigue brought on by standing. Itching may occur above the ankle or over the veins. The dilated, tortuous veins of the thigh and calf are visible and palpable when the patient stands, and may be tender.

Long-standing varicose veins can progress to chronic venous insufficiency.

cards.t: Diagnosing and managing varicose veins
q: how are varicose veins diagnosed
how are varicose veins treated
when is ablation offered
cards.x:
Varicose veins are diagnosed clinically: examine the leg in a dependent position (hanging down). Venous duplex (Doppler) ultrasound confirms the diagnosis and classifies the location and extent of reflux.

Isolated varicose veins (no edema, skin changes or ulcer) are managed conservatively, the same way as chronic venous insufficiency: leg elevation, exercise and compression, remembering to rule out arterial disease before starting compression. A trial of stockings usually continues for weeks to months before a procedure to close off the vein (ablation) is offered. The goal is to improve symptoms and appearance, and varicose veins often recur.

Procedures:
- Sclerotherapy: injecting a sclerosing agent that scars and closes the vein (fibrose and obliterate it).
- Surgical reflux treatment: vein stripping, or a laser or radiofrequency catheter.

cards.t: Atherosclerosis: how a plaque builds and what it does
q: what is atherosclerosis
how does plaque rupture cause an occlusion
what are the three ways atherosclerosis causes disease
cards.x:
Arteriosclerosis is the general term for "hardening of the arteries." The most dominant type is atherosclerosis, which leads to the major causes of death in the United States. The word breaks down neatly: athero means gruel or paste, the fatty core of the plaque, and sclerosis means hardness, the stiffening from fibrous tissue that forms over it.

A plaque builds in steps: a fatty streak inside the intima (the inner layer, just under the lining cells); a stable plaque with a thick fibrous shell; a vulnerable plaque with a fatty core and a thin shell; then rupture into the bloodstream; a clot starting at the rupture site; and finally occlusion, so the tissue below the block dies. Lesions favor arterial bifurcations and places of turbulence, and they develop over many decades.

A plaque can therefore hurt in three ways: it narrows or blocks the artery (stenosis), a clot forms on it (thrombus), or pieces break off and travel (atheroemboli). The arterial diseases in this topic begin in one of these three ways.

cards.t: The three layers of the artery wall
q: what are the layers of an artery
what is the tunica intima
which layer is made of smooth muscle
cards.x:
An artery wall has three layers, from the inside out. The tunica intima is the innermost layer, lined with endothelial cells (the cells that touch the blood) sitting on a matrix of collagen and elastic fibers. The tunica media is the muscular middle layer, made of connective tissue and smooth muscle. The tunica adventitia is the fibrous outer layer.

This matters for atherosclerosis, because a plaque starts as a fatty streak inside the intima, just under the lining cells.

cards.t: Peripheral artery disease: what it is
q: what is peripheral artery disease
how does PAD cause leg pain
which arteries does PAD affect
cards.x:
Peripheral artery disease is a shortage of blood flow to muscle relative to what the muscle needs, producing pain in the affected muscle groups. Think of it as the leg's version of coronary artery disease: the pathophysiology is similar, and 50% of patients with it also have coronary artery disease.

The chain of events is simple: less flow to the leg, less tissue perfusion, less oxygen and nutrients for the muscle, then tissue damage and pain. How bad the symptoms are depends on how narrow the artery is, how many arteries are involved, and how active the patient is.

In the legs, the narrowing sits at three levels: aortoiliac (the aorta and iliac arteries), femoral-popliteal, and tibial.

Many patients with risk factors have few or no symptoms, so ask about functional capacity and any decline in activity.

cards.t: Risk factors for peripheral artery disease
q: what are the risk factors for PAD
how much does smoking raise PAD risk
what is the age cutoff for PAD
cards.x:
Peripheral artery disease is a disease of atherosclerosis, so its risk factors are the usual vascular ones.

- Age: older than 60 with no other risk factors, or 50 with risk factors (smoking, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, sedentary lifestyle, obesity).
- Male sex, and a family history of peripheral artery disease, cardiovascular disease or stroke.
- Cigarette smoking, which carries three times the risk of nonsmokers. Smoking cessation heads the list of risk-reduction measures for every patient with the disease.
- Diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia (abnormal blood fats), hypertension and obesity.
- Elevated homocysteine, an amino acid associated with earlier-onset atherosclerosis.

Notice the overlap with coronary disease: the underlying process is similar, and half of these patients have coronary artery disease as well.

cards.t: Intermittent claudication and what the pain location tells you
q: what is intermittent claudication
how does pain location map to the blocked artery
how is claudication like angina
cards.x:
Intermittent claudication (from the Latin for 'to limp') is pain in one or more leg muscle groups brought on by activity and relieved by rest, usually within about 10 minutes. It can be an ache, cramp, numbness or fatigue. It is analogous to angina in the heart. The muscle asks for more blood during exertion than the narrowed artery can deliver. How severe it is depends on the degree of stenosis, the collateral circulation and how hard the patient exercises.

The site of the pain names the level of the block:
- Buttock and hip: aortoiliac, with a diminished femoral pulse.
- Thigh: common femoral artery, with normal femoral pulses but decreased distal pulses.
- Upper two-thirds of the calf: superficial femoral artery. Pain in the upper two-thirds of the calf is the most common.
- Lower third of the calf: popliteal artery.
- Foot: tibial and peroneal arteries.

The history should cover where the pain is and how far the patient can walk before it starts. It should also cover whether that distance has changed and how long rest takes to relieve it.

cards.t: Leriche syndrome
k: claudication erectile dysfunction absent femoral pulses
q: what is Leriche syndrome
what is the triad of Leriche syndrome
why does aortoiliac disease cause erectile dysfunction
cards.x:
Leriche syndrome is the picture of blockage at the aortoiliac level (the aorta where it divides into the iliac arteries). It is a triad of three findings: claudication, absent or diminished femoral pulses, and erectile dysfunction.

It follows from where the block sits. Pain in the buttock and hip with walking points to aortoiliac disease, and a diminished femoral pulse on one or both sides is the pulse finding. In severe aortoiliac disease, erectile dysfunction is the third piece.

If a case combines buttock or hip claudication, weak groin pulses and erectile dysfunction, the level of the block is the aortoiliac segment.

cards.t: Critical limb ischemia and the rest pain paradox
q: what is critical limb ischemia
why does rest pain improve when the leg hangs down
how is rest pain different from claudication
cards.x:
Critical limb ischemia is the most advanced end of peripheral artery disease: ischemic rest pain, skin ulceration and gangrene.

Ischemic rest pain is constant, throbbing, burning or shooting, with cool feet, localized to the forefoot and toes. It is worse when the leg is elevated or the patient lies back, because gravity no longer helps blood reach the foot. It is not controlled by analgesics, even narcotics. It wakes the patient at night, and some sleep in a recliner.

The paradox is that it is relieved by hanging the leg over the edge of the bed or by walking around. That works because a dependent leg uses gravity to push blood into the foot. That is the opposite of claudication, which is brought on by walking and relieved by resting.

Useful history questions: night pain, recliner use, response to pain medication, and nonhealing toe wounds.

cards.t: Ischemic ulcers and gangrene (dry vs wet)
q: what does an ischemic ulcer look like
what is the difference between dry and wet gangrene
why is wet gangrene an emergency
cards.x:
Ischemic ulcers form because the blood supply cannot meet the extra demands of healing. They often begin as minor trauma and are painful. They show up where arteries end and pressure is high: the tips of the toes, between the digits, and over the metatarsal heads. They look dry and punched out, bleed little, and are often ringed by black necrotic (dead) tissue. They can lead to osteomyelitis (bone infection).

Dry gangrene is hard and dry, usually in the distal toes, with a clear demarcation line between healthy and dead tissue. It is common in peripheral artery disease.

Wet gangrene is a surgical emergency. It is moist, swollen and blistering, with bacterial infection and a risk of sepsis. It is usually a mixed bacterial infection of the dead tissue; when spore-forming Clostridium species are involved they release toxins and gas, and that form is called gas gangrene.

The contrast to remember: dry gangrene is hard with a clear edge, wet gangrene is moist, swollen and infected.

cards.t: Physical exam findings in peripheral artery disease
q: what do you find on exam in PAD
what is dependent rubor
what is reactive hyperemia
cards.x:
When flow is severely reduced the exam shows dry, thin, brittle, shiny skin, loss of hair and toenails, brittle nails, muscle atrophy (wasting) and poor wound healing.

Temperature is the marker for perfusion: check with the back of the hand. The ischemic limb is cool, and the line where the temperature changes roughly marks the level of the block.

Pulses (brachial, radial, aorta, femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial) are diminished or absent below the stenosis. If a pulse is hard to feel, use a handheld Doppler. Capillary refill takes longer than 2 seconds. Listen for bruits over the abdominal aorta and the iliac, femoral and popliteal arteries.

Two color terms: reactive hyperemia is the temporary rise in blood flow after a short period of ischemia, caused by metabolites building up and dilating the vessels. Dependent rubor is the reddish color the skin takes when the leg hangs down.

cards.t: The Buerger test
q: how do you do the Buerger test
what is a positive Buerger test
cards.x:
The Buerger test checks whether a leg's arteries can keep up with gravity. With the patient lying down, raise one leg to 45 degrees for 1 minute. If the arterial supply is poor, blood cannot overcome gravity and the foot turns pale (pallor; cyanosis, a blue color, in severe cases). Then have the patient sit up with the legs hanging over the edge of the bed. Dependent rubor, a deep red color from post-hypoxic vasodilation (vessels that opened wide after being starved of oxygen), appears. In severe cases cyanosis may come before the rubor.

A positive test is pallor on elevation followed by dependent rubor.

cards.t: Other causes of leg pain that mimic claudication
q: how do you tell claudication from spinal stenosis
what else causes leg pain with walking
how does neuropathy pain differ from claudication
cards.x:
Not every leg pain with walking is arterial. The pattern of what brings it on and what relieves it usually separates them.

- Thrombus at a plaque or an embolism: embolic debris from a proximal source gives acute pain.
- Venous insufficiency: calf swelling and discomfort with standing; swelling is worse with prolonged walking.
- Peripheral neuropathy: seen in the elderly with diabetes or alcoholism; continuous burning in the foot that is unaffected by exercise.
- Osteoarthritis of the hip or knee: often present at rest and worse with exercise; better when weight is off the joint.
- Spinal stenosis: claudication-like pain with numbness and weakness, relieved by rest and by sitting down or leaning forward.

True arterial claudication is brought on by activity and relieved by rest. Neuropathy burns continuously whatever you do, joint pain eases when weight is off the joint, and spinal stenosis eases with sitting or leaning forward.

cards.t: Ankle-brachial index: how to calculate and read it
q: how do you calculate the ankle-brachial index
what ABI means claudication
what does an ABI above 1.3 mean
cards.x:
The ankle-brachial index (ABI) is a simple bedside test and the important initial test for peripheral artery disease. It compares blood pressure in the ankle with blood pressure in the arm. For each leg, take the higher ankle pressure (posterior tibial or dorsalis pedis) and divide it by the higher arm pressure. The lower of the two legs is the patient's overall index.

How to read it:
- 0.9 to 1.3: normal.
- 0.4 to 0.9: claudication.
- 0 to 0.4: rest pain and tissue loss (ulcer, gangrene).
- Above 1.3: abnormal, because calcified, noncompressible arteries (for example in a diabetic patient) give a falsely high reading.

So a high number is not reassuring. It can mean the arteries are calcified and too stiff to compress. Also remember the arm side: check blood pressure in both arms and use the higher reading.

cards.t: Imaging and other tests for peripheral artery disease
q: what imaging is first for PAD
what is the gold standard test for PAD
when is CT angiography contraindicated
cards.x:
After the ankle-brachial index, the options build in complexity.

- Plethysmography (pulse volume measurement) is done in a vascular laboratory. Pneumatic cuffs sense volume changes with each pulse and locate the site and severity of disease.
- Duplex ultrasound is the mainstay and initial imaging when stenosis or obstruction is suspected. It is noninvasive, shows flow, and needs no contrast or radiation.
- Computed tomography angiography shows the anatomy with contrast, so contrast allergy or decreased kidney function is a relative contraindication (a caution that may steer you to another study).
- Magnetic resonance angiography is the alternative with contrast allergy. Pacemakers and intracranial aneurysm clips are contraindications.
- Conventional angiography is the gold standard and the most accurate. It is invasive (a vascular puncture, a catheter at the stenosis, contrast injected).

Computed tomography angiography, magnetic resonance angiography and conventional angiography are used mainly to guide a planned intervention, not as the first test. Laboratory tests in the work-up include an electrocardiogram, blood count, lipid profile, metabolic panel with fasting glucose, and renal function (these patients are at risk of renal insufficiency). They also include hemoglobin A1c (average glucose over three months).

cards.t: Treating peripheral artery disease: risk factors and drugs
q: how do you treat PAD
what drugs are used for claudication
what is the blood pressure goal in PAD
cards.x:
Treatment starts with reducing risk factors for everyone:
- Stop smoking.
- Blood pressure below 130/80 mmHg in current guidance. Older teaching used below 140/90 mmHg, or below 130/80 mmHg with diabetes or renal failure.
- Control diabetes and weight.
- Exercise therapy: refer to an exercise rehabilitation program. Supervised programs work better than home-based. Consistent moderate exercise improves walking distance, at least 30 to 45 minutes three times a week.

Drug therapy (names only):
- Antiplatelets: aspirin or clopidogrel lower the risk of heart attack and stroke. Cilostazol (also a vasodilator) is added to improve walking distance.
- Statins. Older teaching names simvastatin and pravastatin, while current guidance prefers high-intensity statins such as atorvastatin or rosuvastatin. The low-density lipoprotein target was classically below 100 mg/dL, or below 70 mg/dL at high risk (diabetes, continued smoking). Current guidance favors below 70 mg/dL.
- Pentoxifylline, a xanthine derivative, helps blood flow through narrowed arteries.
- Folic acid with cobalamin and pyridoxine for hyperhomocysteinemia (high homocysteine). It lowers homocysteine but has not been shown to reduce heart attacks or strokes, so it is not a proven treatment.

cards.t: Revascularization options for peripheral artery disease
q: when is revascularization done in PAD
what is the difference between angioplasty and bypass
what is a bypass graft used for
cards.x:
Revascularization means restoring blood flow. It is recommended for claudication when the patient has severe functional disability and has not responded enough to exercise or drug therapy.

- Endovascular procedures are minimally invasive, like a heart catheterization. They include percutaneous transluminal angioplasty with or without a stent, and atherectomy.
- Bypass graft (using a saphenous vein or a synthetic graft) is invasive but highly effective. It is used principally for severe critical limb ischemia. Complications include heart attack and stroke, graft infection and peripheral embolization.
- Endarterectomy removes plaque from inside the artery by open surgery.

cards.t: Acute limb ischemia and the six P's
k: pain pallor pulselessness paresthesia paralysis poikilothermia
q: what is acute limb ischemia
what are the six P's
how do you treat acute limb ischemia
cards.x:
Acute limb ischemia is the sudden blockage of an artery that was open before, causing abrupt severe pain and absent pulses. It is a vascular emergency.

The blockage comes either from a thrombus forming locally in an artery that was already narrowed, or from an embolus (a piece that breaks off, travels downstream and plugs a smaller artery). Most emboli are thromboemboli, dislodged clots. The heart is their source in 80 to 90% of cases (atrial fibrillation, or a clot in the left ventricle after a heart attack). The history is sudden onset, with or without earlier claudication.

The six P's: pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, and poikilothermia (difficulty regulating temperature). The limb is cold and cyanotic with absent pulses beyond the block. Light-touch sensory fibers are very sensitive to ischemia. So loss of feeling over the top of the foot is often the earliest neurologic sign.

Treatment options:
- Immediate vascular surgery consult.
- Intravenous heparin.
- Catheter-directed thrombolysis if the ischemia is under 14 days old.
- Thromboembolectomy.
- Arterial bypass.
- Amputation.

cards.t: Rutherford categories of acute limb ischemia
q: what are the Rutherford categories
which category goes to the operating room
which category does not need imaging
cards.x:
The Rutherford classification sorts an acutely ischemic limb by how much time you have, and that decides what happens next.

- I, viable: no immediate threat, no sensory loss or weakness. There is time for imaging, for example computed tomography angiography.
- IIA (marginally threatened): salvageable if treated promptly, with no sensory loss or weakness, or only minimal toe symptoms. There is time for imaging.
- IIB (immediately threatened): salvageable only with immediate revascularization. Sensory loss goes beyond the toes, with rest pain and mild to moderate weakness. Go straight to a surgical suite for evaluation and treatment, with no delay.
- III, irreversible: major tissue loss or permanent nerve damage, with profound sensory loss and paralysis. It needs a major amputation whatever the therapy, and imaging is not immediately needed.

The idea: the more threatened the limb, the less time you can spend on tests.

cards.t: Atheroembolism (blue toe syndrome)
q: what is blue toe syndrome
why are pulses preserved in atheroembolism
how is atheroembolism different from a big embolus
cards.x:
Atheroembolism, also called blue toe syndrome, is a shower of tiny emboli: multiple small deposits of fibrin, platelets and cholesterol debris that break off from proximal atherosclerotic plaques (an abdominal aortic aneurysm can do it too).

The key is the size of what lands. These bits lodge in the small vessels of muscle and skin and may not block the large vessels. So the distal pulses usually stay palpable, unlike acute limb ischemia from a big embolus, where pulses are lost.

The patient has acute pain and tenderness where the emboli land. Blockage of the digit's small vessels gives ischemia and the "blue toe," and digital necrosis and gangrene may follow. Look for localized tenderness, pallor and livedo reticularis (a mottled, net-like skin pattern).

A painful blue toe with palpable distal pulses points to this rather than to a large artery occlusion.

cards.t: Carotid artery disease
q: what is carotid artery disease
how does carotid disease cause stroke
how common is asymptomatic carotid stenosis
cards.x:
Carotid artery disease is atherosclerosis of the extracranial carotid artery, the neck artery that feeds the brain. Atherosclerosis favors the carotid bifurcation and bulb, where flow recirculates in a low-shear region (blood swirls back on itself with little force on the wall). The plaque causes stenosis, embolization and thrombosis.

As the internal carotid narrows, flow becomes more turbulent and the risk of atheroembolization rises. Strokes come most often from plaque rupture, not from the artery being blocked by thrombosis.

Patients with significant narrowing and no stroke or transient ischemic attack in the past six months are called asymptomatic. They outnumber symptomatic patients 4 to 1. That is why the narrowing is often present before any attack or stroke.

cards.t: Symptomatic carotid disease: transient ischemic attack, six-month window
q: what counts as a symptomatic carotid
what is a transient ischemic attack
how do you examine the carotids
cards.x:
Carotid disease is symptomatic when it causes focal neurologic symptoms: a transient ischemic attack or a stroke. A transient ischemic attack is a brief focal loss of neurologic function that fully clears with no lasting damage. It was classically defined as lasting under 24 hours, but current definitions rest on the absence of tissue injury rather than a time cutoff.

The window is six months: a patient with significant narrowing and no stroke or transient ischemic attack in the last six months is classed as asymptomatic.

On exam, inspect the neck pulses. Have the patient hold their breath and listen over each carotid separately, first with the diaphragm and then with the bell, for a bruit (a whooshing sound from turbulent flow). Palpate one side at a time. Add an eye, heart, peripheral vascular, neurologic and musculoskeletal exam.

cards.t: Testing for carotid stenosis
q: what is the first test for carotid stenosis
what test follows carotid disease over time
what is the gold standard for carotid imaging
cards.x:
Duplex ultrasonography is the most widely used initial test for carotid disease. It is also used to follow patients over time for progression or after an intervention. Computed tomography angiography or magnetic resonance angiography image the carotid and vertebral arteries in the neck and inside the skull, and the brain. Digital subtraction angiography is invasive and the gold standard, but it is not used for screening. It is used to guide interventions.

So the test is chosen by the situation: duplex to start or monitor, and angiography for planning an intervention.

cards.t: Treating carotid stenosis: medical care, endarterectomy, stenting
q: when is surgery done for carotid stenosis
endarterectomy vs stenting
how do you treat mild carotid stenosis
cards.x:
The percentage of narrowing and whether there are symptoms decide the plan.

- Stenosis below 50% (symptomatic or not): medical management.
- Symptomatic, stenosis above 70%: surgery.
- Asymptomatic, stenosis above 80% with a life expectancy over 5 years: surgery.

Medical management means:
- Antiplatelets (aspirin, clopidogrel).
- Treating hypertension, diabetes (glycemic control) and high cholesterol (statins).
- Quitting smoking (smoking nearly doubles stroke risk).
- A healthy diet, regular exercise and weight loss.

Two operations exist. Carotid endarterectomy removes the plaque through an incision and is the gold standard for high-grade stenosis. Its complications are stroke or nerve damage. Carotid angioplasty with stenting, usually through the femoral artery, is less invasive and is for poor surgical candidates.

cards.t: Aneurysm: definition and types (true, saccular, fusiform, false)
q: what is an aneurysm
what is the difference between saccular and fusiform
where are most aortic aneurysms
cards.x:
An aneurysm is a pathologic dilation of a segment of a blood vessel: a localized widening of more than 50% of the normal diameter. The infrarenal abdominal aorta averages 2 cm, and above 3 cm is aneurysmal.

A true aneurysm involves all three layers of the wall. Its shape is either saccular (only part of the circumference bulges, an outpouching) or fusiform (the whole circumference, a diffusely dilated segment).

A false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm) is different: the wall is thin and the outline irregular, with surrounding hematoma, while a true aneurysm has a thick wall and a smooth outline.

By location, a thoracic aortic aneurysm is ascending, arch or descending. An abdominal aortic aneurysm is the most common site, and 90% are infrarenal (below the kidney arteries), usually involving the bifurcation and the common iliac arteries.

cards.t: Abdominal aortic aneurysm: cause and risk factors
q: what causes an abdominal aortic aneurysm
what is the strongest risk factor for AAA
what is protective against AAA
cards.x:
In an abdominal aortic aneurysm the problem is failure of the wall's main structural proteins, elastin and collagen, in the media (the middle layer). The cause is unclear. Genetics play a part: Marfan syndrome (FBN1 gene) and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (COL3A1 gene). Atherosclerosis may also weaken the wall mechanically. Other etiologies: syphilis (which destroys the vasa vasorum, the small vessels that feed the wall of large arteries), vasculitis (Takayasu arteritis, giant cell arteritis), trauma, and congenital causes.

Risk factors:
- Smoking, current or past, is the strongest.
- Male sex (2 to 1 under age 80, 1 to 1 over 80), advancing age, Caucasian race (Caucasian men have the highest incidence).
- Atherosclerosis, hypertension, a family history of the disease, and other large-artery aneurysms (iliac, femoral, popliteal).

Protective: female sex (though women's aneurysms rupture more often), non-Caucasian race, and diabetes (the reason is unknown).

cards.t: Abdominal aortic aneurysm: presentation and rupture
q: how does a ruptured AAA present
what are symptoms of an unruptured AAA
what is Grey Turner sign
cards.x:
Many abdominal aortic aneurysms cause no symptoms and are an incidental finding on exam.

An unruptured one can cause symptoms as it expands: pain, constant or intermittent, in the abdomen (hypogastrium), back or flank, possibly radiating to the low back; isolated groin pain from pressure on the femoral nerve; early satiety; or an embolic "blue toe."

Rupture means blood escapes into the retroperitoneum (the space behind the abdominal cavity). The classic triad, present in 50%, is severe abdominal or back pain, a pulsatile abdominal mass (virtually diagnostic) and hypotension. It is often misdiagnosed as renal colic, diverticulitis, gastrointestinal hemorrhage or ischemic bowel.

On exam, palpate the aorta and estimate its size. An abdominal bruit is nonspecific, meaning it is not reliable evidence of an aneurysm on its own. Grey Turner sign (bruising of the flank) goes with retroperitoneal bleeding.

cards.t: Testing and surveillance for an abdominal aortic aneurysm
q: what is the best test for AAA
how often do you image a 4 cm aneurysm
how is AAA size followed
cards.x:
Abdominal ultrasound is the study of choice for initial screening and for serial documentation of size. An abdominal X-ray may show a calcified outline in 75%, but 25% are not calcified and are not seen. Computed tomography is better than ultrasound for size, involvement of the visceral arteries and extent. Magnetic resonance imaging is comparable without dye or radiation, useful in stable patients with a dye allergy. Computed tomography angiography is the best diagnostic and pre-intervention planning study.

Laboratory tests include an electrocardiogram (cardiac status), a blood count, a metabolic panel (kidney and liver function), and type and crossmatch if a transfusion is possible.

Surveillance depends on size:
- 3.0 to 3.9 cm: ultrasound every 3 years.
- 4.0 to 5.4 cm: ultrasound or computed tomography every 6 to 12 months.

The larger the aneurysm, the shorter the gap between scans.

cards.t: Abdominal aortic aneurysm: when to refer and when to repair
q: when is an AAA repaired
at what size do you refer a AAA
what increases the risk of rupture
cards.x:
Several size cutoffs drive the decisions, and they are easy to blur.

- 4.5 cm or larger: refer to a vascular specialist for observation and assessment. Refer urgently for aneurysmal pain at any size.
- 5.0 cm or larger: consider vascular surgery referral.
- Elective repair: 5.0 cm or larger in women, above 5.5 cm in men, or rapid growth of 0.5 cm in six months.

Rupture is rare until the diameter exceeds 5 cm. The risk rises with a diameter above 5.5 cm, expansion above 0.5 cm in six months, continued smoking and hypertension.

Medical care means managing modifiable risk factors: stop smoking, tight blood pressure control and moderate exercise. Repair is chosen by age and other illnesses. Endovascular repair places a modular graft through the iliac or femoral arteries to line the aorta and exclude the sac; open surgery replaces the diseased segment with a tube or bifurcated prosthetic graft.

A symptomatic, unruptured aneurysm needs assessment of stability, large-bore intravenous catheters, pain control, blood pressure control with beta blockers, and repair unless contraindicated. A ruptured one is a surgical emergency.

cards.t: Thoracic aortic aneurysm
q: what symptoms does a thoracic aortic aneurysm cause
how is a thoracic aneurysm diagnosed
when is a thoracic aneurysm repaired
cards.x:
A thoracic aortic aneurysm can be in the ascending aorta, the arch or the descending aorta. Most are asymptomatic and found incidentally on a chest X-ray, and a history of hypertension is common.

When symptoms do appear, they come from the location and from compression of nearby structures:
- Ascending: aortic regurgitation and heart failure.
- Arch: hoarseness (pressure on the recurrent laryngeal nerve).
- Descending: shortness of breath, stridor, wheezing, cough and trouble swallowing from compressing the trachea or esophagus.

The chest X-ray may show a widened mediastinal shadow or a pushed trachea or left mainstem bronchus. Computed tomography angiography is the most widely used test and shows the entire thoracic and abdominal aorta. Magnetic resonance angiography gives location, extent and size but is time-consuming. Transesophageal echocardiography evaluates the aortic valve and root.

cards.t: Thoracic aortic aneurysm: surveillance and when to repair
q: when is a thoracic aortic aneurysm repaired
how often do you image a thoracic aneurysm
what is the treatment for a thoracic aneurysm
cards.x:
Surveillance for a thoracic aortic aneurysm (root, ascending or descending) depends on size. Below 4.5 cm, image with computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging every 3 to 5 years. At 4.5 to 5.4 cm, image every 6 to 12 months.

Management starts with smoking cessation, beta blockers and aggressive blood pressure control. Chest or back pain in a patient with a known or suspected thoracic aneurysm needs urgent imaging.

Repair all symptomatic thoracic aneurysms. For an asymptomatic one, the decision depends on diameter, location and growth: repair when the ascending aorta is above 5.5 cm, the descending aorta is above 6.0 cm, or growth is above 0.5 cm per year.

The operation depends on the site. Ascending aneurysms often need open surgery with aortic root replacement; descending ones can be repaired open or endovascularly.

cards.t: Pseudoaneurysm (false aneurysm)
q: what is a pseudoaneurysm
how does a pseudoaneurysm form after cardiac catheterization
how is a pseudoaneurysm treated
cards.x:
A pseudoaneurysm (false aneurysm) is a leak rather than a bulge of the artery wall. After an artery is lacerated, blood escapes through the hole into the surrounding connective tissue and forms a blood-filled cavity outside the vessel wall. The cavity seals the leak as it clots (thromboses).

The common story is a laceration of the femoral artery by the access needle during cardiac catheterization. It presents with pain from the pressure of the swelling or from nerve compression.

On imaging, the false aneurysm has a thin wall, an irregular outline and surrounding hematoma, whereas a true aneurysm has a thick wall and a smooth outline.

If it is smaller than 2 cm, watch and wait, because it may clot and regress by itself. Ultrasound-guided thrombin injection is used to seal the leak.

cards.t: Aortic dissection: what it is and how it presents
q: what is an aortic dissection
what does aortic dissection pain feel like
who gets aortic dissection
cards.x:
Aortic dissection starts with a tear in the intima, the inner lining. Blood forces its way through and separates the wall layers, creating a false lumen (a false channel) within the media where blood can pool and may clot.

The most common predisposing factor is degeneration of the media's collagen and elastin, and Marfan syndrome is the classic medial degeneration. Most patients also have a history of hypertension. Typical patients are in their 60s and 70s (Marfan syndrome is the exception), and males more than females.

The presentation is sudden, severe, tearing or ripping chest pain. The location depends on the site and may change as the dissection spreads downstream. Other findings: syncope, hypertension or hypotension, and aortic regurgitation from widening of the aortic root.

The electrocardiogram may be normal, so a normal tracing does not exclude it.

cards.t: Aortic dissection: testing and treatment
q: how do you diagnose aortic dissection
what is the blood pressure target in dissection
which drugs lower pressure in dissection
cards.x:
For diagnosis, computed tomography of the chest and abdomen delineates the extent. Magnetic resonance imaging is good but slower, and transesophageal echocardiography is another option. The electrocardiogram may be normal.

Management aims to stop the dissection from progressing by lowering the pressure on the aortic wall. The systolic blood pressure target is 100 to 120 mmHg, using a beta blocker (esmolol) first, with a vasodilator (nitroprusside) added if pressure is still high. Pain control is part of the plan. Surgery grafts and replaces the diseased aorta.

An acute dissection that is left untreated has a high mortality.

cards.t: Cardiomyopathy: the three structural types compared
q: what is cardiomyopathy
how do dilated, hypertrophic and restrictive cardiomyopathy differ
which cardiomyopathy is most common
cards.x:
Cardiomyopathies are diseases of the myocardium, the muscular middle layer of the heart wall. The muscle is impaired, so the heart cannot fill and/or contract properly. Three structural types matter most, and stress (Takotsubo) cardiomyopathy and myocarditis are taught after them.

Two terms first: systolic failure means the heart cannot squeeze, diastolic failure means it cannot fill, and ejection fraction is the share of blood the left ventricle pumps out with each beat.

- Dilated: an enlarged, thin-walled ventricle. Systolic failure. Ejection fraction reduced, below 40%. Third heart sound. The most common type.
- Hypertrophic: an enlarged, stiff septum. Diastolic failure, with or without outflow obstruction. Ejection fraction normal, and above 75% late. Fourth heart sound. About 1 in 500 people.
- Restrictive: stiff walls, normal-size ventricles and big atria. Diastolic failure. Ejection fraction preserved until late. Fourth heart sound if there is no regurgitation. The least common.

The question to ask of every case is whether it is genetic and congenital, or secondary to something else. Knowing which cardiomyopathy it is gets you past treating only the symptoms of heart failure.

cards.t: Dilated cardiomyopathy: what it is
q: what is dilated cardiomyopathy
what happens to the ventricles in DCM
why does DCM cause mitral regurgitation
cards.x:
Dilated cardiomyopathy is the most common type. The muscle cannot contract effectively, even though there is no severe blockage of the coronary arteries and no pressure or volume overload (such as hypertension or valve disease) to blame. One or both ventricles dilate and contract poorly. The total mass of the heart rises, and the adverse remodeling produces a globular (round) heart. The result is systolic dysfunction: the heart cannot squeeze.

The dilation distorts the valve apparatus, so mitral regurgitation (earlier) and tricuspid regurgitation develop. The rising end-systolic volume (the blood left in the ventricle after each beat) drives further dilation. Arrhythmias and clots (thromboembolism) follow.

In the United States it accounts for 10,000 deaths and 46,000 hospitalizations a year. Most patients present between ages 20 and 60. It is more common in males and has a high rate in African Americans.

cards.t: Causes of dilated cardiomyopathy (including alcohol and peripartum)
q: what causes dilated cardiomyopathy
can alcohol-related dilated cardiomyopathy recover
what is peripartum cardiomyopathy
cards.x:
The complete list of causes is extensive. The main ones:

- Idiopathic (no cause found; common and probably genetic).
- Familial, common (up to 35%), most often autosomal dominant. Research focuses on the lamin A/C gene.
- Infectious myocarditis. It can be viral (coxsackievirus, parvovirus, influenza, human immunodeficiency virus) or parasitic (Trypanosoma cruzi, Chagas disease).
- Chemotherapy.
- Long-term excess alcohol. This is one of the few causes where function can recover if intake is reduced or stopped.
- Thiamine (a B vitamin) deficiency.
- Systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis.
- Peripartum cardiomyopathy, which is rare and occurs from the last trimester of pregnancy to 6 months after delivery.

History matters. Ask about hypertension, angina, coronary disease, anemia, thyroid disease, breast cancer and chemotherapy, prior heart failure, arrhythmias and clots. Also ask about tobacco, alcohol and drugs, and especially about a family history of cardiomyopathy or sudden death.

cards.t: How dilated cardiomyopathy presents: symptoms and exam
q: what are the symptoms of dilated cardiomyopathy
why does the third heart sound happen
what is hepatojugular reflux
cards.x:
The picture is heart failure. Symptoms include:
- Progressive shortness of breath on exertion (ask how far they could walk months ago and now).
- Fatigue, and skipped or fast beats (arrhythmias).
- Orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat) and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (waking short of breath).
- Leg swelling with rising weight and abdominal girth.

The exam reflects how decompensated the patient is, and left heart failure comes before right. Findings include fast breathing and heart rate, high or low blood pressure, and an irregular pulse. Others are a narrow pulse pressure (a low top number reflects a low stroke volume), crackles and pleural effusions, cool extremities, edema, and a laterally displaced point of maximal impulse.

Heart sounds: a third heart sound (a large volume of blood striking a very compliant ventricle), plus mitral and tricuspid regurgitation murmurs. Right-sided clues are jugular venous distension, congestive enlargement of the liver, hepatojugular reflux (neck veins swell when you press firmly on the liver) and ascites.

cards.t: Diagnosing dilated cardiomyopathy: echocardiogram first
q: how is dilated cardiomyopathy diagnosed
what does the echocardiogram show in DCM
when is a biopsy done
cards.x:
Echocardiography decides it. It shows a dilated ventricle with thin walls (the prominent feature), an ejection fraction below 40%, hypokinesis (weak movement), segmental wall-motion abnormalities, and mitral or tricuspid regurgitation. All four chambers may be enlarged, and there may be a clot.

Other tests build the picture:
- Electrocardiogram: usually abnormal, and may show atrial fibrillation, premature ventricular contractions or left bundle branch block.
- Chest X-ray: an enlarged heart, pleural effusions, pulmonary edema, and Kerley B lines (short horizontal lines, 1 to 2 cm long, that meet the lung's edge at right angles).
- Labs: blood count (for anemia), electrolytes and kidney function, liver function, thyroid function.
- Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium finds inflammatory, ischemic or infiltrative processes such as sarcoidosis and hemochromatosis.
- Biopsy is not routine and rarely useful. It is done only for recent, rapidly deteriorating function or a systemic disease that can involve the heart (hemochromatosis, sarcoidosis, amyloidosis).

cards.t: B-type natriuretic peptide in heart failure
q: what does a low BNP mean
why is BNP elevated in heart failure
what BNP level excludes heart failure
cards.x:
B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) is a blood marker released when the filling pressures inside the ventricles are high. So it is elevated in heart failure. A level below 100 pg/mL makes heart failure an unlikely explanation for the current symptoms.

Think of it as a rule-out test: a low number makes a failing heart an unlikely reason for the symptoms, while a high number fits a heart that is struggling against high filling pressure.

cards.t: Treating dilated cardiomyopathy: drugs
q: how do you treat dilated cardiomyopathy
which drugs lower mortality
when should you anticoagulate in DCM
cards.x:
The drug classes and drugs used to manage it:
- Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors.
- Beta blockers.
- Angiotensin receptor blockers.
- An aldosterone receptor blocker (spironolactone).
- Sacubitril/valsartan.
- Nitrates.
- Diuretics.
- Digoxin, which is considered a second-line drug.
- Antiarrhythmics.
- Anticoagulants.
