Education means removing the offending source (alcohol, nutritional deficiency, cardiotoxic agents). It also means restricting sodium to under 2 g a day. Offer genetic counseling when there is a family history.

cards.t: Devices, assist devices, transplant and prognosis in dilated cardiomyopathy
q: when is a defibrillator placed in DCM
what is a left ventricular assist device
what is the prognosis of dilated cardiomyopathy
cards.x:
When drugs are not enough, devices step in.

- A biventricular pacemaker is for moderately severe left ventricular dysfunction.
- An implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (a device that shocks a dangerous rhythm) is placed if the ejection fraction is below 35% after maximum medical therapy. A biventricular defibrillator combines the two.
- A left ventricular assist device pumps blood from the left ventricle into the aorta. It can be a bridge to transplantation or to recovery of function, or destination therapy for those who cannot have a transplant. Patients may live more than 5 years with one.
- Cardiac transplantation is the other option, and idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy is its primary indication.

Prognosis is poor overall and depends on the response to therapy. Once symptoms emerge, there is 50% mortality at 5 years, largely from progressive disease and sudden death from an arrhythmia.

cards.t: Mitral and tricuspid regurgitation murmurs in dilated cardiomyopathy
q: where is the mitral regurgitation murmur heard
how do you tell tricuspid from mitral regurgitation
what makes the mitral regurgitation murmur louder
cards.x:
As the dilated heart stretches, the valve apparatus is distorted and the valves leak backward (regurgitation). Mitral regurgitation comes earlier, and tricuspid regurgitation follows. Both murmurs are holosystolic, meaning they fill all of systole, so the way to tell them apart is where they are loudest and where they travel.

- Mitral regurgitation: holosystolic, loudest at the apex, radiating to the left axilla, and louder with handgrip or squatting.
- Tricuspid regurgitation: holosystolic at the lower left sternal border, radiating to the right sternum and xiphoid but not to the axilla, and slightly louder with inspiration.

A simple way to remember it: mitral goes out to the armpit, tricuspid stays near the breastbone and gets louder when the patient breathes in.

cards.t: Acute myocarditis: what it is and what causes it
q: what is myocarditis
what causes myocarditis
who gets myocarditis
cards.x:
Acute myocarditis is inflammation of the myocardium (the heart muscle), ranging from subtle to devastating. It usually strikes an otherwise healthy person and can cause rapidly progressive, often fatal heart failure and arrhythmia. Young males are particularly susceptible, though men and women are affected about equally, with no race predilection.

In developed countries, viral infection is presumed to be the most frequent cause: parvovirus, human herpesvirus 6, enteroviruses (Coxsackie B), adenoviruses, hepatitis C, cytomegalovirus, human immunodeficiency virus, and coronavirus disease 2019. Viral myocarditis accounts for 20% of dilated cardiomyopathy.

Other causes:
- Rheumatic fever (beta-hemolytic streptococcus; the heart is affected in 50 to 90%).
- Bacteria such as diphtheria and Legionnaires disease.
- Trypanosoma cruzi (Chagas), rickettsia, spirochetes such as Lyme disease, and Candida.
- Drugs (penicillin, thiazide diuretics, tetracycline, methyldopa).
- Toxins (lithium, arsenic, lead, copper).
- Autoimmune disease (lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, myasthenia gravis).

cards.t: How acute myocarditis presents
k: new heart failure in a healthy young person
q: what are the symptoms of myocarditis
what is the classic history for viral myocarditis
what is on the differential for myocarditis
cards.x:
The classic story is acute decompensated heart failure in a person with no underlying heart problem or a low cardiac risk. In viral myocarditis there is often a flulike illness 1 to 2 weeks earlier (fever, muscle aches, fatigue, respiratory symptoms or stomach upset). A flulike illness that clears and is followed by new heart failure symptoms is the big clue.

Then come exercise intolerance, shortness of breath, fluid retention and chest pain. Palpitations, fainting or sudden cardiac death follow too, caused by ventricular arrhythmias or atrioventricular block.

On exam, the patient may be in cardiogenic shock or frank heart failure: fast heart rate, low blood pressure, raised jugular venous pressure, a third heart sound, crackles and swelling.

The differential includes tamponade, cardiogenic shock, cocaine cardiomyopathy, ischemic heart disease, valve disease and coronary atherosclerosis. It also includes the dilated, hypertrophic, peripartum and restrictive cardiomyopathies.

cards.t: Diagnosing myocarditis: troponin, magnetic resonance imaging and biopsy
q: what is the gold standard test for myocarditis
what test shows the extent of inflammation
when is a biopsy done for myocarditis
cards.x:
The work-up shows inflammation and heart muscle damage while excluding other causes.

- Blood count: leukocytosis (a raised white cell count). Sedimentation rate: may be raised.
- Troponin: the indicator of cardiac myonecrosis (heart muscle cell death).
- Electrocardiogram: sinus tachycardia or arrhythmias.
- Echocardiogram, and a chest X-ray that is nonspecific but may show an enlarged heart.
- Cardiac angiography, to rule out coronary ischemia as the cause of new heart failure.
- Gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging shows the extent of inflammation.

Endomyocardial biopsy (a sample of heart muscle) is the gold standard, but only once other causes of heart failure are excluded. It is recommended for acute deterioration of unknown origin that is not responding to treatment.

So there is a split: magnetic resonance imaging is the best test to see the extent, while biopsy is the definitive one that is rarely done.

cards.t: Myocarditis: management and prognosis
q: how is myocarditis treated
what is the prognosis of myocarditis
does myocarditis lead to dilated cardiomyopathy
cards.x:
Many cases of myocarditis are not obvious, so management starts with a high index of suspicion. Supportive care is the mainstay, and aggressive hemodynamic stabilization may be needed in a sick patient. As needed, the team uses vasodilators, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, diuretics, antiarrhythmics and anticoagulation.

The outlook varies. Most patients with mild symptoms recover completely, but one third later develop dilated cardiomyopathy. That is why myocarditis and dilated cardiomyopathy are linked: viral myocarditis accounts for 20% of dilated cardiomyopathy.

cards.t: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: what it is and how it is inherited
q: what is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
how is HCM inherited
why is HCM a cause of sudden death in young people
cards.x:
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is thickening of the left ventricular muscle that is not explained by a cause such as hypertension, aortic valve disease or an infiltrative or storage disease. It is often asymmetric and can involve any region, most often the interventricular septum (the wall between the two ventricles).

It is mostly inherited, autosomal dominant, meaning one mutated copy from an affected parent is enough. There are at least 1,500 mutations, in genes for sarcomere proteins (the proteins that make muscle contract). It affects 1 in 500 people, males more than females.

It carries a high incidence of sudden death. It is the leading cause of sudden death in preadolescent and adolescent children, with extreme exertion linked to those deaths.

cards.t: Obstructive vs nonobstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
q: what is systolic anterior motion
what is the difference between obstructive and nonobstructive HCM
why does HCM cause diastolic dysfunction
cards.x:
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy comes in two types, depending on whether the thick muscle blocks blood flow out of the heart.

Without obstruction, the problem is diastolic dysfunction. The thick muscle resists filling (reduced compliance) and raises the pressure at the end of filling in the left ventricle.

With obstruction (hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy), the thickened septum narrows the subaortic outflow tract (the path out of the left ventricle). On top of that comes systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve: fast flow through the narrowed path pulls the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve into the outflow tract, causing mid-systolic obstruction. This is the telltale sign of the obstructive form on echocardiography.

Chest pain (angina) can occur without coronary disease because of the outflow obstruction plus the higher oxygen demand of thick muscle.

cards.t: Presentation of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: dyspnea, syncope, sudden death
q: what are the symptoms of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
why is syncope important in HCM
what rhythm causes sudden death in HCM
cards.x:
Many patients have no symptoms and are found through family screening, a murmur on routine exam or an abnormal electrocardiogram.

- Dyspnea is the common presenting symptom: high filling pressure in the ventricle backs up into the lungs.
- Palpitations from atrial premature beats, atrial fibrillation or flutter, or supraventricular or ventricular tachycardia.
- Angina without coronary artery disease.
- Syncope (very common; low output on exertion or an arrhythmia) and presyncope on standing that is relieved by lying down. Both identify patients at high risk of sudden death, and the work-up is urgent. Think of a young athlete who simply passes out.
- Sudden cardiac death, highest in preadolescents and adolescents and related to extreme exertion. Over 80% of cases are ventricular fibrillation.

cards.t: Exam findings and murmurs in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
q: what is pulsus bisferiens
where is the HCM murmur heard and where does it radiate
what murmurs are heard in HCM
cards.x:
Blood pressure and heart rate are usually normal. The classic pulse is pulsus bisferiens, Latin for "strike twice": a double systolic peak that matches the outflow obstruction. The apical impulse is forceful and sustained, maybe displaced, and there is a fourth heart sound from the noncompliant (stiff) ventricle.

There are two murmurs.
- The outflow murmur is crescendo-decrescendo and systolic, best heard at the left sternal border in the 3rd or 4th intercostal space. It radiates to the suprasternal notch but not to the carotids or neck.
- The mitral regurgitation murmur, caused by systolic anterior motion, is holosystolic at the apex and radiates to the axilla.

cards.t: How maneuvers change the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy murmur
q: what makes the HCM murmur louder
what makes the HCM murmur softer
does breathing change the HCM murmur
cards.x:
The rule is simple. Anything that puts more blood in the left ventricle softens the murmur. Anything that puts less blood in makes it louder. That is because the amount of blood in the ventricle changes how much the outflow is blocked.

- Rapid squatting and passive leg raising increase preload (the filling volume): the murmur gets softer.
- Handgrip increases afterload (the resistance the ventricle pumps against): softer.
- Valsalva and standing reduce preload: louder.
- Amyl nitrite reduces afterload: louder.
- Inspiration and expiration: no effect.

So standing and Valsalva shrink the filling of the ventricle. That makes the narrowed outflow tighter and the murmur louder. Squatting fills the ventricle and opens things up.

cards.t: Diagnosing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
q: what is the test of choice for HCM
what wall thickness diagnoses HCM
is catheterization needed for HCM
cards.x:
There is no specific blood test. Routine labs only look for things that make it worse, such as anemia, thyroid disease or kidney and liver problems.

Echocardiography is the typical test of choice. The diagnosis is confirmed by unexplained wall thickness of 1.5 cm or more anywhere in the left ventricle. Classic findings:
- Asymmetric septal hypertrophy and a small cavity.
- A normal ejection fraction (above 75% late, as the small ventricle nearly empties).
- Mitral regurgitation, systolic anterior motion and left atrial enlargement.

Other tests:
- Electrocardiogram: hypertrophy, atrial enlargement, conduction abnormalities, prominent Q waves in the inferior and lateral leads, left axis deviation.
- Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging when the echocardiogram is questionable, and exercise echocardiography.
- An ambulatory electrocardiogram for 24 to 48 hours assesses the risk of dangerous arrhythmias and sudden death.
- Catheterization is not needed for diagnosis, only before a pacemaker or surgery. Genetic testing is available but does not change treatment.

The differential includes aortic stenosis, mitral regurgitation, hypertensive heart disease, athletic heart and restrictive cardiomyopathy.

cards.t: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: drugs to use and drugs to avoid
q: what is the first-line drug for obstructive HCM
why avoid nitrates in HCM
what drugs worsen HCM
cards.x:
For outflow obstruction, a beta blocker (for example metoprolol) is the initial medication. The alternative is a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (verapamil or diltiazem).

The drugs to avoid follow from the mechanism. Drugs that lower preload or afterload, such as nitrates, make the obstruction worse. Diuretics are used only with caution to avoid dehydration. Positive inotropes (digoxin, epinephrine, norepinephrine) raise contractility, ischemia risk and arrhythmias, so they are also avoided.

To prevent sudden death, amiodarone is proven to reduce the incidence and risk of sudden cardiac death, with disopyramide the other antiarrhythmic listed, and an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator is also used. Amiodarone also converts atrial fibrillation and flutter and suppresses their recurrence. For atrial fibrillation, anticoagulation prevents embolic stroke, and radiofrequency ablation is another option.

cards.t: Myectomy and alcohol septal ablation
q: what is a septal myectomy
how does alcohol septal ablation work
when is surgery needed in HCM
cards.x:
When medication does not control obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, the thick septum can be reduced in two ways.

- Surgical septal myectomy excises part of the septal muscle that is causing the obstruction. The mitral regurgitation from systolic anterior motion may resolve with the myectomy alone.
- Alcohol septal ablation injects alcohol down the first septal branch of the left anterior descending artery. It creates a therapeutic infarct (a controlled heart attack) of the upper septum, and it takes months for the septum to thin.

If the disease is unresponsive to therapy, transplant is an option.

Patient advice is to stay well hydrated and avoid excess alcohol. Activity advice is individualized: regular mild to moderate exercise is encouraged, and strenuous or competitive sports need a shared decision with a specialist center.

cards.t: Restrictive cardiomyopathy: what it is
q: what is restrictive cardiomyopathy
why does restrictive cardiomyopathy cause right heart failure
why does it cause heart block
cards.x:
Restrictive cardiomyopathy is the rarest cardiomyopathy. The problem is impaired diastolic filling with a reasonably preserved chamber size. The walls are normal or slightly thickened, so the heart is 'stiff, but not necessarily thickened.'

The chain: stiff walls, poor filling, then reduced output because the filling volume is reduced. The ejection fraction is preserved until late and systolic function is usually normal. Both atria enlarge, atrial fibrillation is common, and right heart failure is often more prominent. Fibrosis (scarring) of the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes can cause heart block.

It has the poorest prognosis of all the heart muscle diseases.

cards.t: Causes of restrictive cardiomyopathy (amyloidosis and others)
q: what is the most common cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy
what causes a stiff heart
which treatments can cause restrictive cardiomyopathy
cards.x:
Restrictive cardiomyopathy has several causes to place:

- Idiopathic (no cause found).
- Infiltrative: amyloidosis, the most common in the United States.
- Storage: hemochromatosis, which is iron deposits.
- Genetic, which is less common than in other cardiomyopathies.
- Inflammatory: cardiac sarcoidosis (granulomas).
- Treatment-related: mediastinal radiation and chemotherapy, where inflammation leads to fibrosis (scarring) and then restriction.

Patients often present late, with pronounced symptoms, so ask about prior radiation, chemotherapy or a systemic disease.

cards.t: Restrictive cardiomyopathy: symptoms, exam and Kussmaul sign
q: what is Kussmaul sign
how does restrictive cardiomyopathy present
why is right-sided failure more prominent
cards.x:
It often presents late, with pronounced symptoms. Right-sided failure features: abdominal pain from an enlarged liver, swelling of both feet, ascites. Also progressive exercise intolerance and dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, palpitations from atrial fibrillation (with a risk of atrial clots), fatigue and syncope.

On exam, the patient is more comfortable sitting, jugular venous pressure is elevated, and the heart sounds are normal but perhaps distant. A fourth heart sound is heard if there is no regurgitation. There may be rales, an enlarged congested liver, hepatojugular reflux and ascites.

Kussmaul sign may be present: a paradoxical rise in jugular venous pressure with inspiration, caused by resistance to right ventricular filling. It is also common in constrictive pericarditis, so it does not separate the two.

cards.t: Restrictive cardiomyopathy vs constrictive pericarditis
q: how do you tell restrictive cardiomyopathy from constrictive pericarditis
why can't echocardiography tell them apart
what test separates restrictive from constrictive
cards.x:
Constrictive pericarditis is the look-alike that must be differentiated from restrictive cardiomyopathy. Both leave a heart that cannot fill properly. Both can show Kussmaul sign. In restrictive cardiomyopathy the problem is the heart muscle. In constrictive pericarditis it is the pericardium (the sac around the heart). The cause, treatment and outcome are very different.

The echocardiogram is not definitive on its own, because the two look alike. In restrictive cardiomyopathy it shows a preserved ejection fraction (which may fall late) and marked atrial enlargement. It also shows near-normal ventricular function and cavity size, normal or thick walls, and abnormal diastolic function.

Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging helps separate them. A thickened pericardium points to constrictive pericarditis, though constriction can occur with a normal-thickness pericardium. If imaging and genetic testing are negative, or tissue would change management, an endomyocardial biopsy can be done. Catheterization gives ventricular pressure tracings.

cards.t: Restrictive cardiomyopathy: electrocardiogram, chest X-ray and treatment
q: what does the electrocardiogram show in amyloid heart disease
how do you treat restrictive cardiomyopathy
why be careful with diuretics in restrictive cardiomyopathy
cards.x:
The electrocardiogram depends on the stage and cause. In amyloidosis it shows low QRS (the main spike) voltage, meaning small tracings. Atrial fibrillation and bundle branch blocks are common. The chest X-ray shows an enlarged heart from atrial enlargement, plus congestion and effusions.

Treatment is to treat the underlying disorder, then manage the heart:
- Diuretics for pulmonary and systemic congestion, but with caution. Stiff ventricles depend on preload to keep up their output, and diuretics lower it.
- Beta blockers, and the calcium channel blockers verapamil or diltiazem, may help by lengthening the time the left ventricle has to fill, improving its relaxation and decreasing the compensatory sympathetic stimulation.
- Anticoagulation to prevent embolism from atrial clots.
- A permanent pacemaker for conduction disease.
- Cardiac transplantation.

The prognosis is the poorest of all the heart muscle diseases.

cards.t: Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy: what it is
q: what is Takotsubo cardiomyopathy
why is it called broken heart syndrome
who gets Takotsubo cardiomyopathy
cards.x:
Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, or 'broken heart syndrome,' is temporary weakness of part of the left ventricle's squeeze (transient regional systolic dysfunction). It mimics acute coronary syndrome, yet the coronary arteries show no angiographic disease and there is no acute plaque rupture. The cause is unknown. Takotsubo is Japanese for an octopus trap, a round-bottomed, narrow-necked pot.

About 90% of patients are postmenopausal women. The trigger is a significant emotional or physical stressor: the death of a loved one, bad financial news, a natural disaster, a new diagnosis, surgery, withdrawal from illicit drugs or near drowning. These patients tend to have low or no cardiac risk factors.

The classic abnormality is hypokinesis or akinesis (weak or absent movement) of the mid and apical segments of the left ventricle.

cards.t: Takotsubo: how it looks like a heart attack, tests and management
q: how do you diagnose Takotsubo
how is Takotsubo treated
what is the prognosis of Takotsubo
cards.x:
Chest pain and shortness of breath are the most common symptoms, and there can be palpitations, nausea, vomiting and syncope. The exam is nonspecific. The patient may look like acute coronary syndrome or acute heart failure: anxious and sweaty, with fast or slow rhythm problems.

The tests also look like a heart attack: troponin I and T are usually elevated, B-type natriuretic peptide is frequently elevated, and the electrocardiogram shows ST (a segment of the tracing) elevation and T-wave inversion. The echocardiogram shows hypokinesis or akinesis of the mid and apical segments. Cardiac catheterization confirms the diagnosis, most often showing normal coronary arteries.

Because it mimics a heart attack and there are no reliable early differences, follow the acute coronary syndrome protocols and admit to cardiology. Supportive care is empiric: beta blockers are commonly used but have not been proven to help, anticoagulation if there is a clot in the left ventricle, and diuretics if there is heart failure.

Most patients recover completely.

cards.t: Cardiomyopathy care for adolescents, adults and the elderly
q: how does cardiomyopathy care differ by age
what is done for adolescents with HCM
what is the goal of care in elderly cardiomyopathy
cards.x:
What you emphasize changes with the age group.

- Adolescents: genetic screening for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and activity restriction for high-risk individuals. This is the age at which hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the leading cause of sudden death.
- Adults: guideline-directed medical therapy (angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, beta blockers, angiotensin receptor blockers, diuretics), devices (an implantable defibrillator, a biventricular pacemaker) and lifestyle measures (sodium restriction, alcohol cessation). In advanced disease, consider an assist device or transplant.
- Elderly: therapy tailored to other illnesses and frailty, cautious use of diuretics and vasodilators, and a focus on symptom control and quality of life, with palliative care discussions in advanced stages.

cards.t: Cardiac rehabilitation and palliative care in cardiomyopathy
q: what does cardiac rehabilitation involve
what is palliative care in cardiomyopathy
when is hospice referral appropriate
cards.x:
Two supports sit alongside medical treatment.

Cardiac rehabilitation programs improve exercise tolerance and quality of life. They include education on taking medicines, nutrition and monitoring symptoms, and psychological support for living with a chronic illness. Home-based rehabilitation suits elderly or mobility-limited patients.

Palliative care does not focus on curing. It focuses on making the patient comfortable and letting them enjoy life. It covers symptom management (shortness of breath, fatigue, swelling), advance care planning and goals-of-care discussions, and support for caregivers and family. In end-stage cardiomyopathy it includes referral to hospice.

cards.t: Electrocardiogram paper: box sizes and counting the heart rate
k: how to count heart rate on ECG
q: how long is one small box on an ECG
how do you count the heart rate on a strip
what is the 300 150 100 method
cards.x:
Electrocardiogram (ECG) paper is a grid that turns distance into time. The thin lines are 1 mm apart, and one small box is 0.04 seconds. The thick lines are 5 mm apart, so one large box (five small boxes) is 0.20 seconds, and five large boxes (25 small boxes) make 1 second.

To count the rate quickly, find an R wave that sits on a thick line. Then count off the next thick lines: 300, 150, 100, 75, 60, 50, 43, 37 beats per minute. The thick line where the next R wave lands gives the rate, so a next beat two large boxes away means about 150, and five large boxes away means about 60.

What you are really measuring is the RR interval, the time between beats. It is regular at rest and gets shorter with exercise as the rate rises.

cards.t: Normal electrocardiogram waves and intervals (P wave, PR, QRS, T wave)
q: what does the P wave represent
what is a normal PR interval
how wide should the QRS be
what does the T wave represent
cards.x:
The beat's electrical impulse starts in the sinoatrial (sinus) node, crosses the atria, passes the atrioventricular node, then runs down the bundle of His, the bundle branches and the Purkinje fibers. The waves below show what the atria and ventricles are doing during the beat.

- P wave: the atria depolarizing (firing). Normally under 0.12 seconds (3 small boxes) and under 2.5 mm tall, best judged in V1.
- PR interval: the impulse traveling from the atria through the atrioventricular node into the ventricles. Normally 0.12 to 0.20 seconds (3 to 5 small boxes); it shortens with exercise as the rate rises.
- QRS complex: the ventricles depolarizing. Narrow, under 0.12 seconds; over 0.5 mV in at least one standard lead and over 1.0 mV in at least one precordial (chest) lead, with an upper limit of 2.5 to 3.0 mV.
- T wave: the ventricles repolarizing (resetting). It points the same way as the QRS, so a negative T wave is normal in aVR and V1, where the QRS is negative too.

cards.t: Normal sinus rhythm and how the other sinus rhythms differ
q: what are the criteria for normal sinus rhythm
how do sinus bradycardia and sinus tachycardia differ from normal sinus rhythm
what makes a rhythm a sinus rhythm
cards.x:
Normal sinus rhythm is the heart's normal beat, started by the sinus node: regular, 60 to 100 beats per minute, with a uniform P wave for every QRS, a constant PR interval of 0.12 to 0.20 seconds, and a narrow QRS under 0.12 seconds.

The three other sinus rhythms keep the waves exactly the same (one uniform P wave per QRS, a PR of 0.12 to 0.20, a narrow QRS) and change only the rate or the regularity:
- Sinus arrhythmia: irregular with a pattern, faster with breathing in and slower with breathing out, still 60 to 100.
- Sinus bradycardia: regular, under 60.
- Sinus tachycardia: regular, above 100, up to 160.

So when the P waves, PR and QRS all look normal, the only questions left are how fast and how regular.

cards.t: Sinus arrhythmia
q: what is sinus arrhythmia
is sinus arrhythmia normal
does sinus arrhythmia need treatment
cards.x:
Sinus arrhythmia is a normal, physiologic variant of sinus rhythm in which the beat is irregular, but in a predictable way that follows breathing. The heart rate is faster as you breathe in and slower as you breathe out, so the gaps between beats stretch and shrink in a repeating cycle.

Everything else is normal sinus rhythm: a rate of 60 to 100, a uniform P wave for every QRS, a PR interval of 0.12 to 0.20 seconds and a narrow QRS under 0.12 seconds. Because it is normal, the person needs reassurance and no treatment.

The giveaway on a strip: the irregularity has a pattern tied to breathing, and every beat still has its normal P wave.

cards.t: Sinus bradycardia: definition and causes
q: what is sinus bradycardia
what causes sinus bradycardia
is a slow heart rate normal in athletes
which drugs cause bradycardia
cards.x:
Sinus bradycardia is a regular sinus rhythm under 60 beats per minute. Every beat is otherwise normal: a uniform P wave for every QRS, a PR interval of 0.12 to 0.20 seconds and a narrow QRS. It can be a normal variant or a sign of disease.

- Normal: an adaptive response in healthy people, particularly well-conditioned, active people such as athletes, during sleep, and in adults over age 65.
- Drugs: beta blockers (for example metoprolol), nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem) and digoxin. When a slow rate follows a newly started rate-slowing drug, that drug is the likely cause.
- Other causes: hypothyroidism, sinoatrial node ischemia (poor blood supply to the node), increased intracranial pressure and late-stage infection. Because hypothyroidism is on the list, a slow sinus rhythm in a patient who may be hypothyroid calls for thyroid function tests.

Most people with sinus bradycardia have no symptoms.

cards.t: Treating sinus bradycardia: observation, atropine, pacemaker
q: how do you treat sinus bradycardia
what is first line for unstable bradycardia
when does bradycardia need a pacemaker
cards.x:
Treatment follows the symptoms, not the number alone. Most people with sinus bradycardia have no symptoms, and an asymptomatic patient needs no treatment.

- Acute, symptomatic and hemodynamically unstable: atropine is first line. If atropine does not work, a temporary pacemaker follows.
- Chronic and symptomatic: a permanent pacemaker.

In a patient, instability usually shows as low blood pressure (hypotension) with confusion, drowsiness or fainting.

One trap: a patient who already has symptomatic bradycardia should not be started on another rate-slowing drug. Beta blockers, the nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem) and digoxin all slow the rate further.

cards.t: Sinus tachycardia: definition and causes
q: what is sinus tachycardia
what causes sinus tachycardia
how fast can sinus tachycardia go
when is sinus tachycardia normal
cards.x:
Sinus tachycardia is a regular sinus rhythm above 100, up to 160 beats per minute, with a uniform P wave for every QRS, a PR of 0.12 to 0.20 seconds and a narrow QRS. Above 160 the P waves are lost, and a regular narrow tachycardia is then called supraventricular tachycardia.

It is usually the heart responding to something else. It is the normal response to exercise and to conditions that release more catecholamines (stress hormones). Causes include:
- Physiologic: pain, anxiety.
- Pathologic: hypovolemia (low blood volume), hypotension or shock, anemia, hypoxia (low oxygen), pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction, hyperthyroidism.
- Drugs: stimulants and anticholinergics, and abrupt withdrawal of beta blockers or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers.

So for this appropriate kind you treat the cause, not the rate: treat the bleeding and replace the volume after blood loss, or treat the infection behind a fever. Physiologic sinus tachycardia usually comes with no symptoms such as dizziness or nausea.

cards.t: Appropriate versus inappropriate sinus tachycardia
q: what is inappropriate sinus tachycardia
how is inappropriate sinus tachycardia treated
what is the difference between appropriate and inappropriate sinus tachycardia
how do you treat sinus tachycardia
cards.x:
Appropriate sinus tachycardia has a reason: physiologic stress, an underlying illness or a medication effect. Inappropriate sinus tachycardia is a heart rate that stays high with no explanation after every secondary cause has been excluded. It is a diagnosis of exclusion, meaning you only reach it once everything else is ruled out.

The two are handled differently. For the appropriate kind, treat the underlying cause rather than the rate. For the inappropriate kind, first eliminate every influencing factor, including lifestyle (such as night shifts), illicit drugs and medications, and use behavioral therapy. Beta blockers are not well tolerated. It is generally left untreated, because patients tolerate the symptoms better than the treatment, and the prognosis is usually benign.

cards.t: Sick sinus syndrome: what it is and its three forms
q: what is sick sinus syndrome
what is the difference between sinus exit block and sinus arrest
what does sick sinus syndrome look like on an ECG
cards.x:
Sick sinus syndrome means the sinus node can no longer keep a reliable rhythm. On the strip the rhythm is irregular and the rate wanders through bradycardia, normal sinus rate and tachycardia up to 160. P waves are variable if present, with a shape that depends on whichever rhythm is running; the PR is variable and the QRS is narrow. An ambulatory monitor (a 24-hour tracing the patient wears) catches the pauses.

It comes in three forms:
- Sinus node exit block: the impulse is generated, but it cannot get out of the sinoatrial node.
- Sinus arrest: the impulse is not generated at all, which leads to a junctional rhythm (P waves inverted before or after the QRS, or not visible).
- Tachy-brady syndrome: a fast arrhythmia alternates with symptomatic bradycardia or with pauses.

Quick way to separate the first two: in exit block the beat is made but trapped; in sinus arrest it is never made.

cards.t: Tachy-brady syndrome
k: sick sinus syndrome with atrial fibrillation
q: what is tachy-brady syndrome
what is the most common fast rhythm in tachy-brady syndrome
how is tachy-brady syndrome treated
cards.x:
Tachy-brady syndrome is the form of sick sinus syndrome in which fast and slow rhythms take turns: a tachyarrhythmia (a fast abnormal rhythm) alternates with symptomatic bradycardia or with pauses. The fast rhythm is most commonly atrial fibrillation, so picture fast atrial runs that stop into a pause followed by slow beats.

Tachy-brady syndrome often needs a permanent pacemaker. If the fast rhythm is ventricular tachycardia instead, the patient needs a permanent pacemaker together with an implantable cardioverter defibrillator.

cards.t: Sick sinus syndrome: causes and management
q: what causes sick sinus syndrome
how is sick sinus syndrome treated
when does sick sinus syndrome need a pacemaker
cards.x:
Sick sinus syndrome has these causes:
- Sinoatrial node ischemia (poor blood supply to the node), or injury to the node from cardiac surgery.
- Electrolyte abnormalities and hypothyroidism.
- Medications: beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin.

Management starts with the underlying cause, for example stopping the rate-slowing drugs. Then the key question is whether the symptoms line up with the episodes of bradycardia. If symptoms do not correlate with the bradycardia, observation is appropriate. If the bradycardia is symptomatic, a permanent pacemaker is placed. The tachy-brady form often needs a permanent pacemaker, plus an implantable cardioverter defibrillator if the fast rhythm is ventricular tachycardia.

cards.t: Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT): the umbrella term
q: what is supraventricular tachycardia
which rhythms count as SVT
is SVT narrow or wide
what does SVT look like on an ECG
cards.x:
Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) is a blanket term for any fast abnormal rhythm arising above the level of the bundle of His (the atrioventricular bundle). Under the umbrella sit sinus tachycardia, focal and multifocal atrial tachycardia, the reentry tachycardias (atrioventricular nodal reentry and accessory pathway reentry), atrial flutter and atrial fibrillation. Ventricular tachycardia arises below the bundle of His, so it is not an SVT.

By definition, SVTs are narrow QRS complex tachycardias (under 0.12 seconds). Most are regular; atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular, and flutter with variable conduction and multifocal atrial tachycardia are irregular too.

The classic regular SVT strip: regular, above 160, P waves and PR hidden if present, and a narrow QRS. The one exception to the narrow rule is antidromic accessory pathway reentry, which is wide.

cards.t: Supraventricular tachycardia: symptoms and when it causes collapse
q: what are the symptoms of SVT
does supraventricular tachycardia cause fainting
when is supraventricular tachycardia dangerous

cards.t: Treating stable supraventricular tachycardia: vagal maneuver, then adenosine
q: what is first line for stable SVT
what does adenosine do in SVT
how many times can you give adenosine
how do you treat supraventricular tachycardia
cards.x:
For a stable patient with supraventricular tachycardia, the order is a vagal maneuver first, before any drug, then adenosine if the vagal maneuver fails. Adenosine may be given twice as needed.

Adenosine helps in one of two ways. It may convert the rhythm back to normal sinus rhythm. Or it may at least slow the rate enough that you can see whether P waves are there: at these speeds the atrial activity is hidden, and slowing things down unmasks it, which helps name the rhythm.

A stable patient gets no shock at all. Only a hemodynamically unstable patient, the less common situation, goes straight to immediate synchronized cardioversion.

cards.t: Synchronized cardioversion versus defibrillation
q: what is synchronized cardioversion
what is the difference between cardioversion and defibrillation
how do you treat unstable SVT
cards.x:
Synchronized cardioversion is a timed shock at decreased voltage, delivered in step with the patient's own heartbeat. It is the immediate treatment for hemodynamically unstable supraventricular tachycardia, which is the less common situation.

Defibrillation is something else: an unsynchronized shock for a patient without a pulse. It has no place in a stable supraventricular tachycardia, which gets a vagal maneuver and adenosine and no shock at all.

Quick way to keep them apart: synchronized cardioversion is for a patient who has a pulse but is unstable, so the shock is timed and lower in voltage; defibrillation is for a patient with no pulse, and it is not timed.

cards.t: Focal versus multifocal atrial tachycardia
q: what is the difference between focal and multifocal atrial tachycardia
how many P wave shapes are in multifocal atrial tachycardia
is multifocal atrial tachycardia regular
cards.x:
Both are fast rhythms started by spots in the atria outside the sinoatrial node, both are typically paroxysmal (they come and go), and both run above 100, usually 150 to 250, with a narrow QRS and one P wave for every QRS. The difference is how many spots are firing, and you read that from the P waves.

- Focal atrial tachycardia: a single ectopic focus (one out-of-place spot). Every P wave has the same abnormal shape, and the rhythm is regular.
- Multifocal atrial tachycardia: multiple foci. At least three distinct P-wave shapes in the same lead, and the rhythm is irregular.

Picture one drummer keeping a steady beat versus several drummers taking turns: one drummer gives one sound and an even rhythm, several give different sounds and an uneven one.

cards.t: Focal atrial tachycardia and the adenosine clue
k: atrial tachycardia not stopped by adenosine
q: what is focal atrial tachycardia
why is adenosine diagnostic in focal atrial tachycardia
who gets focal atrial tachycardia
cards.x:
Focal atrial tachycardia is a regular fast rhythm driven by one ectopic spot in the atria outside the sinoatrial node, so every P wave has the same abnormal shape. It is commonly seen in people without heart disease, in the setting of increased metabolic demand, much like the causes of sinus tachycardia. Most people report abrupt-onset palpitations, and it is generally a benign arrhythmia.

Adenosine is an important diagnostic tool here. It is usually less effective at stopping focal atrial tachycardia than at stopping the reentry tachycardias that depend on the atrioventricular node. So if a rhythm with abnormal P waves carries on after adenosine, that points to focal atrial tachycardia.

cards.t: Treating focal atrial tachycardia
q: how is focal atrial tachycardia treated
can focal atrial tachycardia be cured
what is the long-term treatment for focal atrial tachycardia
cards.x:
Treatment of focal atrial tachycardia follows how unstable the patient is and how long the problem has lasted.
- Unstable: synchronized cardioversion (a timed shock).
- Hemodynamically stable and symptomatic: an intravenous beta blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, while the underlying cause and precipitating factors are identified and treated.
- Chronic: an oral beta blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker as initial therapy. Catheter ablation is usually curative (90%).

Chemical cardioversion, which uses a drug instead of a shock to restore the rhythm, may be tried with amiodarone.

cards.t: Multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT)
q: what is multifocal atrial tachycardia
what causes multifocal atrial tachycardia
how do you treat multifocal atrial tachycardia
cards.x:
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is an irregular fast rhythm driven by several spots in the atria, so the P waves keep changing shape: at least three distinct shapes in the same lead, with one P wave for every narrow QRS.

It is usually due to severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or heart failure, with or without respiratory failure, typically when these patients are acutely ill, with right heart stress or pulmonary hypertension. Most people have no symptoms directly caused by the rhythm, but it is a poor prognostic sign, meaning the outlook is worse.

Management is to treat the underlying condition, for example the flare of lung disease. In hospital a beta blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker may be added, but not for long-term use.

Quick contrast: focal atrial tachycardia is generally benign and often seen without heart disease; multifocal is the one in acutely ill lungs and hearts.

cards.t: Atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia (AVRT): accessory pathway reentry
q: what is AVRT
how does an accessory pathway cause tachycardia
what does AVRT look like on an ECG
cards.x:
Atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia (AVRT) is a fast rhythm in a patient with an accessory pathway, an extra connection that lets the atria reach the ventricles, as in Wolff-Parkinson-White. The impulse runs in a loop that uses both the atrioventricular node and the pathway: down one, back up the other. Picture a two-lane racetrack joined at both ends; once a signal starts lapping, it keeps going round.

The loop can turn either way. Orthodromic is more common than antidromic. Patients most commonly present with palpitations.

On the strip the rhythm is regular, above 100 but usually 200 to 300, with P waves hidden or retrograde, a PR that is hidden or short, and usually a narrow QRS under 0.12 seconds (the antidromic kind is the wide exception).

cards.t: Wolff-Parkinson-White: pre-excitation, the delta wave and the bundle of Kent
q: what is Wolff-Parkinson-White
what is a delta wave
what is the accessory pathway called
when can you see a delta wave

cards.t: Orthodromic versus antidromic reentrant tachycardia
q: what is the difference between orthodromic and antidromic AVRT
which AVRT is wide complex
which is more common, orthodromic or antidromic
where is the P wave in orthodromic tachycardia
cards.x:
Both are loops through the atrioventricular node and an accessory pathway. They differ only in which way the loop turns, and that decides what the QRS looks like.

- Orthodromic (more common): down (antegrade) through the atrioventricular node, back up the pathway. The result is a regular, narrow complex tachycardia with no delta wave, and a retrograde (inverted) P wave just after each QRS.
- Antidromic: down the pathway, back (retrograde) through the node. The QRS is wide, with a delta wave. P waves are rarely seen; if visible, they are retrograde and just before the QRS.

Memory hook: orthodromic goes down the normal route, the node, and keeps a normal, narrow QRS. Antidromic goes the other way, down the pathway, and comes out wide.

cards.t: Treating accessory pathway tachycardia: adenosine, procainamide, ablation
q: how do you treat AVRT
why is adenosine dangerous in Wolff-Parkinson-White
what is the treatment for atrial fibrillation with WPW
what is the long-term treatment for Wolff-Parkinson-White
cards.x:
For orthodromic atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia, start as for any stable supraventricular tachycardia: a vagal maneuver, then adenosine, which is first line.

The danger is atrial fibrillation in a patient with Wolff-Parkinson-White. Think of the node and the accessory pathway as two roads into the ventricles. Adenosine blocks the normal road, the atrioventricular node, which leaves the accessory pathway unopposed to carry the fibrillation through. So atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White is treated with intravenous procainamide, and adenosine must never be used. The same switch applies if adenosine slows a rhythm and reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White: give intravenous procainamide, not adenosine.

For the long term, catheter ablation of the accessory pathway is the first-line treatment of Wolff-Parkinson-White.

cards.t: Pre-excited atrial fibrillation (atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White)
q: what is pre-excited atrial fibrillation
how do you tell atrial fibrillation with WPW from ventricular tachycardia
what is the most dangerous rhythm in Wolff-Parkinson-White
cards.x:
Pre-excited atrial fibrillation is atrial fibrillation conducting down an accessory pathway. It produces an irregular, very fast, wide-complex tachycardia, with QRS complexes that vary in shape. For a patient with Wolff-Parkinson-White this is the most dangerous rhythm: rates above 200 are what cause syncope or collapse, and here the rates can approach 300.

Because it is fast and wide, it can look like ventricular tachycardia. Quick way to tell them apart:
- Ventricular tachycardia: regular, 150 to 200 beats per minute.
- Atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White: irregular, with some rates approaching 300.

Treatment is intravenous procainamide; adenosine must never be used, because blocking the node leaves the pathway unopposed to conduct the fibrillation.

cards.t: Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT) and the frog sign
q: what is AVNRT
what is the frog sign
who gets AVNRT
what is the difference between AVNRT and AVRT
cards.x:
Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT) is a reentry circuit within the atrioventricular node itself. It is typically paroxysmal (it comes in sudden episodes), and the slow-fast (typical) type is the most common. On the strip it is regular, usually 140 to 180, with P waves and PR hidden and a narrow QRS under 0.12 seconds.

Women are affected far more than men. It is commonly seen without heart disease and may occur spontaneously or with exertion, caffeine, alcohol, beta-agonists or sympathomimetics. Patients typically complain of sudden-onset palpitations and “neck pulsations”, seen on examination as the frog sign.

Quick contrast with atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia: that loop needs an accessory pathway as well as the node, while this circuit sits entirely within the node.

cards.t: Treating AVNRT: vagal maneuvers, adenosine, pill in the pocket, ablation
q: how is AVNRT treated
what is pill in the pocket
can AVNRT be cured
does AVNRT need urgent care
cards.x:
Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia almost always stops with vagal maneuvers or adenosine. Synchronized cardioversion is rarely required, and episodes are usually well tolerated.

That makes self-management realistic:
- If a patient who has been educated ends an episode at home with a vagal maneuver, urgent medical attention is usually not required.
- “Pill in the pocket” is an option: a beta blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker taken when an episode starts.
- Counseling: caffeine, alcohol and sympathomimetics can set it off, so a patient whose episodes follow them is advised to limit those triggers.

For a select subset of patients, catheter ablation offers a definitive cure (over 95%).

cards.t: Atrial flutter: sawtooth waves, 2:1 block and 1:1 danger
q: what is atrial flutter
what does atrial flutter look like on an ECG
what is the most common conduction ratio in atrial flutter
why is 1:1 atrial flutter dangerous
cards.x:
Atrial flutter is a fast atrial rhythm with an atrial rate of 250 or greater that can approach 300, seen as sawtooth (flutter) waves. There are more flutter waves than QRS complexes: when the atrioventricular node blocks one of every two atrial impulses, the result is 2:1 block, the most common ratio, and 3:1 and 4:1 are also seen. The rhythm is regular and the QRS narrow.

It is commonly seen with atrial scarring or damage (for example after surgery), right-sided heart failure or pulmonary vascular disease, and in patients with atrial fibrillation who are taking an antiarrhythmic. Symptoms are a rapid heart rate, palpitations, chest pain, dyspnea (shortness of breath), dizziness and fatigue. It is usually not directly life-threatening, with generally no hemodynamic collapse or syncope.

The exception is 1:1 atrial flutter, where every atrial impulse gets through: it causes extreme hemodynamic instability and carries a big risk of progressing to ventricular fibrillation.

cards.t: Treating atrial flutter
q: how is atrial flutter treated
is atrial flutter hard to rate control
what is the definitive treatment for atrial flutter
does atrial flutter need anticoagulation
cards.x:
Atrial flutter is managed by stability first:
- Hemodynamically unstable: synchronized cardioversion.
- Hemodynamically stable: rate control with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker.

Rate control is harder to achieve in atrial flutter than in atrial fibrillation, and flutter has a substantial recurrence rate. Ablation is the definitive management.

Anticoagulation is part of flutter management too: outpatient cardioversion is done after 21 days of anticoagulation.

cards.t: Atrial fibrillation: the strip, risk factors and emergencies
q: what is atrial fibrillation
what does atrial fibrillation look like on an ECG
what are the risk factors for atrial fibrillation
when is atrial fibrillation an emergency
cards.x:
Atrial fibrillation is an irregularly irregular rhythm: absent P waves, no PR interval, and beats that follow no pattern. The rate is usually 110 to 160 (it can be under 80 or over 200), and the QRS is narrow.

It is commonly seen with hypertension, diabetes, cardiac disease, a family history of atrial fibrillation, obesity, sleep apnea and excessive alcohol, and in the elderly: older age raises the risk.

Symptoms are a rapid heart rate, palpitations, chest pain, dyspnea (shortness of breath), dizziness and fatigue, and it is usually not directly life-threatening. It becomes a medical emergency with severe heart failure (pulmonary edema, hypotension) or when it occurs in the setting of an acute myocardial infarction.

cards.t: Types of atrial fibrillation: paroxysmal, persistent, long-standing, permanent
q: what is the difference between paroxysmal and persistent atrial fibrillation
how long does persistent atrial fibrillation last
what is permanent atrial fibrillation
cards.x:
Atrial fibrillation is classified by how long it lasts, and in one case by a decision rather than a time:
- Paroxysmal: lasts less than 1 week and usually ends without treatment.
- Persistent: continuous for more than 7 days but less than 1 year; it needs treatment.
- Long-standing persistent: continuous for more than 1 year.
- Permanent: the patient and clinician make a joint decision to stop further attempts to restore or maintain sinus rhythm.

The one that trips people up is permanent: it is defined by that shared decision, not by a length of time.

cards.t: Managing atrial fibrillation: rate control first
q: how do you treat atrial fibrillation
what is the first goal in stable atrial fibrillation
how do you treat atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
when can you cardiovert atrial fibrillation
cards.x:
Treatment depends on stability and on how fast the ventricles are being driven:
- Hemodynamically unstable: synchronized cardioversion.
- Stable but in rapid ventricular response (the ventricles racing): intravenous rate control.
- Stable without rapid ventricular response: rate control by mouth.

In stable atrial fibrillation, controlling the rate is the first goal, not converting the rhythm. Anticoagulation is guided by stroke risk, and the rhythm is restored only electively, later: outpatient cardioversion after 21 days of anticoagulation. Mapping and ablation are also part of management.

Think of the order as rate first, clot protection next, rhythm last.

cards.t: Anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation: stroke risk score and drug choice
q: why do patients with atrial fibrillation need anticoagulation
what CHA2DS2-VASc score needs anticoagulation
what is the bleeding risk score for anticoagulation
what is the INR goal for warfarin in atrial fibrillation
cards.x:
Anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation is there to prevent stroke from a clot. The CHA2DS2-VASc score (a stroke-risk score) assesses that risk. A score of 0 in a man or 1 in a woman is low risk and may not require anticoagulation. Patients above that typically require anticoagulation unless their bleeding risk is high.

Bleeding risk has its own score, which estimates the risk of major bleeding on anticoagulation. A high bleeding score flags bleeding risks to correct and calls for closer review.

For the drug:
- Direct oral anticoagulants are preferred in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation: dabigatran, apixaban, edoxaban or rivaroxaban.
- If warfarin is used, the target international normalized ratio is 2 to 3.

cards.t: Premature beats: atrial, junctional and ventricular, plus bigeminy and trigeminy
q: what are premature beats
how do you tell a PAC from a PJC from a PVC
what is bigeminy
what is trigeminy
cards.x:
A premature beat is an early beat that starts somewhere in the heart other than the sinoatrial node. It is named by where it starts, and each origin leaves its own fingerprint on the strip:
- Premature atrial contraction: begins in the atria, so it shows an early, abnormally shaped P wave.
- Premature junctional contraction: begins in the atrioventricular junction, giving an early, narrow QRS (usually 0.10 seconds or less) with an inverted P wave, a P wave buried in the QRS (no P visible), or a P wave after the QRS.
- Premature ventricular contraction: begins in the ventricles, giving an early, wide, “bizarre” QRS with no P wave.

When every other beat is an early beat, the pattern is bigeminy; when every third beat is, it is trigeminy.

cards.t: Premature atrial contractions (PACs)
q: what is a premature atrial contraction
what causes PACs
how do you treat premature atrial contractions
are PACs dangerous
cards.x:
A premature atrial contraction (PAC) is an early beat from the atria. On the strip the rhythm is regular apart from the early beat, at 60 to 100, and the early P wave has a different shape; there is still one P wave for each QRS, a PR of 0.12 to 0.20 seconds and a narrow QRS.

PACs are common in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and may happen in normal hearts with excessive alcohol, stress or caffeine. In patients with heart disease they may precede paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter.

Most people have no symptoms and need no treatment: counsel them to avoid potential triggers and reassure them the rhythm is benign. If PACs are frequent, look for underlying structural heart disease. If they are persistent and symptomatic, use a beta blocker (metoprolol) if not contraindicated, or catheter ablation if the PACs are frequent or are triggering atrial fibrillation.

cards.t: Premature junctional contractions (PJCs) and where the P wave sits
q: what is a premature junctional contraction
why is the P wave in different places in junctional beats
how do you treat PJCs
where is the P wave in a junctional beat
cards.x:
A premature junctional contraction (PJC) is an early beat from the atrioventricular node area. Where in the node the beat starts decides where the P wave sits, because it decides which chambers fire first:
- From the top: the atria beat first (short PR).
- From the middle: atria and ventricles beat together, so the P wave is buried in the QRS.
- From the bottom: the ventricles beat first, so a retrograde P wave follows the QRS.

The P waves are inverted in leads II, III and aVF, the PR of the early beat is short (under 0.12) or nonexistent, and the QRS is narrow.

Most people have no symptoms. If they are infrequent and cause no symptoms, no treatment is needed and reassurance is often enough. If they are frequent (more than 10 per minute, or multifocal), look for structural heart disease and treat with a beta blocker; persistent symptoms also call for a beta blocker (metoprolol) if not contraindicated.

cards.t: Junctional rhythm: features, causes and management
q: what is a junctional rhythm
what causes a junctional rhythm
how is junctional rhythm treated
when does a junctional rhythm need a pacemaker
cards.x:
A junctional rhythm is a regular rhythm from the atrioventricular junction, usually at 40 to 60 beats per minute, with P waves inverted in II, III and aVF (before, buried in or after the QRS), a short (under 0.12) or nonexistent PR, and a narrow QRS. It is generally well tolerated.

Causes: sinoatrial node dysfunction (for example sick sinus syndrome) or significant bradycardia, inferior myocardial infarction, the acute period after cardiac surgery, and digoxin toxicity. It can also be seen in healthy people with increased vagal tone, such as well-conditioned athletes.

Management depends on the cause:
- Asymptomatic in an otherwise healthy person: no treatment.
- Due to complete or high-grade atrioventricular block, or to sick sinus syndrome: a permanent pacemaker.
- Due to digitalis (digoxin) toxicity: atropine and/or digoxin immune Fab.

cards.t: Supraventricular rhythms in older adults
q: what arrhythmias are common in older adults
what should you check first in an elderly patient with new bradycardia
how does age affect atrial fibrillation risk
cards.x:
Age changes how several of these rhythms show up:
- Sinus bradycardia is common in adults over 65.
- In an older adult with new symptomatic bradycardia, review the medication list first: beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin cause sinus bradycardia and sick sinus syndrome.
- Supraventricular tachycardia symptoms may be more pronounced in the elderly, as they may be in structural heart disease.
- Older age raises the risk of atrial fibrillation, so stroke risk (the CHA2DS2-VASc score) is weighed against bleeding risk when deciding on anticoagulation.
- Chronic symptomatic bradycardia and symptomatic sick sinus syndrome are treated with a permanent pacemaker.

cards.t: Atrioventricular (heart) block: the four degrees compared
k: first second and third degree block
q: what are the types of AV block
how do the degrees of heart block differ
how do I tell Mobitz type I from Mobitz type II
cards.x:
An atrioventricular (AV) block is a delay or failure of the signal passing from the atria (the upper chambers) down to the ventricles (the lower chambers). The four degrees are told apart by two questions: what does the PR interval do, and do any QRS complexes drop?
- First degree: the PR is longer than 0.20 seconds and constant, and no beat ever drops.
- Mobitz type I (Wenckebach): the PR lengthens beat by beat until a QRS drops, then the cycle repeats.
- Mobitz type II: the PR stays constant at 0.12–0.20 seconds and a QRS drops at random.
- Third degree (complete): no P wave is conducted at all, so the atria and ventricles run as two separate regular rhythms; the ventricular rate is usually below 40 per minute and the QRS may be narrow or wide.

In the first three the rate is 60–100 and the QRS is narrow (below 0.12 seconds). The single feature that separates the two Mobitz types is whether the PR lengthens before the dropped beat.

cards.t: Lyme carditis and other causes shared by the heart blocks
q: can Lyme disease cause heart block
which heart blocks does Lyme carditis cause
what causes show up across all the AV blocks
cards.x:
Lyme disease, through Lyme carditis (the Lyme infection inflaming the heart), is a named cause of every degree of atrioventricular block: first-degree block, both kinds of second-degree block (Mobitz type I and Mobitz type II) and complete (third-degree) block. It sits on all four cause lists, which makes it an easy one to remember.

Two other causes also recur on more than one of those lists: ischemia of the atrioventricular node or ischemic heart disease, especially a myocardial infarction (heart attack), and cardiac ablation.

cards.t: First-degree atrioventricular block
q: what is first degree heart block
what does first degree AV block look like on an ECG
what causes first degree heart block
does first degree heart block need treatment
cards.x:
First-degree atrioventricular block is simply a prolonged PR interval: longer than 0.20 seconds and the same length every beat. Every P wave is still conducted, so there is one P wave for every QRS, no beat ever drops, the rhythm is regular at 60–100 and the QRS is narrow (below 0.12 seconds). Think of a slow toll booth: every car gets through, each one just waits a little longer.

The vast majority of patients have no symptoms; symptoms usually appear once the PR is longer than 0.3 seconds (fatigue, shortness of breath, palpitations, chest pain). The most common cause is age-related wear of the conduction system. Others are increased vagal tone from an overreactive vagus nerve; beta blockers, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin; hypokalemia (low potassium); ischemia of the atrioventricular node, usually after a myocardial infarction (heart attack); chronic hypertension; and Lyme disease. No treatment is needed unless there are debilitating or heart failure symptoms, and a permanent pacemaker is considered for symptomatic patients.

cards.t: Second-degree block, Mobitz type I (Wenckebach)
q: what is Wenckebach
what does Mobitz type 1 look like on an ECG
what causes Mobitz type I
does Wenckebach need a pacemaker
cards.x:
Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) is a second-degree block in which some, but not all, P waves reach the ventricles. The PR interval stretches a little more with each beat until one P wave is not followed by a QRS complex (the dropped beat); then the cycle repeats. The QRS is narrow, the P waves are uniform and outnumber the QRS complexes, and the rate is 60–100.

It is usually asymptomatic; when symptoms occur they are dizziness, fatigue, exertional intolerance and syncope (fainting). Causes: increased vagal tone; rate-slowing atrioventricular nodal blocking drugs (beta blockers, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, digoxin); Lyme carditis; ischemia of the atrioventricular node, usually after a myocardial infarction (heart attack); and cardiac ablation. No treatment is needed unless symptoms are debilitating or from heart failure. A permanent pacemaker is considered for symptomatic patients: symptoms such as fainting, not the dropped beats themselves, make someone a pacemaker candidate.

cards.t: Second-degree block, Mobitz type II
k: type II second degree AV block
q: what is Mobitz type 2
what does Mobitz II look like on an ECG
how is Mobitz II different from Wenckebach
cards.x:
Mobitz type II is a second-degree block with a constant PR interval and QRS complexes that drop at random. The PR stays the same, 0.12–0.20 seconds, beat after beat, and there is no PR lengthening before a dropped beat: a P wave arrives right on schedule and simply has no QRS after it.

The rhythm looks regular apart from those random gaps, the P waves outnumber the QRS complexes, and the QRS is narrow. Quick way to tell it from Mobitz type I (Wenckebach): the PR never stretches before the drop, so the dropped beat comes with no warning.

cards.t: Mobitz type II: causes, symptoms and Stokes-Adams attacks
q: what causes Mobitz type II
what is a Stokes-Adams attack
what symptoms does Mobitz II cause
cards.x:
The most common cause of Mobitz type II is acquired disease of the His-Purkinje system (part of the heart's conduction wiring), especially degenerative changes from old age, chronic hypertension and diabetes. Other causes are Lyme carditis; inflammatory disease such as myocarditis and reactive arthritis; ischemic heart disease, especially myocardial infarction (heart attack); and ablation.

Symptoms come from the slow heart rate (bradycardia) and reduced cardiac output: exertional intolerance, fatigue, dizziness, presyncope (nearly fainting) and syncope (fainting). Mobitz type II can also lead to a Stokes-Adams attack, a sudden fainting spell or seizure from a rapid, temporary drop in blood flow to the brain.

cards.t: Why Mobitz type II is dangerous, and why it gets a pacemaker
q: why is Mobitz type 2 dangerous
what is the treatment for Mobitz II
does asymptomatic Mobitz II need a pacemaker
cards.x:
Mobitz type II is dangerous because it carries a higher risk of progressing to complete (third-degree) heart block and of sudden cardiac death. It usually originates at the bundle of His, so the backup escape rhythm that would take over is weak and unreliable. Because its progression is unpredictable and the prognosis poor, American College of Cardiology and American Heart Association guidelines treat it as dangerous even without symptoms.

Treatment has two steps: emergently, transcutaneous pacing (pacing through the skin); definitively, a permanent pacemaker. So even an asymptomatic Mobitz type II block is referred for a permanent pacemaker, and simply watching it without pacing is the approach to avoid.

cards.t: Third-degree (complete) heart block
q: what is complete heart block
what does third degree heart block look like on an ECG
what is AV dissociation
cards.x:
In third-degree (complete) block, no P waves get through to the ventricles at all. The atria and ventricles are completely dissociated: each runs its own regular rhythm at its own rate and ignores the other. Picture two drummers in separate rooms, each keeping steady time with no idea what the other is doing.

On the tracing, the ventricular rate is usually below 40 per minute. The P waves are uniform but have no relationship to the QRS complexes, and they may even be buried in a QRS complex, ST segment or T wave. Because the two rhythms are unrelated, the PR interval is random, and the QRS may be narrow or wide.

cards.t: Complete heart block: symptoms, syncope and treatment
q: what symptoms does complete heart block cause
why is syncope important in complete heart block
how do you treat third degree heart block
cards.x:
Symptoms in complete block range from none to severe. How bad they are depends on the ventricular escape rate (the backup rhythm the ventricles fall back on), where that escape rhythm starts, and whether there is underlying heart disease. They include presyncope, syncope, dizziness, exertional intolerance, heart failure symptoms, altered mental status and sudden cardiac arrest.

Syncope (fainting) is a particularly important symptom, because it is associated with an increased risk of sudden death. Treatment: emergent transcutaneous pacing (pacing through the skin) is the immediate measure, and once that has stabilized the patient, the definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker.

cards.t: Causes of complete heart block, including Chagas disease
k: causes of third degree heart block
q: what causes complete heart block
can Chagas disease cause heart block
how can endocarditis cause heart block
cards.x:
The most common cause of complete heart block is acquired disease of the cardiac conduction system, especially degenerative changes from old age, chronic hypertension and diabetes. The other named causes:
- Chagas disease, a parasitic infection.
- Lyme carditis.
- Bacterial endocarditis with an associated abscess: an abscess beside the valve (a perivalvular abscess) that reaches the conduction tissue.
- Inflammatory and infiltrative disease: myocarditis, amyloidosis and sarcoidosis (granulomatous infiltration of the heart).

cards.t: Naming the waves of the QRS complex (Q, R, R-prime, S)
k: Q wave R wave S wave
q: how do you name the QRS waves
what is an R prime
what is the difference between a Q wave and an S wave
cards.x:
The waves inside a QRS complex are named by their direction and their order. If the very first wave points down (negative), it is a Q wave. Every wave that points up (positive) is an R wave: the first is R, and a second one is R-prime, written R'. Any downward wave that comes after an upward wave is an S wave.

So a Q wave and an S wave are both negative; what separates them is position. A negative wave before any R is a Q; a negative wave after an R is an S.

cards.t: Bundle branch blocks and fascicular blocks (intraventricular delays)
q: what is a bundle branch block
what is a fascicular block
how wide is the QRS in a bundle branch block
cards.x:
Intraventricular delays are a complete or partial interruption of conduction in the wiring that carries the signal through the ventricles. A block in the left or right bundle branch is a bundle branch block. The left bundle branch divides into an anterior and a posterior fascicle, and a block in one of those is a fascicular block.

The rest of the tracing looks normal: a regular rhythm at 60–100, one P wave for each QRS, and a constant PR of 0.12–0.20 seconds. What changes is the QRS, which is wide: a complete bundle branch block widens it to 0.12 seconds or more.

cards.t: Left bundle branch block: what happens and how it looks
q: what does left bundle branch block look like on an ECG
how do you recognize LBBB
what happens in left bundle branch block
cards.x:
In left bundle branch block, conduction through the left bundle is delayed, so the left ventricle is not activated through its own branch. Instead, it is activated by electricity crossing the septum from the right side of the heart.

What to look for on the electrocardiogram:
- A wide QRS, 0.12 seconds or more.
- A dominant S wave in V1 (an rS pattern).
- A prolonged R wave peak, over 0.06.
- A broad, monophasic R in the lateral leads.
- Absent Q waves in leads I, V5 and V6.

cards.t: Left bundle branch block: causes, symptoms, treatment and a new block
q: what causes left bundle branch block
what does a new left bundle branch block mean
how is LBBB treated
what does it mean if LBBB causes symptoms
cards.x:
Causes of left bundle branch block: chronic hypertension; chronic ischemic heart disease and severe coronary artery disease; dilated non-ischemic cardiomyopathy; valvular heart disease, with aortic stenosis singled out; and Lenègre–Lev disease, a degenerative, fibrotic disease of the conduction system.

Patients are usually asymptomatic. One who develops symptoms usually has severe underlying heart disease and does not tolerate the block well; the symptoms resemble a heart failure flare (dizziness, shortness of breath, breathlessness on exertion). Prognosis depends on the type and severity of that underlying disease and on any other conduction disturbances. The block is usually left untreated, except that symptomatic left bundle branch block with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction gets a biventricular pacemaker. A new left bundle branch block should always be considered a sign of pathology, so the patient is evaluated for underlying heart disease.

cards.t: Right bundle branch block: what happens and how it looks
q: what does right bundle branch block look like on an ECG
what are bunny ears on an ECG
why is the QRS wide in right bundle branch block
cards.x:
In right bundle branch block the left side works normally: the left ventricle is activated through the left bundle branch, and the septum depolarizes normally via the left bundle too. The right ventricle has to be activated by electricity crossing the septum instead, which takes longer and widens the QRS.

What to look for:
- An rsR' pattern, nicknamed bunny ears, in V1, V2 and V3, the right-sided chest leads, where the delay shows best.
- A slurred S wave in leads I and aVL.

cards.t: Right bundle branch block: causes, symptoms and treatment
k: pulmonary embolism right bundle branch block
q: what causes right bundle branch block
is a new right bundle branch block dangerous
how is RBBB treated
cards.x:
Causes of right bundle branch block include age-related degeneration of the conduction system; chronic ischemic heart disease; pulmonary hypertension; a sudden rise in right ventricular pressure, such as a pulmonary embolism; cardiac ischemia; dilated or hypertrophic cardiomyopathies; and inflammatory or infiltrative heart disease such as myocarditis and amyloidosis.

Most patients are asymptomatic. When it does cause symptoms, it usually points to severe underlying heart disease, and the symptoms resemble a heart failure flare (dizziness, shortness of breath, breathlessness on exertion) or worsening cardiomyopathy. Prognosis depends on whether there is underlying heart disease and what type, and treatment means treating any underlying condition. A new right bundle branch block is not always pathological: it can occur in a patient with no apparent heart disease.

cards.t: Premature beats (atrial, junctional, ventricular), bigeminy and trigeminy
q: what is a PVC
what is the difference between a PAC and a PVC
what is ventricular bigeminy
what is a premature junctional contraction
cards.x:
Premature (early) beats are extra beats that start somewhere other than the sinoatrial node, the heart's normal pacemaker, and they are named by where they start:
- Premature atrial contraction (from the atria): an early, abnormally shaped P wave.
- Premature junctional contraction (from the atrioventricular junction): an early, narrow QRS, usually 0.10 seconds or less, with a P wave that is inverted, buried in the QRS or after it.
- Premature ventricular contraction (from the ventricles): an early, wide and bizarre QRS (over 0.12 seconds) with no P wave; the rhythm is otherwise regular.

When ventricular beats fall into a fixed pattern they get their own names: in ventricular bigeminy every other beat is ectopic (an early beat from the wrong place), and in trigeminy every third beat is.

cards.t: Premature ventricular contractions: causes and what to check first
q: what causes PVCs
what should I check first in a patient with frequent PVCs
what triggers premature ventricular contractions
what symptoms do PVCs cause
cards.x:
The main causes to look for behind premature ventricular contractions are hypoxemia (low oxygen in the blood) and electrolyte imbalances: hypokalemia (low potassium), hypomagnesemia (low magnesium) and hypercalcemia (high calcium). So with frequent ones, the first moves are to check oxygenation (a blood gas) and the electrolytes, potassium and magnesium, and to correct the hypoxemia.

They occur in people with or without structural heart disease, and alcohol, caffeine and stimulants are triggers. Most patients have no symptoms; when there is one, it is palpitations, often felt in the neck.

cards.t: Managing premature ventricular contractions by risk and burden
q: how are PVCs treated
when do PVCs need ablation
what makes PVCs high risk
what is PVC burden
cards.x:
Treatment is sorted into three groups by risk and burden (the share of all heartbeats that are premature ventricular contractions):
- Low risk, low burden (under 1% of beats, or 1,000 a day), no structural heart disease and no symptoms: reassurance and removing triggers (cut alcohol, caffeine and stimulants).
- Low risk with symptoms: a beta blocker is first-line; catheter ablation if symptoms are refractory or the patient cannot tolerate the drug.
- High risk: a burden over 15% of beats (or 15,000 a day), cardiomyopathy caused by the premature beats, pre-existing structural or electrical conduction disease, or a history of syncope. The first step is a beta blocker plus optimizing treatment of the underlying heart disease, but isolated premature beat-induced cardiomyopathy with heart failure symptoms goes to catheter ablation.

cards.t: Sudden cardiac death and the four cardiac arrest rhythms
q: what is sudden cardiac death
what are the four rhythms of cardiac arrest
what is the most common predisposing condition for sudden cardiac death
cards.x:
Sudden cardiac death is an unexpected natural death from a cardiac cause within one hour of the person collapsing. Four rhythms cause cardiac arrest: ventricular fibrillation, pulseless ventricular tachycardia, pulseless electrical activity, and ventricular standstill (asystole).

The most common predisposing condition is coronary artery disease, and that holds even for someone who has never had a myocardial infarction (heart attack). So coronary artery disease alone raises the risk; a past heart attack is not required.

cards.t: Implantable cardioverter defibrillator and the wearable vest
k: secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death
q: what does an implantable cardioverter defibrillator do
who needs an ICD after ventricular tachycardia
what is a LifeVest
cards.x:
An implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) prevents sudden cardiac death from arrhythmias. Its sensing electrodes detect a fatal arrhythmia and the device delivers a shock. Newer devices can also act as pacemakers. Think of it as a smoke detector wired to its own sprinkler: always watching, and acting only when the dangerous rhythm appears.

There is also a wearable, external cardioverter defibrillator worn as a vest (LifeVest) that detects and shocks a fatal ventricular rhythm. After unstable or pulseless ventricular tachycardia, once the patient is stabilized, most need an implantable defibrillator for secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death (protection for someone who has already had a dangerous rhythm).

cards.t: Ventricular tachycardia: definition and ECG features
q: what is ventricular tachycardia
what does VT look like on an ECG
how many PVCs in a row make ventricular tachycardia
cards.x:
Ventricular tachycardia is three or more premature ventricular contractions in a row: a run of early beats that start in the ventricles. On the tracing it is a regular rhythm at 100–250 per minute with wide QRS complexes (over 0.12 seconds), no PR interval, and no P wave tied to the QRS.

It is then sorted two ways: by how long it lasts (non-sustained or sustained) and by QRS shape (monomorphic, all the same, or polymorphic, varying). A recognizable picture is sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, often seen after a myocardial infarction (heart attack): a regular wide-QRS rhythm of 100 to 250 per minute with identical complexes lasting over 30 seconds.

cards.t: Sustained versus non-sustained ventricular tachycardia
q: what is the difference between sustained and non-sustained VT
how long does VT have to last to be sustained
is a short run of VT that causes collapse sustained
cards.x:
Ventricular tachycardia is split by how long it lasts. Non-sustained ventricular tachycardia lasts under 30 seconds. Sustained ventricular tachycardia lasts 30 seconds or more, or causes hemodynamic collapse (the circulation fails) in under 30 seconds.
