That second clause is the trap. A run that collapses the patient is sustained however short it is, so the 30-second line does not rescue an unstable patient from the sustained label.

cards.t: Monomorphic versus polymorphic ventricular tachycardia
q: what is the difference between monomorphic and polymorphic VT
what causes polymorphic VT
what causes monomorphic ventricular tachycardia
cards.x:
What separates the two is whether the QRS shapes vary. In monomorphic ventricular tachycardia every QRS complex has the same shape; in polymorphic ventricular tachycardia the shape varies.

Their usual causes differ too:
- Monomorphic most often occurs with existing heart disease: heart failure, cardiomyopathy or a past myocardial infarction (heart attack).
- Polymorphic without a prolonged QT is most commonly due to acute myocardial ischemia (heart muscle suddenly short of blood); it is also common with cardiomyopathy.
- Polymorphic with a prolonged QT is torsades de pointes.

Either kind can cause palpitations, chest pain, dyspnea (breathlessness), syncope or presyncope.

cards.t: Treating non-sustained ventricular tachycardia
q: how do you treat non-sustained VT
does non-sustained ventricular tachycardia need an ICD
what is first line for symptomatic NSVT
cards.x:
Treatment of non-sustained ventricular tachycardia depends on whether it causes symptoms.
- Symptomatic: a beta blocker (metoprolol, carvedilol) is the first-line drug therapy. If it is not effective or not tolerated, catheter ablation is a primary alternative to antiarrhythmic drugs. If a beta blocker and catheter ablation are not options, try an antiarrhythmic drug (amiodarone, lidocaine or procainamide).
- Asymptomatic: optimize treatment of the underlying heart conditions, such as heart failure.

Non-sustained ventricular tachycardia is not, by itself, a reason for an implantable defibrillator, though some patients are candidates for one for primary prevention (to prevent a first life-threatening event).

cards.t: Treating stable sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia
q: how do you treat stable sustained VT
which drugs are used for stable monomorphic VT
when should procainamide be avoided
cards.x:
Every patient with sustained ventricular tachycardia gets the same initial setup: a cardiac monitor, intravenous access, a 12-lead electrocardiogram, supplemental oxygen and appropriate labs.

If the patient is hemodynamically stable (none of chest pain, altered mental status, shortness of breath or hypotension) and the rhythm is monomorphic, the treatment is pharmacologic cardioversion, meaning a drug converts the rhythm: an intravenous antiarrhythmic, either lidocaine, amiodarone or procainamide. Procainamide is avoided when there is a prolonged QT or heart failure.

If the patient is unstable, the first treatment is a shock instead; polymorphic rhythms are treated separately.

cards.t: Unstable ventricular tachycardia: synchronized cardioversion or defibrillation
q: what counts as hemodynamically unstable
when do you cardiovert versus defibrillate VT
how do you treat unstable ventricular tachycardia with a pulse
cards.x:
Hemodynamic instability means any one of four signs: chest pain, altered mental status, shortness of breath or hypotension. One is enough, so a patient who is alert with a normal blood pressure but has new chest pain is unstable.

For unstable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, the pulse decides the shock:
- With a pulse: synchronized cardioversion, a shock timed to the heart's own beats.
- Without a pulse: defibrillation (unsynchronized cardioversion), as for ventricular fibrillation.

Once stabilized, most patients need an implantable defibrillator for secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death.

cards.t: Treating polymorphic ventricular tachycardia
q: how do you treat polymorphic VT
do you defibrillate polymorphic VT if the patient has a pulse
what happens after defibrillation for polymorphic VT
cards.x:
Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never truly stable, even if the patient looks well and has a pulse, so it is treated with defibrillation (an unsynchronized shock).

After defibrillation comes urgent coronary angiography with possible revascularization in the cardiac catheterization laboratory. An antiarrhythmic or beta blocker may be added, usually intravenous metoprolol or intravenous amiodarone. Quick contrast with monomorphic: a stable monomorphic rhythm gets intravenous drugs, and an unstable one with a pulse gets synchronized cardioversion.

Torsades de pointes is the polymorphic form that comes with a prolonged QT, and it is covered separately.

cards.t: Torsades de pointes and QT prolongation
q: what is torsades de pointes
what causes QT prolongation
what causes torsades de pointes
cards.x:
Torsades de pointes is a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia in the setting of a prolonged QT interval: the QRS complexes keep changing and seem to twist around the baseline. A long QT interval is the key risk factor.

The long QT syndrome behind it is either congenital (present from birth) or acquired, and most torsades comes from the acquired kind. Acquired QT prolongation comes from:
- Drugs: many classes, including several antiarrhythmics, antidepressants, antipsychotics and antimicrobials.
- Electrolyte disturbances: hypokalemia (low potassium) and hypocalcemia (low calcium).

Quick way to place it: torsades is polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, but specifically the kind that comes with a long QT.

cards.t: Treating torsades de pointes: magnesium, and what to avoid
q: how do you treat torsades de pointes
why not give amiodarone for torsades
why are beta blockers avoided in torsades
which antiarrhythmic can be used in torsades
cards.x:
In a conscious patient, intravenous magnesium is the first treatment: an intravenous push to break the torsades, then more magnesium as an infusion, continued when runs keep recurring after the first dose. If the patient is hemodynamically unstable, the treatment is defibrillation (an unsynchronized shock).

What to avoid follows from the problem, a QT that is already too long:
- Amiodarone and procainamide prolong the QT interval, so they are out.
- Beta blockers such as metoprolol prolong it indirectly: the slow heart rate they cause lengthens the R-to-R interval and with it the QT. This applies to acquired, drug-induced torsades.
- Intravenous lidocaine is the antiarrhythmic that can be used, though there is not much evidence for it.

cards.t: Ventricular fibrillation
q: what is ventricular fibrillation
can ventricular fibrillation have a pulse
how does ventricular fibrillation look on the monitor
cards.x:
Ventricular fibrillation is uncoordinated electrical activity and nothing else: no pulse and no perfusion (no blood being pumped to the body). On the monitor the rate is 0, and there is no rhythm, no P waves, no PR interval and no QRS complexes. The activity may be coarse or fine. Think of a crowd where everyone claps at random: plenty of activity, but never one coordinated beat.

Because there is no pulse, a patient in ventricular fibrillation is in cardiac arrest. It is one of the two shockable arrest rhythms, along with pulseless ventricular tachycardia, and immediate defibrillation is the first treatment.

cards.t: Shockable versus unshockable cardiac arrest rhythms
q: which cardiac arrest rhythms are shockable
can you shock asystole
is pulseless electrical activity shockable
cards.x:
Of the four cardiac arrest rhythms, two are shockable and two are not.
- Shockable: ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia. They are handled together: treat as cardiac arrest (start cardiopulmonary resuscitation, give oxygen, attach the monitor/defibrillator) and defibrillate, with an unsynchronized shock, as soon as possible.
- Unshockable: pulseless electrical activity and asystole. A shock is not part of their treatment.

So the rhythm on the monitor decides whether the defibrillator is used.

cards.t: Treating ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia
q: what is the order of treatment for ventricular fibrillation
when do you give amiodarone in cardiac arrest
how often is epinephrine given in VF
cards.x:
Ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia are treated as cardiac arrest, in this order:
- Start cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), give oxygen and attach the monitor/defibrillator. Defibrillate (unsynchronized) as soon as possible: immediate defibrillation is the first treatment.
- Give 2 minutes of CPR after each shock, and epinephrine repeatedly, every 3 to 5 minutes, alongside the shocks and CPR. Still in the rhythm: a second shock.
- Consider intubating. Once an advanced airway is in place, give continuous chest compressions with one breath every 6 seconds.
- Still in ventricular fibrillation after shocks: amiodarone, which can be repeated.
- Refractory to shocks after that antiarrhythmic: consider lidocaine.

cards.t: Asystole versus pulseless electrical activity
q: what is pulseless electrical activity
what is the difference between asystole and PEA
what is the prognosis of asystole
cards.x:
Asystole is a flat line: no rate (0), no rhythm, no P waves, no PR interval and no QRS complexes.

Pulseless electrical activity (PEA) is not the same thing. The monitor shows an organized rhythm you would expect to come with a pulse, for example normal sinus rhythm, yet there is no pulse and no perfusing beats. The electrical signal looks fine; the pump is not delivering.

Both carry a poor prognosis; they are usually end-of-life rhythms. The arrest rhythms with the best prognosis are ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation, so a ventricular fibrillation that degrades to asystole has moved to a much worse prognosis.

cards.t: Pulseless electrical activity and asystole: causes and treatment
q: how do you treat asystole
what are the main causes of PEA
do you shock pulseless electrical activity
cards.x:
Pulseless electrical activity and asystole are both unshockable, so the response is to start chest compressions immediately. The mainstays of treatment are cardiopulmonary resuscitation with high-quality chest compressions and epinephrine every 3 to 5 minutes, and intubation should be considered early.

Pulseless electrical activity also has two leading causes in adults: hypovolemia (too little blood volume) and hypoxia (too little oxygen). In a bleeding patient, the hypovolemia must be addressed urgently.

cards.t: Left versus right bundle branch block
k: left vs right bundle branch block
q: how do I tell LBBB from RBBB
what's the difference between left and right bundle branch block
which new bundle branch block is a sign of disease
cards.x:
Both widen the QRS; what separates them is which ventricle is activated late, the leads that show it, and what a new one means.
- Left: the left ventricle is activated across the septum from the right. Look for a dominant S wave in V1 (rS) and absent Q waves in I, V5 and V6.
- Right: the septum and left ventricle activate normally via the left bundle, and the right ventricle is activated late across the septum. Look for rsR' (bunny ears) in V1, V2 and V3 and a slurred S in I and aVL.
- A new left bundle branch block is a sign of pathology, so evaluate for heart disease. A new right bundle branch block is not always pathological; it can occur with no apparent heart disease.
- Both are usually asymptomatic, and symptoms in either usually point to severe underlying heart disease.

cards.t: Heart block in elderly patients
q: why is heart block more common in the elderly
does an elderly patient with asymptomatic Mobitz II need a pacemaker
what is the most common cause of heart block in older patients
cards.x:
Atrioventricular block is more common in elderly patients because of degenerative conduction system disease: the wiring wears with age. Age-related degeneration is the most common cause of first-degree block, and degenerative His-Purkinje (conduction system) disease of old age tops the cause list for both Mobitz type II and complete block. Age-related degeneration of the conduction system is also a named cause of right bundle branch block.

Age does not soften the rule for Mobitz type II: an elderly patient with an incidental, asymptomatic Mobitz type II block still needs a permanent pacemaker, because the block is dangerous even without symptoms.

cards.t: Pericardial disease: the three ways it presents
q: what are the types of pericardial disease
what is a pericardial compressive syndrome
what is the most common pericardial disorder
cards.x:
Pericardial disease shows up in one of three ways: acute or recurrent pericarditis (inflammation of the sac around the heart); a pericardial effusion (extra fluid in that sac) without major hemodynamic compromise, meaning it is not seriously disturbing the circulation; or a compressive syndrome, where the heart itself gets squeezed. Acute pericarditis is the most common disorder of the pericardium.

The three compressive syndromes differ in what does the squeezing:
- Cardiac tamponade: fluid under pressure compresses the heart.
- Constrictive pericarditis: the sac scars, loses its elasticity and can no longer give (noncompliance).
- Effusive-constrictive pericarditis: an underlying constriction plus an effusion, usually with tamponade; the constriction persists after the fluid is drained.

cards.t: Acute, incessant, recurrent and chronic pericarditis: the time frames
q: what is the difference between incessant and recurrent pericarditis
how long does acute pericarditis last
when is pericarditis called chronic
cards.x:
Pericarditis is named by how long it lasts and whether it settles in between.
- Acute: inflammation of the pericardial sac lasting less than 4 to 6 weeks.
- Incessant: symptoms persist for more than 4 to 6 weeks, up to 3 months, without a sustained remission.
- Recurrent: symptoms of acute pericarditis return after a symptom-free interval of 4 to 6 weeks or longer.
- Chronic: symptoms persist for more than 3 months.

Incessant versus recurrent is the pair to keep straight. Incessant pericarditis never really switches off, while recurrent pericarditis has a genuine symptom-free gap of 4 to 6 weeks or longer before the symptoms return. Recurrence is common: it affects about 15 to 30% of patients with acute pericarditis.

cards.t: How common pericarditis, effusion and tamponade are
q: how common is acute pericarditis
how often does pericarditis come back
how common is cardiac tamponade
cards.x:
Acute pericarditis is the most common pericardial disorder, with an incidence of about 27.7 per 100,000 people a year. It is recorded in about 5% of patients admitted through the emergency department for nonischemic chest pain, meaning chest pain that is not from poor blood flow to the heart muscle.

How often the others turn up:
- Recurrent pericarditis: about 15 to 30% of patients with acute pericarditis.
- Pericardial effusion: Framingham cohort data suggest one may be present in up to 6.5% of the general adult population.
- Cardiac tamponade: about 0.05% of hospital admissions.
- Constrictive pericarditis: true population prevalence is unknown; it is uncommon after viral pericarditis.

Once someone has had acute pericarditis, a return is common.

cards.t: What causes pericarditis: idiopathic, viral, and tuberculosis by region
q: what is the most common cause of pericarditis
which viruses cause pericarditis
when should I think of tuberculosis in pericarditis
cards.x:
Pericardial disease is most often idiopathic (no cause is found), and most idiopathic cases are likely viral: a virus is probably behind it even though none is identified. The viruses named are coxsackieviruses and echoviruses in children, and cytomegalovirus and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) in adults. Viral pericarditis is typically preceded by an upper respiratory infection, and the list also includes Epstein-Barr virus, influenza, and hepatitis A and B.

Where the patient lives changes the picture. In a Western European series, idiopathic disease was 55% of acute pericarditis and tuberculosis under 1%. In an African series, idiopathic disease was only 13.7%, and tuberculosis caused about 69.5%. So tuberculosis, especially in developing countries, belongs on the list wherever it is prevalent.

cards.t: Other causes of acute pericarditis, and treating the cause
q: what are the causes of acute pericarditis
what BUN level causes uremic pericarditis
how is uremic pericarditis treated
cards.x:
Beyond viruses, acute pericarditis has a long list of causes:
- Infection: bacteria (Staphylococcus, Pneumococcus, Streptococcus in rheumatic pancarditis, Haemophilus, Mycoplasma, Mycobacterium tuberculosis), fungi (Histoplasma, Aspergillus, Blastomyces, Coccidioides, Candida) and parasites (Echinococcus, amebic, Toxoplasma).
- Heart injury: myocardial infarction (peri-infarction pericarditis and Dressler syndrome) or cardiac surgery.
- Autoimmune disease (systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis), neoplasm (metastatic, primary, paraneoplastic) and uremia (blood urea nitrogen above 60 mg/dL).
- Iatrogenic causes: trauma, radiation therapy to the chest, and drug-induced lupus from procainamide and hydralazine.

The cause steers treatment: uremic pericarditis is treated with dialysis, autoimmune pericarditis with steroids, tamponade with pericardiocentesis (draining the fluid), and the usual inflammation with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs plus colchicine.

cards.t: Dressler syndrome (pericarditis after a heart attack or heart surgery)
q: what is Dressler syndrome
when does Dressler syndrome happen after an MI
can pericarditis follow heart surgery
cards.x:
Dressler syndrome is pericarditis that develops as a result of a myocardial infarction (heart attack) or after cardiac surgery (post-cardiotomy). It typically appears about 2 to 3 weeks after the myocardial infarction, so the pericarditis comes after a delay rather than at the time of the heart injury.

It belongs to the post-myocardial infarction group of causes, alongside peri-infarction pericarditis. Dressler syndrome is also on the list of causes of pericardial effusion, together with fluid after a myocardial infarction or after cardiac surgery.

Quick way to place it: pericarditis-type chest pain a couple of weeks after a heart attack points to Dressler syndrome.

cards.t: Causes of pericardial effusion
k: why fluid collects around the heart
q: what causes a pericardial effusion
why should I think of cancer with a large pericardial effusion
can hypothyroidism cause a pericardial effusion
cards.x:
A pericardial effusion (extra fluid around the heart) shares many causes with pericarditis, plus some metabolic ones:
- Idiopathic, and infection (human immunodeficiency virus, Lyme disease, coxsackievirus, tuberculosis).
- Malignancy, and trauma.
- Cardiac: after a myocardial infarction, Dressler syndrome, after cardiac surgery.
- Metabolic: uremia and hypothyroidism.
- Rheumatologic and endocrine: systemic lupus erythematosus, and thyroid disease with myxedema.
- Medications.

Cancer deserves special attention. Malignancy is an important underlying cause especially of pericardial effusion and cardiac tamponade, and across five case series of moderate to large effusions it was a leading identified cause, at 13 to 38%. The others in those series were idiopathic, iatrogenic, infectious, uremic, collagen vascular, post-infarction and hypothyroid causes.

cards.t: Medications that cause pericardial effusion or pericarditis
q: which drugs cause pericardial effusion
how do hydralazine and procainamide cause pericarditis
what is drug-induced lupus pericarditis
cards.x:
Five medications are listed as causes of pericardial effusion: doxorubicin, minoxidil, phenytoin, hydralazine and procainamide. Two of them act through a middle step. Hydralazine and procainamide cause drug-induced lupus, and that is how they lead to an effusion; the same drug-induced lupus is also listed as an iatrogenic (treatment-caused) cause of acute pericarditis.

Quick way to keep them straight: the lupus pair, hydralazine and procainamide, shows up under both pericarditis and effusion, while doxorubicin, minoxidil and phenytoin are listed as causes of effusion.

cards.t: Acute pericarditis: the chest pain and its differential
q: what does pericarditis pain feel like
what makes pericarditis pain better or worse
what else can look like pericarditis
cards.x:
The classic complaint is pleuritic chest pain: sharp, substernal (behind the breastbone), worse when lying flat (supine) and when breathing in, and relieved by leaning forward. Patients may also develop a fever.

Sharp pain that worsens with breathing and changes with position is what sets pericardial pain apart from a myocardial infarction (heart attack). Even so, angina and myocardial ischemia or infarction stay on the differential, with:
- Lungs: pleuritis, pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax.
- Gut: acute esophagitis or gastritis, gastro-esophageal reflux disease, peptic ulcer disease, esophageal spasm, esophageal rupture.
- Aorta: aortic dissection.

cards.t: Diagnosing acute pericarditis: two of four criteria
q: what are the diagnostic criteria for acute pericarditis
is troponin one of the pericarditis criteria
do you need a friction rub to diagnose pericarditis
cards.x:
The diagnosis of idiopathic or viral pericarditis is usually clinical. Two of these four criteria must be present:
- Sharp substernal chest pain.
- A pericardial friction rub.
- Suggestive electrocardiogram changes (widespread ST elevation).
- A new or worsening pericardial effusion.

Troponin is not one of the four. So a patient with the typical pain and widespread ST elevation already has two criteria, even when no rub is heard.

Because it is primarily a clinical diagnosis, most patients with acute pericarditis do not need an invasive workup such as pericardiocentesis or a pericardial biopsy.

cards.t: Acute pericarditis workup: labs, echocardiogram and chest X-ray
q: what tests do you order for suspected pericarditis
what does an elevated troponin mean in pericarditis
why check C-reactive protein in pericarditis
cards.x:
The initial workup is a history and physical examination, an electrocardiogram, a chest radiograph, a transthoracic echocardiogram, and labs: complete blood count, troponins, erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein. Further testing is decided case by case.

What to expect:
- Echocardiogram: often normal unless there is an effusion. In typical, low-risk pericarditis it is normal or shows only a small effusion; a moderate to large effusion is itself a high-risk feature.
- Chest radiograph: typically normal.
- Troponin: may be raised if the heart muscle is also affected (myopericarditis).
- Laboratory signs of inflammation are common, with leukocytosis (a raised white cell count).

C-reactive protein matters beyond diagnosis: it is checked at presentation and then weekly to guide when treatment is tapered.

cards.t: Pericardial friction rub, and how to tell it from a pleural rub
q: what does a pericardial friction rub sound like
where is a pericardial rub heard best
how do you tell a pleural rub from a pericardial rub
cards.x:
A pericardial friction rub is a superficial, scratchy or squeaking sound over the heart, and it is highly specific for acute pericarditis. Classically it is triphasic (it has three parts), and its intensity waxes and wanes.

How to hear it best:
- Listen at the left sternal border with the diaphragm of the stethoscope.
- It gets louder with the patient leaning forward, holding a breath, and with firm pressure of the diaphragm.

The held breath is also how you tell it from a pleural rub. A pleural rub is tied to breathing and heard as the patient breathes in, so it stops when the breath is held. A pericardial rub keeps going, and can even get louder, while the breath is held: the lungs have stopped, but the heart keeps beating.

cards.t: Pericarditis on the electrocardiogram: widespread ST elevation, PR depression
q: what does pericarditis look like on an ECG
what happens in lead aVR in pericarditis
what is Spodick sign
cards.x:
The electrocardiogram in acute pericarditis shows ST elevation spread across most leads rather than in one area. Expect widespread concave (scooped) ST elevation with PR depression in most limb leads (I, II, III, aVL, aVF) and the chest leads V2 to V6. Lead aVR, and sometimes V1, shows the mirror image: reciprocal ST depression and PR elevation.

Sinus tachycardia is also common, from pain and/or a pericardial effusion.

Another finding is the Spodick sign: a downsloping segment between the T wave and the next P wave, best seen in II and V4 to V6. It can also be seen in acute myocardial infarction, so it is not unique to pericarditis.

cards.t: The four electrocardiogram stages of pericarditis
q: what are the four stages of pericarditis on ECG
why does a patient with pericarditis have T wave inversion
how does the pericarditis ECG change over time
cards.x:
The electrocardiogram in pericarditis changes over the course of the illness in four stages:
- Stage 1: widespread ST elevation and PR depression, with reciprocal changes in aVR.
- Stage 2: the ST changes normalize and the T waves flatten everywhere.
- Stage 3: the flattened T waves become inverted.
- Stage 4: the tracing returns to normal.

This matters for timing. A patient seen weeks into the illness may show widespread T-wave inversion without any ST elevation. When troponin is normal, that is a later stage of pericarditis, the expected evolution of the illness, not a new myocardial infarction (heart attack).

cards.t: When pericarditis needs pericardiocentesis or a pericardial biopsy
q: when do you do a pericardiocentesis in pericarditis
when is a pericardial biopsy needed
does every pericarditis patient need a pericardiocentesis
cards.x:
Most patients with acute pericarditis do not need an invasive workup, because it is primarily a clinical diagnosis. Draining the fluid or sampling the tissue is kept for specific situations.

Pericardiocentesis (draining the pericardial fluid) is for cardiac tamponade, for moderate to large effusions that are refractory to medical therapy and causing severe symptoms, and for suspected bacterial or neoplastic (cancer-related) pericarditis.

Pericardial biopsy and pericardioscopy (looking inside the pericardium with a scope) are for:
- Cardiac tamponade that keeps relapsing.
- Suspected bacterial or neoplastic pericarditis.
- Pericarditis that worsens despite medical therapy, without a specific diagnosis.

The common thread: you go invasive when there is dangerous fluid, a bacterial or cancerous cause to prove, or a course that is not settling with treatment.

cards.t: High-risk features in acute pericarditis (who may need hospital)
q: when should a patient with pericarditis be admitted
what are the high-risk features of pericarditis
which pericarditis patients may need hospitalization
cards.x:
These features mark acute pericarditis as higher risk, with a potential need for hospitalization:
- Fever above 38 degrees Celsius (100.4 degrees Fahrenheit), or a subacute course over days to weeks without an acute onset of chest pain.
- Evidence suggesting cardiac tamponade, or a moderate to large pericardial effusion.
- Immunosuppression, oral anticoagulants, or acute trauma.
- No clinical improvement after 7 days of appropriately dosed anti-inflammatory and colchicine therapy.
- Elevated cardiac troponin, which suggests myopericarditis (the heart muscle is involved too).

Tamponade is the urgent one: a patient in an office or urgent care with signs of tamponade belongs in the emergency department now.

cards.t: Treating acute pericarditis: anti-inflammatory plus colchicine, then prednisone
q: what is the first-line treatment for acute pericarditis
how long is colchicine given for pericarditis
what if the patient cannot take NSAIDs
cards.x:
First-line therapy for most acute idiopathic or viral pericarditis is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (aspirin, ibuprofen or indomethacin) plus colchicine. For a first episode, the anti-inflammatory is given until the chest pain resolves and C-reactive protein is normal. Colchicine runs longer: about 3 months after a first episode, and 6 months or more after a recurrence. Add gastrointestinal protection, for example a proton pump inhibitor, during the anti-inflammatory course.

If the patient cannot take nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, prednisone takes their place. The ladder:
- First line: anti-inflammatory plus colchicine.
- Second line, for refractory cases or a contraindication to anti-inflammatories: prednisone plus colchicine.
- Third line: second-line therapy plus a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug.

Patients should finish the full course to prevent recurrence, not stop when the pain eases.

cards.t: Pericarditis after a myocardial infarction: aspirin plus colchicine
q: how do you treat pericarditis after a heart attack
can you give ibuprofen for pericarditis after an MI
how is Dressler syndrome treated
cards.x:
After a myocardial infarction (heart attack), the usual anti-inflammatory choice changes. Other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are not given: ibuprofen and indomethacin are avoided, and glucocorticoids (steroids) are also avoided in peri-infarction pericarditis. Aspirin is used instead, with colchicine added.

So the regimen for post-infarction pericarditis, including Dressler syndrome, is aspirin plus colchicine. Quick way to remember it: of the three first-line anti-inflammatories (aspirin, ibuprofen, indomethacin), aspirin is the one that stays after a heart attack.

cards.t: Pericarditis: activity restriction and when to taper treatment
q: when can a patient exercise after pericarditis
when do you start tapering pericarditis treatment
how is C-reactive protein used to guide tapering
cards.x:
Patients should avoid strenuous physical activity until their symptoms resolve and their biomarkers (C-reactive protein) are normal: for at least 1 month after diagnosis, keeping the maximal heart rate under 100 beats per minute. Counseling covers both the reason for the restriction and how long it lasts.

Tapering can follow one of two approaches:
- Symptom-based: tapering starts once the patient has been symptom-free for at least 24 hours.
- C-reactive protein-based: the level is checked at presentation and then weekly, and tapering starts when the patient is symptom-free and the C-reactive protein has normalized.

Either way, colchicine continues for its full course.

cards.t: Treatment failure in acute pericarditis
q: what if pericarditis doesn't improve with treatment
what counts as treatment failure in pericarditis
what does no response in a week mean in pericarditis
cards.x:
If a patient does not respond to a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug plus colchicine within 1 week, that suggests a cause other than idiopathic or viral pericarditis.

Treatment failure is defined as any of:
- Persistent fever.
- Persistent pleuritic chest pain.
- A new pericardial effusion.
- Worsening of general illness.

A patient failing therapy is admitted and evaluated for another cause. Lack of response after a week of treatment is also one of the high-risk features and one of the markers of the poorest prognosis.

cards.t: Surgery for pericarditis (pericardiectomy) and cardiac magnetic resonance
q: when is surgery considered for pericarditis
why get a cardiac MRI before pericardiectomy
what is cardiac MRI used for in recurrent pericarditis
cards.x:
Pericardiocentesis (draining the fluid) or pericardiectomy (surgically removing pericardium) may be considered for:
- A moderate to large effusion, particularly if it is hemodynamically significant (straining the circulation) and causing tamponade, or symptomatic and refractory to medical therapy.
- A suspected neoplastic or bacterial cause with a moderate to large effusion.
- Frequent, highly symptomatic recurrences with effusion.
- Evidence of constrictive pericarditis, which is a late occurrence.

Before committing a patient to pericardiectomy, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showing edema or late gadolinium enhancement helps identify constriction that is inflammatory and potentially reversible. Cardiac magnetic resonance is now also recommended for risk stratification of complicated or recurrent pericarditis.

cards.t: Prognosis of acute pericarditis
q: what is the prognosis of acute pericarditis
which pericarditis patients do worst
what predicts a poor outcome in pericarditis
cards.x:
The poorest prognosis falls in about 15% of patients: those with at least one of these features.
- Fever above 38 degrees Celsius, or a subacute onset.
- A large effusion, with or without tamponade.
- No response to anti-inflammatory medicines after 1 week.
- Myopericarditis or traumatic pericarditis.
- Oral anticoagulation.

Most of these features also appear among the high-risk features that can call for hospitalization.

cards.t: Pericarditis follow-up, referral and patient counseling
k: when to refer pericarditis to cardiology
q: what should I tell a patient with pericarditis
when do you refer pericarditis to cardiology
what symptoms should send a pericarditis patient to the emergency department
cards.x:
Counseling covers a few practical points:
- Keep the head of the bed elevated, since the pain is worse lying flat.
- Take the full treatment course to prevent recurrence; do not stop when the pain eases.
- Follow the activity restriction, with its reason and duration explained.
- Discuss the response to conservative therapy and the medicines' side effects.
- Red-flag symptoms of recurrence or tamponade, such as shortness of breath, lightheadedness or falling exercise tolerance from low cardiac output, need the emergency department, not a routine appointment.

Refer to cardiology when there is no response to conservative management, when the pericarditis recurs, or when constrictive pericarditis develops.

cards.t: Recurrent pericarditis: definition, first-recurrence treatment and risk
q: what is recurrent pericarditis
how do you treat a first recurrence of pericarditis
what increases the risk of multiple recurrences
cards.x:
Recurrent pericarditis is the return of pericarditis symptoms after a symptom-free interval of 4 to 6 weeks or longer. It follows about 15 to 30% of acute episodes.

A first recurrence is treated with a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug until the chest pain resolves and inflammatory markers are normal, plus colchicine for 6 months or more.

Three things raise the risk of multiple recurrences:
- How high the C-reactive protein rises.
- How severe the pericardial late gadolinium enhancement is on imaging.
- An autoimmune cause.

Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging stratifies the risk of recurrent pericarditis, and a recurrence is a reason to refer to cardiology.

cards.t: Anti-interleukin-1 therapy (anakinra, rilonacept) for recurrent pericarditis
q: when is anakinra or rilonacept used in pericarditis
what is the inflammatory phenotype of pericarditis
how is a second recurrence of pericarditis treated
cards.x:
Anakinra and rilonacept are anti-interleukin-1 agents. For recurrent, colchicine-resistant or steroid-dependent pericarditis with an inflammatory phenotype, anti-interleukin-1 therapy is preferred, and the 2025 guidelines support starting it earlier in these patients.

The inflammatory phenotype means a high C-reactive protein (above 10 mg/L), fever, and evidence of pericardial inflammation on imaging.

At a second recurrence the path splits:
- Idiopathic pericarditis or post-cardiac injury syndrome that is colchicine-resistant, with a history of raised C-reactive protein: add an interleukin-1 blocker.
- An underlying systemic autoimmune disease: low-to-moderate prednisone.

Azathioprine and intravenous immunoglobulin are later-line options.

cards.t: Constrictive pericarditis: what it is and what causes it
q: what is constrictive pericarditis
why does constrictive pericarditis look like heart failure
what causes constrictive pericarditis
cards.x:
In constrictive pericarditis the pericardium has scarred and lost its elasticity, so it acts like a stiff shell that limits how much the heart can fill. The symptoms come from:
- Fluid overload: peripheral edema and anasarca (generalized swelling).
- Diminished cardiac output: fatigue and dyspnea on exertion (breathlessness with effort).

That is why it looks like heart failure.

More than 50% of cases are idiopathic or viral. Others follow cardiac surgery, prior radiation therapy, infection, connective tissue disease or uremia, or a prior history of pericarditis, trauma, surgery or systemic disease that affects the pericardium.

cards.t: Constrictive pericarditis on examination: Kussmaul sign and pericardial knock
k: jugular venous pressure rises on inspiration
q: what is a pericardial knock
what exam findings suggest constrictive pericarditis
what is Kussmaul sign in constrictive pericarditis
cards.x:
Most patients have an elevated jugular venous pressure. Two findings to know:
- Kussmaul sign: the jugular venous pressure increases when the patient breathes in, rather than decreasing.
- Pericardial knock: an early diastolic sound, occurring slightly earlier than a third heart sound would. It is pathognomonic (it clinches the diagnosis) when present, but rare.

Pericardial calcification is highly specific but uncommon. With more severe constriction, peripheral edema, ascites, pleural effusion, pulsatile hepatomegaly (an enlarged, pulsing liver) and cachexia (wasting) are common.

Quick way to remember the knock and the calcification: convincing when you find them, but usually you won't.

cards.t: Constrictive pericarditis: echocardiogram, electrocardiogram and imaging
q: how is constrictive pericarditis diagnosed
what does the echo show in constrictive pericarditis
does a chest x-ray without calcification rule out constriction
cards.x:
Constrictive pericarditis is usually diagnosed clinically with typical echocardiogram features, and echocardiography confirms it in many patients. Look for:
- Increased pericardial thickness.
- Abnormal septal motion, or a septal bounce toward the left ventricle.
- Pronounced respiratory variation in ventricular filling.
- Moderate enlargement of both atria.

The electrocardiogram commonly shows nonspecific ST and T-wave changes and tachycardia; low voltage may be present, and atrial fibrillation is common in advanced cases. On a chest radiograph, pericardial calcification with the right clinical picture is highly consistent with constriction, but most patients have none, so a film without calcium does not exclude it.

When it is suspected but unconfirmed, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging or computed tomography evaluates pericardial thickness, and magnetic resonance or positron emission tomography can show acute inflammation. Coronary angiography with right heart catheterization is occasionally needed to confirm.

cards.t: Constrictive pericarditis: its mimics and the natriuretic peptide clue
q: what mimics constrictive pericarditis
why can cirrhosis look like constrictive pericarditis
is BNP useful in constrictive pericarditis
cards.x:
Three conditions are on the differential:
- Subacute cardiac tamponade.
- Restrictive cardiomyopathy, the key cardiac mimic.
- Cirrhosis, the noncardiac mimic, because both cause ascites and fluid overload.

The workup is a history and examination, electrocardiogram, chest radiograph, complete blood count, sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, B-type natriuretic peptide and a transthoracic echocardiogram.

Labs help only partly. The sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein are often elevated. No B-type natriuretic peptide threshold confirms or excludes constriction, but the level is likely lower in constrictive pericarditis than in restrictive cardiomyopathy. So a lower value leans toward constriction rather than restrictive cardiomyopathy, without settling the question.

cards.t: Constrictive pericarditis: pericardiectomy, a medical trial, and prognosis
q: how is constrictive pericarditis treated
what is the survival after pericardiectomy
can constrictive pericarditis be treated with medicine
cards.x:
Constrictive pericarditis is often a surgical disease. The definitive treatment is pericardiectomy, surgical removal of part or most of the pericardium, done by cardiothoracic surgery with cardiology. If surgery is planned, diuretics should be used sparingly beforehand.

Early, hemodynamically stable constriction may first get a 2-to-3-month trial of the acute pericarditis medicines used for longer: diuretics for fluid overload, plus nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and colchicine. If tuberculosis is the cause, treating it may significantly reduce progression to constriction.

Prognosis:
- Untreated, survival is low; when surgery is needed, earlier intervention is associated with better outcomes.
- After pericardiectomy, 5-year survival is nearly 80% and 10-year survival nearly 60%.
- Prior ionizing radiation is associated with the worst survival.
- Older age, worse functional class and comorbidities (such as kidney dysfunction, pulmonary hypertension or hyponatremia) predict a poor long-term outcome.

cards.t: Pericardial effusion: symptoms of small and large effusions
q: what are the symptoms of a pericardial effusion
why does a large pericardial effusion cause hoarseness
can a pericardial effusion have no symptoms
cards.x:
What a pericardial effusion (fluid around the heart) causes depends on its size.
- A small effusion may cause no symptoms, or only vague ones: a dull ache in the chest, fatigue, decreased exercise tolerance, dyspnea (shortness of breath).
- A large effusion is associated with dysphagia (trouble swallowing), nausea, hiccups, cough, and hoarseness from impingement on the recurrent laryngeal nerve, the nerve to the voice box.

The bigger danger is tamponade, when the fluid compresses the heart itself, and whether that happens depends heavily on how fast the fluid collects.

cards.t: Why a small, fast effusion can cause tamponade but a large, slow one may not
q: why can a small effusion cause tamponade
how can a large effusion not cause tamponade
how much fluid causes tamponade
cards.x:
With a pericardial effusion, speed matters as much as size, because the pericardium can stretch, but only over time.
- Acute effusion: the fluid collects fast and the pericardium has no time to stretch, so even a small amount, under 200 mL, can cause hemodynamic compromise (tamponade).
- Chronic effusion: the fluid builds slowly, the pericardium stretches over time, and a large amount can accumulate without tamponade.

Think of the pericardium as a sleeve that can be eased larger slowly but not all at once. So when judging an effusion, ask how fast it came, not only how big it is.

cards.t: Diagnosing a pericardial effusion and finding its cause
q: how do you diagnose a pericardial effusion
what labs do you order for a pericardial effusion
why check an ANA in a young woman with an effusion
cards.x:
Clinical evaluation, an electrocardiogram and a chest radiograph may suggest an effusion, but an echocardiogram is required to confirm it. The echocardiogram is sensitive and specific for the fluid and shows its hemodynamic significance (how much it affects the circulation); with moderate to large effusions the heart may be seen swinging in the fluid.

Initial labs are a complete blood count, basic metabolic panel (chemistry and kidney function), thyroid-stimulating hormone and troponins, possibly with an antinuclear antibody test, for example in a young woman with an effusion (lupus).

Then hunt for the cause from the history, examination and medication list:
- Thyroid function tests (myxedema).
- A rheumatologic workup.
- Human immunodeficiency virus and Lyme serology, and a tuberculin skin test.
- Albumin and urine protein (nephrotic syndrome).
- An evaluation for malignancy, for example breast or lung cancer.

cards.t: Diagnostic pericardiocentesis: when to tap and what to send the fluid for
q: what tests do you send pericardial fluid for
when is a diagnostic pericardiocentesis done
is the pericardial fluid cell count helpful
cards.x:
Diagnostic pericardiocentesis means draining pericardial fluid, by a needle through the skin or surgically, to help find the cause. Consider it in patients already undergoing therapeutic drainage for tamponade, in those with a high suspicion of neoplastic, purulent (pus-forming) or tuberculous pericarditis, and in those with a moderate-to-large effusion of unknown cause.

Each fluid study answers a different question:
- Gram stain and bacterial and fungal cultures: bacterial (purulent) or fungal infection, and the organism's sensitivities.
- Acid-fast bacilli stain and mycobacterial culture: tuberculosis.
- Cytology: malignant cells, when cancer is suspected.
- Cell count and differential: rarely helpful in establishing the diagnosis.

cards.t: Pericardial effusion: management, prognosis and follow-up
q: how is a pericardial effusion treated
when is a pericardial window done
what is the prognosis of a malignant pericardial effusion
cards.x:
Management follows the cause: the effusion gets whatever medical therapy its underlying etiology needs, for example for cancer, tuberculosis or infection. A pericardial window or pericardiectomy is performed for recurrent effusions and for loculated (walled-off) effusions, especially those located posteriorly that cannot be reached with a needle through the skin.

Prognosis depends on the underlying cause. A symptomatic malignant pericardial effusion carries a limited life expectancy, a median of 2 to 4 months, and often recurs within that time; a palliative care consult is recommended to improve clinical outcomes and quality of life.

Follow-up is close and with the specialty that matches the cause: cardiology, infectious disease (for example tuberculosis), nephrology (uremia), oncology or rheumatology. All large pericardial effusions should be followed with serial transthoracic echocardiograms.

cards.t: Cardiac tamponade: what it is and what causes it
q: what is cardiac tamponade
why does tamponade lower cardiac output
what causes cardiac tamponade
cards.x:
Cardiac tamponade is pericardial fluid under pressure compressing the heart. The squeezed heart mechanically cannot fill properly (impaired diastolic filling), so it has less blood to pump and cardiac output falls.

Causes:
- Acute pericarditis.
- Iatrogenic injury (caused by medical care) and penetrating trauma.
- Free-wall rupture after a myocardial infarction.
- Malignancy.
- Aortic dissection.

Tamponade is an emergency. Evidence suggesting tamponade is a high-risk feature that requires hospitalization, so a patient with these signs outside the hospital is sent to the emergency department.

cards.t: Beck triad
k: muffled heart sounds distended neck veins hypotension
q: what is Beck triad
what are the three classic signs of cardiac tamponade
what does Beck triad point to
cards.x:
Beck triad is the classic three-part picture of cardiac tamponade:
- Distant (muffled) heart sounds.
- Distended jugular veins.
- Decreased arterial blood pressure (hypotension).

A handy hook is the three Ds: distant, distended, decreased. The low blood pressure follows from the core problem in tamponade: fluid under pressure stops the heart filling, so cardiac output falls. Look for the triad alongside the other tamponade findings, such as pulsus paradoxus and tachycardia.

cards.t: Pulsus paradoxus and the other examination findings in tamponade
q: what is pulsus paradoxus
what are the exam findings in cardiac tamponade
what does sinus tachycardia mean in tamponade
cards.x:
Pulsus paradoxus is a 10 mmHg (millimeters of mercury) drop in blood pressure when the patient breathes in. It goes with a marked fall in left ventricular stroke volume (the blood pumped per beat) during inspiration.

Other findings, in both acute and subacute tamponade:
- Elevated jugular venous pressure.
- Hypotension and tachycardia.
- Chest pain or discomfort, dyspnea or tachypnea (fast breathing), syncope or presyncope (fainting or nearly fainting), and peripheral edema.
- On the venous waveform, a prominent x descent and an absent y descent.

Take sinus tachycardia seriously: it may indicate significant hemodynamic compromise and is an indication for immediate pericardiocentesis.

cards.t: Diagnosing tamponade: a clinical diagnosis confirmed by drainage
q: how is cardiac tamponade diagnosed
what does the echo show in tamponade
what confirms cardiac tamponade
cards.x:
Tamponade is a clinical diagnosis: you recognize it at the bedside. It is confirmed only by the hemodynamic and clinical response to draining the pericardial fluid (pericardiocentesis). A patient whose blood pressure and breathing recover after drainage has had the diagnosis confirmed.

Tests support the suspicion:
- Echocardiogram: identifies the effusion and its hemodynamic significance. Right ventricular diastolic collapse (the right ventricle caving in while it should be filling) is evident with tamponade, and absent in a pericardial effusion alone.
- Cardiac catheterization: equalization of pressures in all chambers of the heart.

Quick contrast: an effusion is fluid around the heart; tamponade is that fluid under enough pressure to compress the heart, which is what the collapsing right ventricle shows.

cards.t: Tamponade: electrocardiogram and chest X-ray findings
q: what is electrical alternans
what does tamponade look like on a chest x-ray
can tamponade have a normal-size heart on x-ray
cards.x:
On the electrocardiogram, tamponade shows a low-voltage QRS, tachycardia and electrical alternans: the QRS amplitude alternates from beat to beat as the heart swings in the fluid. Electrical alternans is fairly specific for cardiac tamponade, but it can rarely be seen with very large effusions.

On the chest radiograph, a large effusion gives cardiomegaly with a globular, water-bottle shaped heart, and the lung fields may be clear on both sides, unlike heart failure. But at least 200 mL of fluid must accumulate before the heart shadow enlarges. So a small effusion that builds up quickly can cause tamponade while the heart still looks normal-sized on the film.

cards.t: What mimics cardiac tamponade (differential diagnosis)
q: what is the differential for cardiac tamponade
what can mimic acute tamponade
what conditions look like tamponade
cards.x:
Several conditions can mimic acute cardiac tamponade:
- Myocardial infarction, especially with right ventricular involvement.
- Aortic dissection.
- Massive pulmonary embolism, which causes hemodynamic compromise through right ventricular overload.

The differential also includes constrictive pericarditis, congestive heart failure and cirrhosis. Keep all of these in mind before settling on tamponade, since the diagnosis is a clinical one, confirmed by the patient's response to drainage.

cards.t: Treating cardiac tamponade: pericardiocentesis, fluids, and no diuretics
q: how is cardiac tamponade treated
why give IV fluids in tamponade
why are diuretics avoided in tamponade
cards.x:
Expedient (prompt) pericardiocentesis is the definitive treatment for cardiac tamponade. It is therapeutic, and the fluid is sent for diagnostic studies at the same time.

Until drainage, intravenous fluids are given to increase preload (the blood filling the heart) and prevent collapse of the right ventricle. This is a temporizing, stabilizing measure, not the cure. For the same reason, diuretics, which lower preload, are avoided before drainage: the compressed heart depends on preload.

Nonhemorrhagic tamponade is treated with pericardiocentesis; hemorrhagic tamponade from trauma needs emergent surgery to repair the injury.

With prompt recognition and treatment, the short-term outcome is often good. The long-term prognosis depends on the underlying cause: a malignant effusion carries a far worse outlook than a viral one.

cards.t: Effusive-constrictive pericarditis
k: jugular venous pressure stays high after pericardiocentesis
q: what is effusive-constrictive pericarditis
why does the jugular venous pressure stay high after draining an effusion
how is effusive-constrictive pericarditis recognized
cards.x:
Effusive-constrictive pericarditis is two problems at once: an underlying constrictive pericarditis (a scarred pericardium that has lost its elasticity) with a coexisting pericardial effusion, usually with cardiac tamponade.

Its defining feature appears after the fluid is drained. The tamponade is treated, but the constriction persists. So the jugular venous pressure stays elevated after drainage, with the Kussmaul sign of constriction (a jugular venous pressure that rises on inspiration). The course runs tamponade first, then persistent constrictive physiology.

Quick way to spot it: if the jugular venous pressure stays high after a pericardial effusion has been drained, think of a stiff pericardium hiding under the fluid.

cards.t: Pericardial disease in older adults: drug cautions and cancer suspicion
q: how is pericarditis managed differently in the elderly
why are NSAIDs a concern in older adults with pericarditis
should I think of cancer in an older adult with an effusion
cards.x:
Older adults need a few adjustments:
- Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are on the Beers list of potentially inappropriate medications, so use them with caution (bleeding, kidney injury). Colchicine also needs caution: consider a dose reduction.
- Corticosteroids increase osteoporosis risk, a particular concern on prolonged courses.
- Keep a higher index of suspicion for malignancy, especially with an effusion or tamponade.
- Surgical interventions (pericardiocentesis, windows, pericardiectomy) carry higher morbidity and mortality, and recovery from a prolonged illness or procedures often needs rehabilitation.
- Consults: cardiology, and cardiothoracic surgery, which performs pericardiectomy and pericardial windows.

Older age also predicts a worse long-term outcome in constrictive pericarditis.

cards.t: Infective endocarditis: what it is and where it takes hold
q: what is infective endocarditis
where does endocarditis usually occur
what is bacteremia
cards.x:
Endocarditis is inflammation of the endocardium, the inner membrane that lines the heart's chambers and covers the cusps of the heart valves. In infective endocarditis the damaged lining carries bacterial growths called vegetations. A closely related term is bacteremia: bacteria in the bloodstream, identified by any true-positive blood culture. Blood should be sterile, so real growth matters.

Where it takes hold:
- Heart valves, the most common site.
- The low-pressure side of a ventricular septal defect (a hole between the two ventricles). The right side is the low-pressure side.
- Endocardium damaged by abnormal (aberrant) jets of blood or by foreign bodies.
- Intracardiac devices.

cards.t: Types of endocarditis: native, prosthetic, device and health care-associated
q: what are the types of infective endocarditis
what is health care-associated endocarditis
how is endocarditis classified
cards.x:
Infective endocarditis is labeled by where the vegetation sits and, for one type, where the infection was picked up:
- Native valve: vegetation on the patient's own heart valves.
- Prosthetic valve: vegetation on an artificial valve.
- Cardiovascular implantable electronic device: vegetation on a pacemaker or an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, for example on a lead.
- Health care-associated: less common. Suspect it in a hospitalized patient who develops fevers and positive blood cultures with no apparent source. Staphylococcus aureus causes about half of these cases.

The full classification uses four axes together: the timing (acute versus subacute), the site (native valve, prosthetic valve or implantable device), the cause, such as the organism (methicillin-resistant or methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus), and predisposing risk factors, such as injection drug use.

cards.t: Who gets infective endocarditis: risk factors
q: what are the risk factors for endocarditis
what is the leading predisposing condition for endocarditis
who is most at risk of infective endocarditis
cards.x:
Endocarditis takes hold where the heart is already abnormal, or where something gives bacteria a way into the blood. The recognized risk factors:
- Heart conditions: congenital heart disease, rheumatic heart disease, degenerative valve disease, intracardiac devices and prosthetic valves.
- Ways in for bacteria: injection drug use, and poor dentition or dental infections.
- A weaker immune system: immunocompromised status and human immunodeficiency virus infection.

In high-income countries, degenerative valve disease (valves worn down over time) and intracardiac devices are now the leading predisposing conditions. Age matters: risk is increased among the elderly, and patients over 60 make up more than 50% of cases, though endocarditis can occur at any age. Men are affected more often than women. In people who inject drugs, Staphylococcus aureus causes more than 60% of all their endocarditis and 80–90% of cases where the tricuspid valve is infected.

cards.t: Prosthetic valve and device endocarditis: when the risk is highest
q: when is the risk of prosthetic valve endocarditis highest
how soon after a pacemaker can endocarditis happen
how much native valve endocarditis is health care-associated
cards.x:
Prosthetic valve infections make up 16–35% of endocarditis cases. The greatest risk is within the first year after the valve is replaced. After that the risk gradually declines until it is similar to the risk for a native valve.

Pacemaker or implantable defibrillator endocarditis can occur within weeks of implantation or of a generator change.

Hospital care matters for native valves too: about 25–35% of native valve endocarditis is health care-associated.

cards.t: How an endocarditis vegetation forms
q: what is a vegetation made of
how does a vegetation form in endocarditis
what are the steps of vegetation formation
cards.x:
A vegetation is the infected growth that infective endocarditis produces: a mass of platelets, fibrin (the protein mesh of a clot), micro-colonies of microorganisms and inflammatory cells. It results when microorganisms invade and colonize the endocardial structures and inflammation follows.

It builds in four steps:
- Normal endothelium (the healthy inner lining) resists pathogens.
- Bacteria adhere where there is a risk factor, such as a prosthetic valve, an implantable electronic device, congenital heart disease or intravenous drug use.
- An inflammatory response draws in platelets, monocytes and cytokines.
- Thrombosis (clotting) builds the vegetation.

Think of it as a clot built up around a colony of bacteria.

cards.t: Acute versus subacute infective endocarditis
q: what is the difference between acute and subacute endocarditis
how fast does acute endocarditis progress
what does subacute endocarditis look like
cards.x:
The split is about speed and how aggressive the organism is. Acute endocarditis is a hectically febrile illness from a virulent, invasive organism. Subacute endocarditis has an indolent, slow-burning course.
- Tempo: acute typically develops over 3–10 days, with rapid onset, high fevers and systemic toxicity. Subacute brings lower fevers, generalized malaise and weight loss over weeks or months.
- The heart: acute rapidly damages cardiac structures. Subacute is slow to cause structural damage, if it does at all.
- Spread: acute seeds sites outside the heart. Subacute rarely metastasizes.
- Untreated course: acute progresses to death within weeks. Subacute is gradually progressive unless a major embolic event or a ruptured mycotic (infected) aneurysm complicates it.

Quick way to hold it: acute is a very sick patient within days; subacute is a patient who has felt run down and lost weight for weeks.

cards.t: Which organisms cause acute versus subacute endocarditis
q: which bacteria cause acute endocarditis
which bacteria cause subacute endocarditis
is viridans strep acute or subacute
cards.x:
The organism sets the pace. A virulent organism such as Staphylococcus aureus or a beta-hemolytic streptococcus gives the abrupt, toxic, high-fever course of acute endocarditis.
- Acute: beta-hemolytic streptococci; Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-susceptible or methicillin-resistant); sometimes Staphylococcus lugdunensis, a coagulase-negative staphylococcus; enterococci.
- Subacute: viridans streptococci; enterococci; coagulase-negative staphylococci; and the HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) group.

Enterococci appear on both lists, so they don't settle the question by themselves. The cleanest pairing to remember is Staphylococcus aureus for acute and viridans streptococci for subacute.

cards.t: Symptoms of infective endocarditis
q: what are the symptoms of endocarditis
what is the most common symptom of endocarditis
why can endocarditis cause confusion
cards.x:
Fever is the most common symptom of infective endocarditis. After that come chills, sweats, myalgias (muscle aches), neurologic deficits, headache, anorexia (loss of appetite) and weight loss, malaise, and cough, which is linked to people who inject drugs.

The odd symptoms make sense once you picture what the infection sends around the body. Septic emboli, infected fragments carried in the blood, can reach the brain and produce neurologic deficits such as new confusion. So a heart infection can show up as a change in thinking.

cards.t: Where endocarditis spreads: complications organ by organ
q: what are the complications of endocarditis
what organs does endocarditis affect
can endocarditis cause a stroke
cards.x:
Endocarditis is a heart infection that shows up all over the body. Organ by organ:
- Brain: ischemic stroke, abscess, intracranial hemorrhage, meningitis and infective intracranial aneurysms.
- Eye: Roth spots. Skin: Janeway lesions and Osler nodes.
- Heart: congestive heart failure, valvular dysfunction, arrhythmias, myocardial abscesses and myocardial infarction.
- Kidney: acute kidney injury, glomerulonephritis and infarction.
- Embolic sites: spleen, lung, kidney, liver, and splinter hemorrhages. Musculoskeletal: myalgias, arthralgias (joint pain) and osteomyelitis (bone infection).

Other findings include fever, hepatosplenomegaly (an enlarged liver and spleen) and metastatic infection, meaning infection seeded at a distant site.

cards.t: Osler nodes versus Janeway lesions
q: what is the difference between Osler nodes and Janeway lesions
which is painful, Osler nodes or Janeway lesions
are Janeway lesions immunologic or embolic
cards.x:
Both are skin signs of endocarditis on the hands and feet, and one difference separates them: Osler nodes are painful, Janeway lesions are painless. The pain follows the mechanism.
- Osler nodes: painful red nodules on the pads of the fingers and toes. They may be microscopic abscesses, appear in crops and fade in 2–3 days. They are an immunologic phenomenon.
- Janeway lesions: painless (nontender), flat hemorrhagic macules, meaning flat, bloody spots, on the palms of the hands and soles of the feet. They are a vascular (embolic) phenomenon from septic emboli, and they are associated with acute infective endocarditis.

One hook: Osler, "ouch," on the finger pads; Janeway, painless and flat, on the palms and soles.

cards.t: Roth spots, splinter hemorrhages and petechiae
q: what are Roth spots
what do splinter hemorrhages look like
where do petechiae appear in endocarditis
cards.x:
These are the other peripheral signs of endocarditis, small bleeds you can spot on examination.
- Roth spots: white-centered hemorrhages in the retina, from vasculitis (inflammation) of the small retinal arteries. They count as an immunologic phenomenon.
- Splinter hemorrhages: thin dark lines under the fingernails and toenails, in the proximal portion of the nail plate. They are an embolic, and so vascular, phenomenon.
- Petechiae: minute, pinpoint hemorrhages that can be transient, found in the mouth (buccal mucosa, palate), on the conjunctiva and on the skin of the extremities. Conjunctival hemorrhages count as a vascular phenomenon.

To sort them: Roth spots sit with Osler nodes as immunologic signs; splinter hemorrhages, conjunctival hemorrhages and Janeway lesions are vascular.

cards.t: Endocarditis in people who inject drugs: the tricuspid valve and the lungs
q: which valve is affected in people who inject drugs
why do people who inject drugs get cough with endocarditis
what organism causes tricuspid endocarditis
cards.x:
In people who inject drugs, the valve to remember is the tricuspid valve, and Staphylococcus aureus causes 80–90% of the cases where it is infected.

The tricuspid valve sits on the right side of the heart, and the right side of the heart sends blood on to the lungs. That fits with the lung appearing among the embolic complications, with cough being the symptom linked to people who inject drugs, and with septic pulmonary infarcts (patches of lung tissue killed off by infected emboli) counting as a vascular phenomenon.

cards.t: Cardiac complications: new murmur, heart failure and perivalvular abscess
q: why does endocarditis cause a new murmur
what is a perivalvular abscess
why can endocarditis cause heart block
cards.x:
Inside the heart, the infection can do damage in these ways.
- A new murmur: the infection damages the valve or ruptures the chordae tendineae (the cords that hold the valve leaflets), so the valve leaks backward. That leak is regurgitation.
- Congestive heart failure: it follows from the valve no longer working properly (valvular dysfunction).
- Perivalvular abscess: the infection extends beyond the valve leaflets into the heart muscle. Where it goes next decides the problem. Into the epicardium (the heart's outer layer), it causes pericarditis. Into the upper ventricular septum, it interrupts the conduction system and produces a new conduction block.

So in a patient with endocarditis, a new conduction block can point to an abscess that has reached the septum.

cards.t: Endocarditis organisms by where they enter the body
k: early versus late prosthetic valve endocarditis organisms
q: what organism causes endocarditis after dental work
which organism causes endocarditis from a gut source
what causes early versus late prosthetic valve endocarditis
cards.x:
The organism is easiest to predict by asking where it got into the blood. Most infective endocarditis is bacterial. Fungal endocarditis is caused by Candida (and Aspergillus).

- Mouth (dental procedures, poor dentition): viridans streptococci.
- Skin (injection drug use, surgery, device pockets): staphylococci.
- Upper respiratory tract: the HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) group.
- Gastrointestinal tract: Streptococcus gallolyticus.
- Genitourinary tract: enterococci.

Prosthetic valves split by timing. Early infection is the skin staphylococci: coagulase-negative staphylococci (Staphylococcus epidermidis) and Staphylococcus aureus. Late infection is viridans streptococci.

cards.t: The HACEK organisms
q: what are the HACEK organisms
are HACEK organisms gram negative
where do HACEK organisms come from
cards.x:
HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) is a memory word for five kinds of bacteria that cause endocarditis: Haemophilus aphrophilus, Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans, Cardiobacterium hominis, Eikenella corrodens and Kingella species. Their source is the upper respiratory tract.

What sets them apart is the Gram stain. These organisms are gram-negative, specifically fastidious (hard to grow) gram-negative coccobacilli, while the other usual causes, staphylococci, streptococci and enterococci, are gram-positive. They are a small share of cases: about 3% of community-acquired native valve endocarditis.

cards.t: Which organism leads in each setting of endocarditis
q: which organism causes most health care-associated endocarditis
what is the most common organism in pacemaker endocarditis
what causes community-acquired native valve endocarditis
cards.x:
The leading organism in endocarditis shifts with the setting, although across all forms staphylococci are 30–70% of cases:
- Community-acquired native valve: streptococci about 40%, then Staphylococcus aureus about 28% and enterococci about 9%.
- Health care-associated native valve: Staphylococcus aureus about 52%, the largest share, then enterococci about 16%, streptococci about 13% and coagulase-negative staphylococci about 11%.
- Prosthetic valve: coagulase-negative staphylococci are the top listed cause under 2 months after surgery (about 33%) and at 2–12 months (about 35%); after 12 months streptococci are (about 31%, with Staphylococcus aureus about 18%).
- Implantable electronic device: coagulase-negative staphylococci about 41%, then Staphylococcus aureus about 36%.
- People who inject drugs: Staphylococcus aureus causes more than 60% of all their endocarditis.

Methicillin resistance is common among these Staphylococcus aureus strains, and vancomycin is in every empiric regimen.

cards.t: What else can look like endocarditis (differential diagnosis)
q: what is the differential diagnosis for endocarditis
what can mimic infective endocarditis
how is atrial myxoma different from endocarditis
cards.x:
Several conditions share endocarditis's fever, rash, aches or valve findings:
- Systemic lupus erythematosus: can present with non-infective (Libman-Sacks) endocarditis.
- Antiphospholipid syndrome: thromboemboli and heart valve disease.
- Vasculitis: petechiae-like spots from inflamed vessels.
- Polymyalgia rheumatica: muscle aches with raised inflammatory markers (erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein).
- Reactive arthritis (joint symptoms), Lyme disease (fever and, rarely, myocarditis), meningitis (fever and rash) and tuberculosis (fever, night sweats and weight loss).

Atrial myxoma is the tumor that mimics it: fever plus a new murmur, either a tumor plop or a mid-diastolic rumble. Because it is a cardiac tumor and not an infection, blood cultures stay negative.

cards.t: Modified Duke criteria: the two major criteria
q: what are the major Duke criteria
what counts as a positive blood culture in the Duke criteria
does a change in an old murmur count as a major criterion
cards.x:
There are only two major criteria, one from the blood and one from the heart.

Positive blood culture: a typical organism from two separate blood cultures. The typical organisms are viridans streptococci, Streptococcus gallolyticus, HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organisms, Staphylococcus aureus, or community-acquired enterococci without a primary focus. A persistently positive blood culture also counts: positive cultures drawn more than 12 hours apart, or all of 3 (or a majority of 4 or more) separate cultures with the first and last drawn at least 1 hour apart.

Evidence of endocardial involvement: a positive echocardiogram showing an oscillating mass inside the heart on a valve, its supporting structures or implanted material; an abscess; or new partial dehiscence (separation) of a prosthetic valve. New valvular regurgitation also counts, but an increase or change in a murmur that was already there is not sufficient.

Transesophageal echocardiography, which is highly sensitive and specific, is required for optimal assessment of possible prosthetic valve endocarditis or complicated endocarditis.

cards.t: Modified Duke criteria: the minor criteria
q: what are the minor Duke criteria
which positive blood cultures don't count in the Duke criteria
which heart conditions count as a predisposition
cards.x:
The minor criteria are the supporting clues, and there are five of them:
- Predisposition: a predisposing heart condition or injection drug use. The heart conditions are valve disease with stenosis or regurgitation, a prosthetic valve, congenital heart disease (except an isolated atrial septal defect, a repaired ventricular septal defect or a closed patent ductus), prior endocarditis, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
- Fever: 38.0 °C (100.4 °F) or more.
- Vascular phenomena, such as major arterial emboli and Janeway lesions.
- Immunologic phenomena, such as Osler nodes and Roth spots.
- Microbiologic evidence: a positive blood culture that does not meet the major criterion, or serologic (blood test) evidence of active infection with a typical organism.

Some single positive cultures don't count: coagulase-negative staphylococci and diphtheroids, because they are common culture contaminants, and organisms that rarely cause endocarditis, such as gram-negative bacilli.

cards.t: Vascular versus immunologic phenomena in the Duke criteria
q: which endocarditis signs are vascular and which are immunologic
what counts as an immunologic phenomenon in the Duke criteria
is a Janeway lesion a vascular or immunologic phenomenon
cards.x:
Two of the minor criteria sort the body-wide signs of endocarditis into two groups, and each group counts as one minor criterion.
- Vascular phenomena: major arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial hemorrhage, conjunctival hemorrhages and Janeway lesions.
- Immunologic phenomena: glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots and rheumatoid factor.

The pair that is easy to mix up is the two hand-and-foot signs: Janeway lesions belong to the vascular group, Osler nodes to the immunologic group. Roth spots, in the eye, are also immunologic.

cards.t: Modified Duke criteria: definite versus possible endocarditis
k: how to use the Duke criteria
q: how many Duke criteria do you need for definite endocarditis
what makes endocarditis possible rather than definite
do you need minor criteria if you have two major criteria
cards.x:
The modified Duke criteria label a case definite or possible by counting major and minor criteria.
- Definite: two major criteria, or one major and three minor, or five minor. Two major criteria alone are enough; no minor criteria are needed.
- Possible: one major and one minor, or three minor.

Here's how it plays out. A typical organism in separate blood cultures plus a vegetation or an oscillating mass on echocardiogram is two major criteria, so the case is definite. Now take a patient with a predisposing heart condition, a fever and painful finger-pad nodules: three minor criteria, so endocarditis is possible. The next step is drawing blood cultures, three sets from separate sites, before any antibiotic. If they grow a typical organism, that adds a major criterion, and one major plus three minor makes it definite.

cards.t: Blood cultures and basic labs in suspected endocarditis
q: how many blood cultures for endocarditis
how fast should cultures be drawn in acute endocarditis
what labs are abnormal in endocarditis
cards.x:
Blood cultures come first, and they always come before antibiotics. Draw three sets from separate sites, within 24 hours. If the presentation suggests acute endocarditis, draw two cultures within the first 1–2 hours, then start empiric antibiotics (treatment aimed at the likely organisms before the results are back).

Other labs fill in the picture:
- Complete blood count with differential: leukocytosis (a high white cell count) and anemia of chronic disease with a normal mean corpuscular volume, so a normocytic anemia (normal-sized red cells).
- Urinalysis: hematuria, proteinuria and pyuria (blood, protein and white cells in the urine), reflecting kidney involvement such as glomerulonephritis or emboli.

cards.t: Transesophageal echocardiogram in endocarditis
q: why is a transesophageal echo used for endocarditis
does a normal TEE rule out endocarditis
what does an echocardiogram show in endocarditis
cards.x:
A transesophageal echocardiogram is an ultrasound of the heart taken from a probe in the esophagus, which sits right behind the heart. It is highly sensitive and specific for endocarditis: it detects vegetations on the valve leaflets and defines the extent of the disease.

The catch: a normal transesophageal echocardiogram does not necessarily rule out endocarditis. A clean result does not settle the question on its own.

cards.t: How endocarditis is treated: bactericidal, prolonged, intravenous
q: how long are antibiotics given for endocarditis
when does the antibiotic clock start in endocarditis
why must endocarditis antibiotics be bactericidal
does endocarditis need hospital admission
cards.x:
Every bacterium in the vegetation must be killed, so therapy must be bactericidal (it kills bacteria rather than just stopping their growth) and prolonged. Treatment typically runs 4–6 weeks, counted from the first negative blood culture: not from admission, the first dose, the first positive culture or the end of fever.

The rest of the plan:
- Antibiotics are given parenterally, meaning intravenously.
- The patient is admitted to the hospital, with close monitoring of labs, kidney function and cardiovascular status by a multidisciplinary team.
- Empiric therapy starts only after blood cultures have been drawn.
- The team considers whether surgery is indicated: valve replacement, vegetectomy (removing the vegetation) or valve repair.

cards.t: Empiric antibiotics for endocarditis
q: what is the empiric treatment for endocarditis
what empiric antibiotics for a prosthetic valve less than a year old
why is vancomycin in empiric endocarditis therapy
cards.x:
Empiric therapy, started after blood cultures are drawn but before the organism is known, covers the three big groups: staphylococci, streptococci and enterococci. The choice depends on the valve:
- Native valve endocarditis, a subacute presentation, or a prosthetic valve in place more than 1 year: vancomycin plus ceftriaxone.
- A prosthetic valve in place 1 year or less: vancomycin plus gentamicin plus cefepime.

Vancomycin is in both. Methicillin resistance is common among Staphylococcus aureus strains in endocarditis, and vancomycin is the standard drug for methicillin-resistant strains. Antibiotics are planned with an infectious disease consult.

cards.t: Treating Staphylococcus aureus endocarditis: susceptible versus resistant
q: what is the treatment for MRSA endocarditis
what is the treatment for MSSA endocarditis
how is staph aureus prosthetic valve endocarditis treated
cards.x:
The one difference to remember: methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus gets nafcillin or oxacillin, while methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus gets vancomycin.
- Susceptible strain, native valve: nafcillin or oxacillin, or cefazolin. Vancomycin is only the alternative when these beta-lactams can't be used.
- Resistant strain, native valve: vancomycin or daptomycin.
- Prosthetic valve: rifampin and gentamicin are added to the antistaphylococcal drug, so vancomycin plus rifampin plus gentamicin. If cultures show a susceptible strain, nafcillin or oxacillin can replace the vancomycin.

So vancomycin is the standard drug for resistant strains and only a backup for susceptible ones.

cards.t: Treating viridans streptococcal, enterococcal and HACEK endocarditis
q: how is viridans strep endocarditis treated
when can a 2-week regimen be used for endocarditis
how is enterococcal endocarditis treated
what treats HACEK endocarditis
cards.x:
Once cultures name the organism, therapy is directed at it.
- Viridans streptococci: penicillin G or ceftriaxone, with or without gentamicin; or vancomycin.
