- Enterococci: ampicillin (or penicillin G) plus gentamicin; ampicillin plus ceftriaxone; or vancomycin plus gentamicin.
- HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organisms: ceftriaxone, or ampicillin-sulbactam.

Viridans streptococci can sometimes get a short 2-week regimen, penicillin G or ceftriaxone plus gentamicin, but only for uncomplicated endocarditis with a rapid response to therapy and no chronic kidney disease. Gentamicin is nephrotoxic (it damages the kidneys), which is why chronic kidney disease rules it out, and an abscess makes the case complicated.

cards.t: When endocarditis needs surgery
q: what is the most common indication for surgery in endocarditis
when does endocarditis need surgery
why does fungal endocarditis need surgery
cards.x:
Heart failure caused by a failing valve is the most common reason to operate. The indications:
- Heart failure due to valvular dysfunction, the most common.
- Infection not resolving with appropriate antibiotic therapy, meaning cultures stay positive on a regimen that matches the organism.
- Abscess.
- Fungal infection, because it is difficult to cure with medication alone.

The common thread is that antibiotics alone are not enough: the valve is failing, the infection is not clearing, or the organism is hard to cure with drugs. Those patients are referred to cardiothoracic surgery.

cards.t: Anticoagulation in endocarditis
q: should you anticoagulate a patient with endocarditis
does anticoagulation prevent septic emboli
what about anticoagulation with a prosthetic valve and endocarditis
cards.x:
Anticoagulation is not beneficial in patients with native valve endocarditis. It can seem logical to thin the blood when pieces of infection are breaking off as emboli, but anticoagulation does not prevent septic emboli and does not dissolve vegetations, so it should not be started for that reason.

With a prosthetic valve, anticoagulation is controversial. Whether a patient needs anticoagulation is part of the cardiothoracic surgery evaluation.

cards.t: Who to involve: referrals and disposition in endocarditis
q: which consults does an endocarditis patient need
why consult addiction medicine for endocarditis
where does an endocarditis patient go after the hospital
cards.x:
Endocarditis is managed by a team, and each member has a defined job.
- Infectious disease: antibiotic therapy and outpatient monitoring until the patient's disposition is settled.
- Cardiothoracic surgery: evaluation for surgery and for anticoagulation needs.
- Addiction medicine: harm reduction for people who inject drugs.
- The multidisciplinary team: disposition, meaning where the patient goes next. That may be rehabilitation, for example a deconditioned older patient finishing intravenous antibiotics, or palliative care.

cards.t: Who needs endocarditis prophylaxis: the high-risk heart conditions
q: who needs antibiotic prophylaxis for endocarditis
does a coronary stent need endocarditis prophylaxis
does a pacemaker need endocarditis prophylaxis
cards.x:
Prophylaxis is reserved for high-risk cardiac conditions:
- Prosthetic heart valves, including transcatheter-implanted prostheses and homografts, and prosthetic material used for valve repair (annuloplasty rings, chords, clips).
- Previous infective endocarditis.
- Unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease (including palliative shunts and conduits), or repaired congenital heart disease with residual shunts or valve regurgitation at or next to a prosthetic patch or device.
- The first 6 months after congenital heart disease repair with prosthetic material or a device.
- A cardiac transplant with valve regurgitation from a structurally abnormal valve.

Conditions not on the list do not call for prophylaxis, including coronary artery stents, prior coronary bypass grafting, controlled hypertension, an innocent murmur, a history of rheumatic fever without a high-risk condition, and a pacemaker without valve disease.

cards.t: Which procedures need endocarditis prophylaxis
q: which dental procedures need endocarditis prophylaxis
does a colonoscopy need endocarditis prophylaxis
do braces adjustments need prophylaxis
cards.x:
For a high-risk patient, prophylaxis is given for these procedures:
- Dental procedures that manipulate the gum tissue or the periapical region (around the root tips) of the teeth, or perforate the lining of the mouth: dental cleaning, root canals, extractions, a gum biopsy.
- Invasive respiratory tract procedures that cut or biopsy the respiratory lining, such as tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy.

Not needed: bronchoscopy (unless it involves cutting the lining, such as a biopsy), routine anesthetic injections through noninfected tissue, dental X-rays, placing removable prosthodontic (denture-type) or orthodontic appliances, adjusting braces or placing brackets, and bleeding from trauma to the lips or mouth. Gastrointestinal and genitourinary procedures such as cystoscopy, upper endoscopy and colonoscopy, and transesophageal echocardiography, don't need it either, in the absence of active infection.

cards.t: Endocarditis prophylaxis: which drug and when
q: what antibiotic is used for endocarditis prophylaxis
when is the prophylaxis dose given
why amoxicillin for dental prophylaxis
what if the patient can't take oral medication
cards.x:
The standard is a single dose of oral amoxicillin, given 30–60 minutes before the procedure, so the drug is already circulating when the transient bacteremia happens. It is one dose: never a course of days, never a dose afterward. Amoxicillin is chosen because it covers the likely organism after dental work, viridans streptococci.

By situation:
- No penicillin allergy, can take oral medication: oral amoxicillin.
- No penicillin allergy, can't take oral medication: ampicillin by intramuscular or intravenous injection (or cefazolin or ceftriaxone).
- Penicillin allergy, can take oral medication: azithromycin or clarithromycin; doxycycline; or cephalexin.
- Penicillin allergy, can't take oral medication: cefazolin or ceftriaxone by intramuscular or intravenous injection.

In the allergy rows, the cephalosporins are not used after anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria (hives).

cards.t: Penicillin allergy and prophylaxis: cephalosporins, and why not clindamycin
q: why is clindamycin no longer used for endocarditis prophylaxis
can a penicillin-allergic patient get cephalexin
what prophylaxis after anaphylaxis to penicillin
cards.x:
Clindamycin is no longer recommended for endocarditis prophylaxis because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection. A patient carrying an old card that lists clindamycin needs an alternative such as azithromycin.

With penicillin allergy, the question is what the reaction was:
- Anaphylaxis, angioedema (swelling) or urticaria (hives) to penicillin or ampicillin: no cephalosporins (cephalexin, cefazolin, ceftriaxone). Azithromycin, clarithromycin and doxycycline remain appropriate even after anaphylaxis.
- A mild delayed rash without hives, swelling or anaphylaxis: cephalosporins are not excluded.

Amoxicillin and ampicillin are themselves penicillins, so they are avoided in penicillin allergy. Vancomycin is not part of the adult prophylaxis table.

cards.t: Prognosis of endocarditis by organism
q: which organism has the worst prognosis in endocarditis
what is the prognosis of viridans strep endocarditis
what is the most likely complication of fungal endocarditis
cards.x:
How endocarditis goes depends on the organism.
- Staphylococcus aureus: the most lethal organism. Mortality is highest in prosthetic valve endocarditis (about 50%), about 30% in people who do not inject drugs, and lowest in people who inject drugs (about 5%).
- Viridans streptococci: a relatively good prognosis if antibiotic treatment is started before complications occur.
- Enterococci: difficult to treat because of antibiotic resistance, with major complications and the need for valve replacement in about 30–40%.
- Fungi: the most likely complication is embolism, with occlusion of larger peripheral arteries.

Speed matters too: untreated acute endocarditis can be fatal within weeks.

cards.t: Infective endocarditis in children: how it differs from adults
q: what is the main risk factor for endocarditis in children
how is pediatric endocarditis different from adult endocarditis
how common is endocarditis in children
cards.x:
In children, endocarditis is driven mainly by congenital heart disease and indwelling central venous catheters, rather than degenerative valve disease. Congenital heart disease is the dominant substrate in developed countries (about 53–68% of pediatric cases), having replaced rheumatic heart disease, though up to about 46% of affected children have no underlying cardiac lesion. It is low incidence but high mortality: about 0.05–0.12 per 1000 admissions, with mortality of 5–16%.

Compared with adults, pediatric and adolescent endocarditis is:
- More often right-sided.
- Higher in septic embolism (up to about 40%).
- Less likely to cause heart failure.
- Considerably less common to show the classic peripheral signs (Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, Roth spots, splinter hemorrhages, splenomegaly).

In a child with cyanotic congenital heart disease and a systemic-to-pulmonary shunt, the murmur may not change; falling oxygen saturation can be the signal of shunt infection instead.

cards.t: Endocarditis in infants: organisms and the sepsis-like picture
q: what causes endocarditis in infants
how does endocarditis present in a newborn
what raises the risk of fungal endocarditis in infants
cards.x:
In infants (under 1 year), endocarditis often looks like sepsis. The illness is nonspecific and often indistinguishable from sepsis or heart failure: feeding difficulty, respiratory distress, tachycardia (a fast heart rate), hypotension, and a new or changing murmur. Septic emboli are common, producing osteomyelitis, meningitis or pneumonia, and neurologic signs such as seizures, hemiparesis (weakness of one side) and apnea (pauses in breathing) are frequent.

The organisms are Staphylococcus aureus, coagulase-negative staphylococci and Candida; less often group B streptococci, enteric gram-negative rods and Streptococcus pneumoniae. Fungal disease is tied to central venous catheters, hyperalimentation (intravenous feeding) and neonatal intensive care or prematurity.

cards.t: Endocarditis in older children and adolescents
q: what organism causes endocarditis in children with congenital heart disease
how does endocarditis present in older children
what causes endocarditis in adolescents
cards.x:
In children over 1 year with congenital heart disease, viridans group streptococci (Streptococcus sanguis, mitis and mutans) are the most common cause, Staphylococcus aureus comes next, and enterococci are less common than in adults. The course is usually indolent: a prolonged low-grade fever with fatigue, joint and muscle aches, weight loss, rigors (shaking chills) and sweating. A fulminant presentation with high spiking fevers instead suggests Streptococcus pneumoniae or Staphylococcus aureus.

Adolescents increasingly resemble adults: viridans group streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus, including Staphylococcus aureus disease linked to injection drug use. At any age, prosthetic material or surgery within 60 days points to Staphylococcus aureus and coagulase-negative staphylococci, with infection of the device, graft or valve.

cards.t: Treating and preventing endocarditis in children
q: how is endocarditis treated in children
which children need endocarditis prophylaxis
does a repaired ventricular septal defect need prophylaxis
cards.x:
Treatment in children is essentially the same as in adults, with the same empiric therapy: antibiotics that are prolonged, bactericidal, parenteral (intravenous, not intramuscular), directed at the organism and weight-based, with infectious disease and cardiology or cardiothoracic surgery input.

Prophylaxis is reserved for high-risk conditions: a prosthetic valve or prosthetic material (transcatheter prostheses, homografts); prior endocarditis; unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease (palliative shunts and conduits); repaired congenital heart disease with residual defects next to prosthetic material; a cardiac transplant with valvulopathy (valve disease); and the first 6 months after repair with prosthetic material or a device. A repair with no residual defect is high risk only in that first 6 months, so a ventricular septal defect closed with a prosthetic patch 4 months earlier still qualifies.

It is given for dental procedures with gum or periapical manipulation or perforation of the mouth lining, invasive respiratory procedures with mucosal incision (tonsillectomy, adenoidectomy), or procedures on infected skin or musculoskeletal tissue.
